reviews.advice: You have outdated management filled with "yes men/women". Management will complain behind closed doors but press on those below them regardless of performance (there's no incentive to excel if you will be treated like the low performers anyway). You need young, educated leaders who are not afraid to speak up and look out for their team as needed. Current management is an older generation, often with no more than a high school diploma, afraid to lose their lifelong job. So they don't speak up during meetings even when they clearly have questions, suggestions, or disagreements. The company has the tools needed to make this a better place, it truly does. However, management doesn't know how to use or implement those tools in the workforce.
reviews.cons:
It's a pretty easy interview. It seems like they are probing for who will stick through the abuse. Nothing technical in the interview but more about how you would react in certain situations and how badly you want the job. That said, the job doesn't have to be as stressful as they make it, but uneducated/outdated management that has done nothing else in their career may be stuck in old, outdated ways to treat employees. I did very well in the position, but I am glad that another company saw my true potential and gave me a chance.

Lastly, you will have to do something outrageous to get fired. If you are a good employee don't expect any recognition that holds any value. Nothing beyond a "thank you" on a daily meeting is to be expected. Most management doesn't know how to work the company award system anyway.
reviews.pros: Good teammates for the most part.

reviews.advice: Stop micromanaging the FCM's and let them run the business according to their own FC clientele. Not everything that works at one center will work across every FC. There has to be some flexibility and stop promoting unqualified individuals to lead teams when they themselves prove to be unfit for leadership. It's really a "protect our own" environment and has really turned into a "gotcha" management style within the FC's.
reviews.cons: Micromanagement from senior leaders. Unrealistic expectations that stress not only the FCM out but the team as well because expectations change almost weekly and the "sales" are just "behaviors" now and former "sales" people are trying to manage "behaviors" when they themselves did not possess these "behaviors".
reviews.pros: Pay. Pay is good no doubt. Benefits are good as well but that's expected given the size of the company.

reviews.advice: Be realistic in your expectations! Behind closed doors, managers will complain to each other about policies and procedures they disagree with or they feel are unrealistic themselves - but then they’ll push those same new policies, procedures, and best practices down the throats of their own team without the slightest hesitation.
reviews.cons: Brand-Brand-Brand. It’s shoved down your throat from Day 1. Which is simply another way of saying - be sure to well liked by everyone, play politics or you’ll never get promoted beyond your entry level position, and most of all - be sure to brown nose the managers, especially your DM!
reviews.pros: Great starting hourly pay, solid annual raises between 3-8%, at the end of the day - the work really isnt all that difficult. However, the work can become quite repetitive, mundane, and for certain personality types - you’ll likely become bored very quickly in your role!
reviews.summary: No one cares how proficient you are in your role, but more so about how well liked you are by management!

reviews.advice: Bank of America needs to do a thorough assessment and employee survey about management. While much has been made about how the hybrid in office/remote work schedule has made it easier for some team members to hide/not do their part, the same observations about their direct managers has not been mentioned nearly enough. Employee development and cross training is at an all time low, managers who were not providing development opportunities or even sufficient training for their team members appear to have gotten even worse. At this critical juncture in time,  now that companies are establishing their formal and more permanent remote work policies, its is beyond vital to have the management team make employee development and training a key area of focus and priority going forward.

- No longer a great place for career development, neither by way of strong training or mentorship. Primary example(s), i.e. NOT isolated incidents: Manager blocks their own team member from a promotion/raise offered by another departments despite their not being able to offer a similar opportunity with their team. This happened a shockingly high number of times, enough times to make it seem less the action of a bad manager and more about poor culture company wide
- Compensation falls far below main rivals
- Culture of fear permeates throughout each organization, promoted by management’s lack of presence and endorsement of their team members
- the culture of favoritism, a longstanding problem well before the pandemic, has seemingly become more pervasive in the aftermath of the return to office. What previously may have only given the appearance of different rules for different employees has become embarrassingly transparent that some rules do not apply to some employees

Really vague instruction from the people who are supposed to be qualified trainers that talk like it is supposed to be easy. reviews.advice:
Customers spend $15 to $100K on cabinets and countertops.  

Providing accurate designs/orders is key to customer satisfaction, referrals, Pro retention, and the long-term building of your business.  

Providing a work location away from trash compactors, receiving bays, and non-stop, non-cabinetry customers would increase order accuracy and greatly shorten design time.

The notion that a kitchen can be designed in two, 2-hour meetings is false.  A complex kitchen can take 40+ hours to design and another 4-10 hours of order follow-through.

Standard working days would improve work-life balance and we could remember the day of the week.

Finally, give designers two monitors; they shouldn't have to share a single monitor with customers; similarly, customers shouldn't be forced to sit immediately next to the specialist during the design process.
reviews.cons:
The noise and interruptions are not conducive to the concentration and attention to detail required for this position. There is no quiet space provided to work. Design software is only loaded on the computers in the department. Designers are 'basically' chained to their chairs and serve as the 'store information desk' for every customer walking by.

Due to flash sales, the workload is often heavier than what can reasonably be accomplished in 40 hours and OT is rarely an option. As a result, skipped lunches and disappointed customers are the norm. 

No one else in the store is trained in this position and store/upper management does not understand what the job entails.
reviews.pros: The company stands behind its sales/customers. Coworkers are smart, considerate, and helpful. The cabinetry specialist position is challenging and interesting. 401K and ESPP plans are great. I learned a lot during my time in this position.

reviews.cons:
The training process could use some improvement. For your first couple of shifts, you're just sitting in the training room watching videos and answering questions. However, while transitioning to the floor of your assigned department, it often feels like the information from the training doesn't stick, leaving you feeling unprepared when faced with real customer interactions.

Additionally, staffing shortages in many departments mean that you might be asked to cover areas you're not familiar with. This becomes particularly demanding when a customer asks for assistance with a specific product or service, but you don't have the tools to help them or call for support. So you end up just walking around the store looking for someone to help, only to find that either no one is available or the other staff members are already stretched thin, assisting multiple other customers simultaneously.

reviews.advice:

Most common responses "well, we can't change that on this level" and "we'll look into it" followed by never hearing from it again. The in house tool for approving programs and ideals is even worse, cause you don't even get that. 

So suggestion to management? Why bother, not like anyone will listen anyway.
reviews.cons:
"We don't approve working when not clocked in, it's against policy" followed shortly by "we suggest you get here 15-30 minutes early to get your computer on, programs running, and log into the phone system before clocking in"

Pretty much tells you all the info you need about how contradictory many policies and suggestions are... Such as don't hang up on a customer (even when they're being abusive), but you still somehow don't have to take abuse from the customer. Then any call that you do wind up forwarding to a supervisor is met with a lecture on ho2 you need to work harder to descalate the situation even though it only happens once every couple months... 

Hoping they changed a lot since I worked there, but I doubt it. Glad I left when I did before it drove me insane, I still get moody when someone says the words "metrics" in reference to any data point.

You get a real "worker bee" vibe here, it's a step above feeling like a cog, but not enough to make you feel like your opinions matter in any way.

We are human, they cannot be avoided completely. There’s a weight on those errors with three classes. Class 1 is when it involves the member to be affected by the mistake. Now the next are Class 2 and 3. These are very minor and don’t really cause a delay in treatment. You are only allowed 7 in a rolling calendar year. These are mistakes where there is a # in a ste or apt number. They don’t want you to use the #. So, again, these are mistakes that really don’t need to be addressed as a quality issue. Get 7 of those and you will be on a program where you have to be clear of all mistakes in. 6 month period. You make any mistake, you are terminated. Additionally, if you are excellent with members for several years, and make one mistake because you react poorly to a member one time, you not only CAN be terminated, you WILL be terminated. It’s agreed we need to put your best foot forward, but we all have our bad days. 1 member over a 3-year span of being Exceptional with every interaction, exceeding expectations across the board. None of that means anything to management.

reviews.advice:
- Less talking, more doing.
- Collaborate with other leaders. It is not the responsibility of the Teams doing the work. 
- Find fulfilling hobbies outside of work and stop taking pride in making everyone so miserable.
- Get rid of Mike Hutchins.
- Remote work is not the enemy. The old white dude mentality of people having to be sitting in a chair because you said so is out of touch and you will continue to lose top talent in droves to companies with remote options.
reviews.cons:
- The political games that are being played among senior leadership have over shadowed the mission and values of the company. 
- We have teams that are no longer directly reporting to the CISO, yet still have "a dotted line" in which they are accountable and have to meet with the CISO who disagrees with what the leadership approach of their organization has decided. Instead of senior leadership doing their job and sitting in a room for 30 minutes to hash it out, it is the Tech teams executing the work who are constantly punished.
- Regularly occurring meetings are scheduled during lunch time and employees are expected to attend.
- After hours (5-8 PM) issue management meetings have become the norm and you are expected to attend. No, you are not compensated in any way for your time after hours.
- Instead of acknowledging the constant feedback that is given in real time (during All Hands, Town Halls, etc.) by employees who would like more flexible hybrid/remote options comparable to Fannie Mae, leadership has taken a sneaky, backdoor approach to rolling back remote work to avoid headlines and having to pay folks severance packages. They are re-classifying previous "remote" job families, and have updated documentation to include that even if you live 50+ miles for the office, that is not a reasonable justification for remote status. Translation: they are forcing folks to resign so they will not have to pay severance.
- Newly instituted arbitrary rules in the name of "cyber security" have been implemented so Tech performers with high privilege roles and permissions are not allowed to use them off-site. Yet another way to oust remote employees.
- Reclassifying job families so existing remote employees cannot be promoted (i.e. to Manager) without committing to a hybrid work schedule.
- There has been record high turnover in Q1 2024 across all levels of leadership and employees. It has not been addressed by leadership, no open roles have been posted.
- Little to no room for growth or mobility. They do not grow their existing workforce, they would rather bring in an outside hire.

reviews.advice:
Bring in seasoned merchandisers to help design routes.

Try to balance out the extra stores among the staff rather than relying on the same 10-20 merchandisers to pick up the slack everywhere. 

Trainees aren't "help". No extra stores for trainers with trainees unless they finish they're route early and specifically ask for more work.

Talk to merchandisers like they know what their doing; if a problem arises ask the merch about it and don't manipulate or tsk-tsk them about it. If something is an ongoing problem then reprimand, no need to create an anxious work environment.
reviews.cons:
At worst, way more work than any one human being can handle, be ready for 14-16 hour days and perhaps having to come in on your days off if you're low on the seniority list.

The product line has become so vast that if you are a high quality, thorough merchandiser a heavy delivery day at a store can easily turn into 7-10 hours just in that one store (expect to do 2-4 stores a day, plus perhaps having to pick up someone else's store depending on how short we are on people).

Managers are for the most part okay (they need to get every store in the region covered so I'm not totally unsympathetic to their plight) but can get manipulative and try to coax (or flat out demand) you into doing extra stores on days when there's no way you could handle such requests.

You need to be selective in which areas you want to work as some sales reps are A LOT better than others. They need to make a living too/are being pressured to sell, sell, sell but if you get someone pushing a lot of excess product into stores that can't move it out you'll be maneuvering product around the back room all day and catching an earful from the grocery manager about it.

Some stores don't allow pallets on the floor after certain hours which makes it near-impossible to do the job efficiently when you have other stores to get to or if the no-pallets store is not the first stop.

Avoid merchandising Hy-Vee's at all costs. Cramped backrooms, 1-3 day sales where they get bombarded with product, no employees ever want to drop your pallets from the racking for you (or try to make you use the forklift to do it, which we aren't to do for insurance reasons, too many accidents). 

Poor route designs where you either have too little to do in your own stores and end up driving all across the Twin Cities covering extra stores, or too heavy of a route with multiple deliveries on the same day trying to navigate cramped back rooms.

Once you get a few years seniority you can probably get a route with decent days (Sun-Wed or Wed-Sat, you usually need around 5 years in to get a Mon-Thurs or Tue-Fri start and if you get one earlier than 5 years get ready to be forced in), but that's almost worse than working opposite a seasoned vet as the merch on your other side will likely be completely terrible, unable to organize, product in the wrong location, displays built wrong or not at all. All new merchandisers get 3 weeks of training but if you're the merch who's training them it's often an excuse to throw extra stores at you (because you now have "help").
reviews.pros:

Very occasional chance to work with other merchandisers who you can commiserate with.

It's a union job so even if you feel like a number there's someone there to back you up and make sure you're taken care of.

reviews.advice:
1. Revise Organizational Structure: Address the issues in the current organizational structure to enhance efficiency and clarity.

2. Process Improvement: Invest in refining and developing processes to streamline operations and reduce challenges for employees.

3. Foster Open Communication: Create a culture that encourages open communication without fear of repercussions. This will contribute to a healthier work environment.

4. Employee Development Programs: Implement programs to develop employees' skills and provide opportunities for career growth.

5. Regular Feedback Mechanism: Establish a systematic and regular feedback mechanism to understand employee concerns and address them promptly.

6. Active Listening to Employees: Prioritize listening to employees who are on the front lines, as they have valuable insights into day-to-day operations. Understand their perspectives on processes, not just the final outcomes, to make informed improvements that resonate with the workforce.

7. Promote Diversity and Inclusion: Specifically, foster an environment that values and respects black women within the workforce. Actively work towards diversity and inclusion initiatives to ensure that every employee, especially black women, feels heard, valued, and supported in their professional journey.

reviews.advice:
I was debating whether I approve of the CEO or not. 

On the one hand, he occasionally sends these excellent emails about business philosophy and avoiding siloing, wasteful meetings, and that managers are there to support their employees, not the other way around. 10/10 on that! When he leads an all-hands meeting, he usually has interesting things to say, especially if you can get him free-form thinking out loud during a Q&A session.

On the other hand, he is a relentless micro-manager and singlehandedly derails production, reduces product quality, makes hundreds of people have to work much harder, and causes massive waste because he wants to see every little detail and change those details at literally the last minute. It’s grossly inefficient and is ruining the company bit by bit. 

My advice to management: The company would work much better if Elon was only an idea man, locked up safely in a room somewhere, with his hands completely off of operations.
reviews.cons:
Rare to be recognized, let alone thanked, for going above and beyond to accomplish something out of the ordinary. Once you've "done the impossible", it's just assumed that you can and will do it again and again from now on. 

Literally hundreds of people in one room, desks on top of each other, as many as possible in every little space. Companies claim that they’re being “modern” and “progressive” by not having offices and cubicles, but they’re just being cheap. Look at pictures of offices from the 1950’s. You’ll see the same hundreds of desks in a room.

Yearly raises are typically less than the cost of living

Work/life balance is mediocre at best

Smallish yearly bonuses in the form of golden handcuffs. RSUs that vest over 4 years, so you’ll wait a long time to benefit from them

Those who were hired before mid-2013 made a lot of money off stock options, but many of those people are leaving now that all of their options are used up. 

Revolving door. It’s hard to last more than a couple of years here. 

It’s always seemingly a few steps away from massive failure

Very few processes in place, so work is done extremely inefficiently

Very common to compose an email and see “This is no longer a valid Tesla address”

The entire Service organization shares one budget. I am scrimping to save $50 on software while a barely-related manager wastes literally tens of thousands of dollars a week on cool toys, and it all comes from the same place.

Everything’s urgent, and people try to name-drop that Elon’s watching this very project so I need to stop everything for them. Luckily those of us who have been around for a while see right through that charade.

Technically, no 401(k) match, though if you’re careful with the health benefits you choose, you can end up with some leftover that can be diverted into the 401(k).

Middle managers are very hit-and-miss. Many were promoted because a manager was needed and they were the only one who knew anything about the department. Much room for improvement here.

Minimal leadership training. No real employee development opportunities. The results are just as bad as you’d expect.

Massive inter-departmental struggles. Most of my problems can be traced to one power-hungry manager of a sister department. It only takes one person to ruin the work lives of many people. 

There are more meetings than I expected from this kind of company. Elon sent a great email about how wasteful meetings are, but people have fallen into old bad habits.

Completely ineffective HR department

Every department is grossly understaffed, just barely above the point of collapse. Nearly everyone has to work harder than they would if they were doing the same job at another company.

Anything that they can do in house, they’ll do, rather than outsourcing to a supplier. There are people who spend their whole careers deciding “make vs. buy”… no need for them here, it seems. This is corporate arrogance, and it reduces quality, wastes human resources, and slows time to market in many cases. A positive side effect is that more products are made here in California than would be if they were outsourced.

Inadequate parking

Note to hiring managers at other companies: Watch out if someone from Tesla has “Project Manager” on their title. Many of these people are just general office workers with no skills beyond harassing people via email.
reviews.pros:
Completely casual dress code

Flexibility to work from home when needed

Always interesting to work at the factory

If you look at the SEC filings, you can see that the top people are basically compensated the same as the other employees, which is a pleasant surprise.

Many “beautiful people” here (male and female). Lots of eye candy.

A lot of people complain about the pay, but they paid me more than my last company, where I had the same title

LGBT friendly

The product is cool, and really fun to drive

If you’re in the right department, you might be able to drive a Tesla somewhat regularly. If not, there is an ongoing contest where you can be randomly selected to take one home for a couple of nights

The company is still growing

There is room to move geographically within Service, since Tesla owns the Service Centers

Lots of “car guy” coworkers to keep conversations interesting

Benefits actually got better and cheaper every year from 2012-2015, and stayed similar after that. I guess this was due to the company growing and getting better group rates. Regardless, not many people can say that.

You’ll frequently come to work that day expecting to work on a certain project and end up on something totally different. This can be good and bad.

Starting hours are typically flexible, which is a really nice perk. Nobody is making sure you’re in your seat at a certain time.

Most employees are surprisingly responsive and friendly.

Very heavy email-based communication, and it mostly works quite well.

You get good at doing the best you can with the resources you have, rather than doing the best possible job. This isn’t necessarily a complaint, since it’s a valuable skill to have, but you should consider if you’re going to be okay in that kind of environment before applying.
reviews.summary: A unique company, but it’s hard to last more than a couple of years here.

reviews.cons:
Unfortunately, I was laid off without notice in the middle of my shift one day. The managers looked truly upset that they were having to let a few of us go. Apparently some people at HQ looked at some metrics from their office and decided who they would let go without consulting with the local managers for their input.

This is a company that has a great local atmosphere at all of the stores I worked at in Southern California, and it can be swept out from under you for absolutely no legitimate reason at any time. If you are going to work here, my best advice is to not be concerned with going above and beyond with helping out around the store and impressing your immediate superiors. You should only be concerned with the metrics you are being judged on for your ONE specific role at the location. If you start helping out with other departments,making the store more cohesive in general, and learning other aspects of the jobs at a location, this may impress your managers, but has zero impact on whether or not you will stay at the company. It will merely give you a false sense of confidence from people who ultimately do not decide if you stay or go.

The managers would give good feedback and let you know when they felt you were doing great / not so great. It was a place that really welcomed innovation within the store rather than sticking to what a manual told us was best.

Tesla targets the best of the best, so when recruiting, it can be challenging to hire people away from other companies due to compensation, at Tesla relies heavily on their equity offering to compensate for lower salaries.

Company doesn’t care about work life balance. Will literally give hour notice of schedule change and expect us to not have issues with it. They dont recognize hard work or even promote it. If you are exceeding expectations expect the bar to change and be given higher expectations so you cannot promote or level up. A lot of people do not push team work or sharing of information. If you get hired expect to have to figure everything out for yourself unless you are deemed as “worthy” of the knowledge.
Also company doesnt support the technician roles getting pay bumps. So expect WAY less technical roles to be making as much or more if you are applying as a technician or even as an engineer. Pay scale is really unbalanced between positions.

reviews.cons:
Timeliness is VERY important at tesla and that can be hard to deal with if you are using public transportation. I had been 10 minutes late due to a delay from BART and was immediately sent home and told to complete a reschedule form and that I would be contacted shortly. Long story short 2 weeks later and I got a letter of termination. The Situation was out of my control as the bart train I took was the earliest train possible. All it took was one day of being late by 10 minutes for me to be bounced from tesla and I cannot re apply for 6 months. 

Other than that there weren't any cons that come to mind, however I would recommend buying your own boots as the Tesla provided boots can be very uncomfortable. So beware if you will be relying on public transport and always have a backup plan if there are any delays as even with proof of what had happened I was still turned away.

reviews.advice: Please focus on what matters and stop regurgitating what you think looks proper on paper. Telling 5 employees across 8 lines each that they need to put in 12 defects a month gives you a library of garbage that means nothing to keep up with. The defects that matter get buried underneath garbage. And that's just for 1 building.
reviews.cons:
"Normal Circumstances" is the thing here. Line speed can wildly vary, and it's down to your luck on if you're on a fast / slow line, and how you handle it. I'm not enjoying the fast pace required of me each day, and my peers hired with me in different areas genuinely have a less intense workday; their own words when comparing line duties. Not really much opportunity to switch things up. You will be where they need / want you.

There are also a large amount of asinine company requirements to keep up with. Logging a total of 20 things online that the company knows is bull, just to keep checking a box and be satisfied. There's more asinine box ticking than I've ever seen at any company, but mainly for higher positions. What you have to deal with as an N1 new hire is not that bad in that regard, but I've seen many higher positions get screwed over in their promotions and shoved into higher responsibilities without proper compensation for far too long.
reviews.pros:
General workflow is easy to understand at a base level. You continuously learn what's expected of you, and it's not hard to keep up under normal circumstances.

My personal management has also been very good and genuinely cares about my progression.

reviews.cons: They constantly talk about how much they value diversity, yet I am someone who struggles with a (new) disability and when this disability occurred (I’m purposely being vague so as not to reveal too much) their disability department made my life a living hell. About two weeks into my month-long hospital stay I got a call telling me my short-term disability claim had been approved, so I didn’t worry about it any longer. So, when about 5 weeks later I got a call saying my disability claim had been denied because my doctor had failed to send them the paper work they had requested (even though I had watched him place it in the fax machine) I was stunned. What followed was months of back and forth, with them requesting more and more paperwork, but nothing was enough for them to approve the claim. I even gave them paperwork showing I had been in the hospital the whole time. THEN they said in order for me to be able to return to work I needed a doctor’s note. So, my doctor wrote a note saying I was fit to return to work now that my stay at the hospital had addressed everything successfully. The disability claim manager called me to say my claim had been denied and closed because, according to my doctor’s most recent letter, I was fit to work. I pointed out that obviously it would have said that because it was written after I had been temporarily disabled for the two months and ready to return for work. She simply repeated that the case was denied and that I had to wait for my denial letter to appeal my case I still haven’t gotten this letter. Every time I call to ask about it, I get the same line - it’s is on the way and when it comes I can appeal it. Because of all of this, I went two months without a paycheck and had to move in with my parents and take out a loan from my 401k to cover childcare. It was a complete and utter mess.

reviews.advice:
Boeing's got plenty of brainpower with high GPAs, but is this enough?  To create great products you’ve got to have the heart in addition to the head.  

Find ways to make Boeing a cool place to be an engineer, where people can feel like they’re doing ‘real engineering’, not just being software jockeys doing production work.  Try to make the place feel less conventional and fuddy-duddy.

All the bonuses and other extrinsic rewards are great. But what really gets people up in the morning? Feeling like they're part of something bigger, that their ideas matter, and that they're not just cogs in the machine. Create space where creativity thrives and unconventional types feel at home.
reviews.cons:
If you're all about tradition, love following rules, and like to settle into a routine where you’re told what to do and how to do it, you might just fit in perfectly here. It’s all about sticking to the script here. It's like working on the production line in an engineering factory.

But if you’re the type who likes to color outside the lines, thrives under creative chaos, and loves to innovate, think again. You’ll likely find yourself butting heads with the status quo and the ‘lifers’, especially the managers who aren't typically fans of shaking things up. It’s like being a square peg in a round hole, and let’s just say not everyone’s going to be thrilled about your groundbreaking ideas.

Dreaming of cutting-edge aerospace work? You might need to adjust your expectations. Aerospace is incredible, but it’s also very cautious by nature and tends to move at a glacial pace when it comes to innovation. You’ll likely spend more time fine-tuning the old than inventing the new.

And about those high-tech tools you were looking forward to? Think more vintage than cutting edge. Upgrading software can be like moving mountains, so don’t hold your breath unless the software is about to become unsupported by the manufacturer. It was a real eye-opener for me when I switched jobs and saw what modern engineering tools could do. It’s way beyond most structural analysis done at Boeing in its sophistication. There’s a whole world of tech out there that makes some of the old stuff still used at Boeing look like child’s play.

Seeing new grad engineers get reduced to spreadsheet jockeys from day one was tough. I kept wanting to tell them, "You sure this is the dream job you were after?" It’s not just about the tools, though. It’s about getting to do real, hands-on engineering, something that’s pretty rare in big aero. Feeling like you’re tethered to a computer all day, every day, and never touching anything real gets old fast for some. Also, at other companies I’ve found a freedom to pursue new ideas I’m interested in, along with an appreciation of my drive for innovation. At Boeing, I found such ideas are typically not appreciated and normally get shut down: “We don’t have the budget”, “we don’t have the staffing”, “that’s not within our scope”.

Sticking around for the steady paycheck and benefits is easy, but don’t let it turn into a trap. Some call it the ‘golden handcuffs’—comfortable, yet limiting. Keep in mind, unless you’re looking to make a career of big aero, working at Boeing probably won’t make you very marketable for the vast majority of employers, most of which don’t have such hyper-specialization in their engineering roles.

Some might consider getting a role on a Phantom Works project to be the dream. Just keep in mind even PW isn’t all about groundbreaking work; most of it is heavily derivative in nature. For me, earning a few patents on a PW project was a highlight, showing that it’s not impossible to innovate.

Looking back at my time with Boeing, it simply didn’t have the fun or happy atmosphere I've found elsewhere. A big reason, I think, is that a lot of people didn't seem all that excited about the work. And can you blame them? When you've been doing the same relatively narrow tasks day in, day out, for years—or even decades—it's no surprise when the job loses its shine. When the intrinsic rewards of the work don’t cut it anymore, people tend to get obsessed with extrinsic rewards, like raises, promotions, bonuses, or any perks that come their way (yes at Boeing there was an obsession compared to other places I’ve worked). The thing is, big extrinsic rewards like promotions and raises are few and far between, and their luster fades quickly as they become the ‘new normal’ .

Finding my way to a job where my knack for innovation is actually celebrated was a game-changer. Now I feel like a valued, trusted, and important part of the whole; not just one of thousands of anonymous units of engineering labor. Also, I feel like a real salaried employee who has agency and is not constantly being ‘watched’. This is a stark contrast to Boeing where I felt salaried in classification only, and had to charge time to the 1/10th of an hour. It’s a reminder that there’s a perfect fit out there for everyone—you just gotta keep looking.

Thinking about the future, with all the hype about AI and automation, there’s lots of potential for shaking things up in aerospace. There’s a lot of moving data from one place to another and doing standard work according to well-established rules and procedures, and we all know those types of things are ripe for disruption by automation. Just something to think about.
Even though this cons section is much longer than the pros section, I’m not trying to put down my old employer. However I do feel I owe prospective employees an honest assessment. Even though I stayed far too long, it was a chapter in my life that set me up for where I am now, working my dream job. Also, this is for you unconventional types who might be feeling a bit out of place wherever you are, wondering if there’s more to engineering than landing a job at a big company. I hope you find that place where your brilliance shines.
reviews.pros:
The benefits are the standout feature to me – healthcare insurance and the 401k are very good. Also in the area of compensation, they pay for overtime, which isn’t typical for engineering jobs. 

Opportunities to move around within the company can be a major plus and help you get promotions and bigger raises faster. Whether it’s projects, roles, or locations, there’s a lot of room to explore.

I believe the compensation is fair for the broader engineering market. However I do question how competitive it is for the industry: I passed up an offer from a competitor that would have raised my pay by nearly 50%. I turned it down because, based on my experience at Boeing (especially the last year) I had no desire to stay in big aero no matter how much the pay.

reviews.advice: Current leadership are micromanagers, provide them training and development, or replace them. Having leaders in place based on equity will never provide great leadership. In summary, having leaders who micromanager can lead to a host of negative consequences, including reduced creativity, morale, and productivity, as well as inhibited growth and increased stress levels within the team or organization. It is generally advisable for leaders to strike a balance between providing guidance and allowing employees the freedom to excel in their roles.
reviews.cons: The Director and above leadership are micromanagers. They claim to provide employees with the tools needed to perform their jobs and think on their own. This is not the case. They constantly scrutinize the employees and they have little to no autonomy in their roles. Employees are not allowed to make decisions or take ownership of their tasks and are disengaged and demotivated. When working with leadership, they provide detailed instructions on how tasks should be done, leaving little room for employees to think critically or find creative solutions to problems. Leadership monitored and criticized. This lead to low morale among team members. Employees felt that their leader lacked trust in their abilities, and they felt undervalued and unappreciated. Leadership often spent an excessive amount of time reviewing and correcting their employees' work based on their logic and process. Leadership constantly watched and evaluated employees and created a high-stress work environment. Employees constantly felt on edge, worried about making mistakes or facing criticism.

reviews.advice: Please retire
reviews.cons:
- My manager was not helpful, only had two one on ones each year and would often make verbal promises that he eventually forgot months later. 
- boring and broken tech; testing your code locally could even be a struggle and there were pointless Java updates
- program clearance took way too long; I was at the company for three years not knowing what I was working before I couldn’t take it anymore
- paradoxical optimizations; teammates would often talk endlessly on how to optimize the broken tech they’ve been assigned to. It all felt kind of pointless
- confused management and lots of cancellations; 4/5 of the projects I worked on were cancelled which was very demoralizing
- clocking in hours on spreadsheets is annoying; often found myself working late because I was lost on a assignment and didn’t want to mischarge. Ended up subtracting my vacation time frequently
- teammates were often bad at explaining things (especially through writing). I recall my software architect explaining dependency injection in a condescending manner to insinuate it’s too difficult to explain. After learning it myself a year later, I’d say it’s not that complicated at all. 
- teammates were a bit backstabby during year end reviews

reviews.cons:
In general, the pro's heavily out weigh the cons.

1. Working with union can be challenging at times
2. May encounter co-workers who seek the spot light vs. working as team 
3. May encounter leadership team members with different views on promotions/years of experience required (e.g. must have "X" years of experience before being promoted to "Y" level, as opposed to promoting based on knowledge, results, etc.)
4. If you're a high performer and leading high profile projects/programs you can find yourself working more than 40+ hours per week. Some may find this as a negative but when you are younger this can truly accelerate your career and be an opportunity for you to deliver results that far exceed your peers.
reviews.pros:
No particular order:

1. Work/Life Balance 
2. Salary
3. Broad range of projects/programs (depending on job function)
4. Ability to "jump" careers within a single company (e.g. RMS, Space, MFC, Aero could be considered sub-companies within LM) and work on everything ranging from quality assurance, failure analysis, software engineering, manufacturing, systems engineering, program management, propulsion systems, radars, combat ships, missiles, satellites, wildfire prevention, and so much more! There are honestly so many diverse roles within a single company it is incredible. 
5. Community Involvement / volunteering opportunities
6. Strong collaboration with academia, different business areas (RMS, Space,...), industry, etc. 
7. Many diverse work locations (Sunnyvale, CA; Palmdale, CA; Ft. Worth, TX; Grand Prarie, TX; Marietta, GA; King of Purssia, PA; Stratford, CT; etc.)
8. The company has over $150B dollars in backlog which will provide years of work for employees. In addition, they continue to grow and secure sizeable contracts from around the world leading to their $67.6B in net sales in 2023. 
9. Job security

reviews.advice: Management must keep in mind that it today's world, which is saturated with brilliant companies that hire top talent, IBM must remain competitive to attract great talent and hold on to it.  In the meanwhile, we're seeing the opposite trend, where great people leave IBM for other companies, be it because of a more competitive package, dropping morale and many other reasons.
reviews.cons:
1. Unfortunately, IBM still uses the "normal distribution" rating system, where at the end of the year each employee is ranked as a top contributor (5%), above average contributor (15%), average contributor (~75%), and bottom contributor (5%).  This curve is difficult to apply in the R&D world, where you may have many members of the team working long and hard hours, and end up being "average contributors" at the end of the year, because there just isn't room for all to be top contributors. 

2. The above may not be so disturbing, if only IBM didn't practically cancelled all raises, performance bonuses and incentive for the non top-performers. I've had a consistent "above average" rating in the last 4-5 years, and my raise and performance bonus were ridiculous mere 1.5-2% of my salary.  Were I rated "average contributor" I would have gotten NOTHING. So you can imagine that people can go year after year without any raise to their salary.

From talking to manager friend, this is IBM's way to eliminate the non-top-performers without having to fire them, as part of its direction of reducing US manpower. 

3. Hiring freeze in many areas - again, as part of IBM's attempt to reduce its workforce across North America and Europe we see many jobs move to the India and Far East markets.  This is of course upsetting to see local teams shrink and disappear, especially when many great local IBM colleagues and experts begin to drop out. From my experience thus far working with India SW teams - they are still very far away from the standards I would have expected from US and Europe based teams. 

4. Poor top down communication about company's and divisions' future.  Employees learn from rumors and news websites what's about to come...

employerResponses.response:
Thanks for sharing your experience, and we're glad that you've had a positive experience working with talented colleagues and taking advantage of IBM's programs.  IBM is in the midst of a major transformation, --our Systems business is going through its own changes  to strengthen competitiveness.  Change is never easy.   As part of our transformation, we just launched a whole new approach for how we are coaching employees, delivering feedback and managing reviews. No distribution guidelines or what some think of as 'stacked rankings." 

What's particularly great is that this was co-designed with our employee base from all over the world... to the tune of hundreds of thousands of page views, comments, on-line debates and discussions.  IBMers even named the new system Checkpoint, to reflect the regular feedback rituals we're adopting.  Managers are more empowered with the new methodology to help them acknowledge the great work of their teams and help their employees develop professionally. 

These steps and more are showing up in our employee surveys as well. So IBMers are feeling the change. We are confident these changes will help us in continuing to attract and retain great talent.

reviews.pros:
Disclaimer: A lot of what I'm writing below of course depends on the work area and management chain.  But I found this to be fairly pervasive policies in IBM in my 9+ years with the company. 
1. IBM's policies and management are very flexible when it comes to working remotely or accommodating various life situations (sick days, doctor visits, etc.).  Management is encouraged to measure an employee by their work and impact, and not by hours spent at their office. 
2. Great colleagues!  Though unfortunately, many have been leaving due to the instability of IBM's HW development business. 
3. At least in my area, there's a high level of flexibility on which projects should I undertake based on my and my management assessment of business impact.

reviews.advice: Don't be so cut-and-dried regarding quota/performance rules. I had one senior colleague who was exceptionally good in her role, who had a bad year and was forced to leave IBM, and then a huge deal she was working on close the following 1Q anyway. She was forced to leave, despite the fact that everyone loved her and she worked hard, just because of some arbitrary performance targets. This system needs to be fixed, because IBM let it's best talent leave, and that's not a great way to sustain growth in the long run.
reviews.cons:
Some of the "old guard" at IBM are stubborn, resistant to change and adapt to clients' needs. But those folks are starting to leave the company. Sales quotas occasionally can be quite aggressive, but if you are a nice/reasonable person and visibly show effort/hustle, management can be lenient on performance targets. Targets are also subject to change at a moment's notice.

Also, promotions can be extremely slow, and you have to fight for every new career opportunity. Management won't guide you in your career - that's up to you and you alone.
reviews.pros:
IBM's training and mentorship are some of the best in the F500 community, and maybe the tech industry as a whole. The people are reasonable, the workload is fast-paced and interesting, but not at the expense of your health. Pay has become more competitive in recent years, leading folks like me to stay for years, even when courted by higher-growth startups. Overall, there's lots to like about IBM.

The new CEO, Arvind Krishna, also seems to have a good handle on what IBM needs to succeed, and he's steering the ship confidently in the right direction, after many years previously of stagnant growth.
reviews.summary: IBM Proves Why it's a Top Employer

reviews.advice: I have been at IBM for a long time and it really pains me to see them going downhill.  Partners cannot sell because the rates IBM is charging for consulting is higher than their competitors, then when people aren't staffed they are being made redundant but calling their termination a performance issue.  The rates and PIP policies are hurting your own people.  We all know what the rates are you charge and yet we're not being paid at the market rate, we're all below it.  This hurts what used to be a great company to work for and I wish upper management would look at these policies to realize that the high turnover rate has everything to do with them.
reviews.cons: In consulting they punish people for things that they are not in control of. IBM will put people on Performance Improvement Plans because their billable rate is on the low side, but if the partners haven't sold work for the consultants it is not a performance issue. It feels like this is a workaround for unemployment and severance. If there isn't work to be done, this should be a reduncancy termination that has severance and a positive leaving experience. That is not how IBM handles this which is a shame.
reviews.pros: IBM is a consistent company that has been around for a long time with several different areas to move into if you want to change your skills and career options
reviews.summary: Good company that could be great

reviews.advice: RTO and layoffs don't align with your stated values of DEI, promoting people from within, or creating career growth opportunities. You would do better to create (and communicate) an actual Talent Strategy that allows employees to opt in or out over the course of a year or 2. For example, instead of mandated RTO, you could say 'no more openings outside of strategic locations.' Or instead of layoffs, you could ask for voluntary early retirement, name roles that have (maybe) a 6 month shelf-life and will not be backfilled, or ask for voluntary LOAs without pay to meet a profit target for a quarter. There needs to be more creativity, strategy, and planning in the way you care for employees.
reviews.cons: IBM's leadership has proven over and over again that it's always going to be profit over people. If IBM ever does anything that confuses you (or looks like it's against its values), just ask yourself if it makes sense from a finance and/or legal perspective. Usually, that's where the decisions come from.
reviews.pros: IBM has the potential to be a leader for good in the way the world works.

reviews.advice: Continue listening and taking action on employee feedback and improving. Understand that many still want flexibility in working from home.
reviews.cons: Lots of moving parts in this company and releases take a long time (6+ months) due to technical debt. Designs can be "handed off" often a year or more before something releases. Also this is relatively unsexy B2B / enterprise work, and the complexity is not for everyone. Learn to embrace it or you won't do well or be happy here.
reviews.pros: Phenomenal place for designers. Robust support system with great design leadership up to the top, as well as a huge network of mentors. As an individual contributor, I rarely have to waste effort trying to explain to my engineering or PM stakeholders that UX is important, but YMMV depending on your team or org. Good people, culture, work life balance, decent benefits and pay, and career growth opportunities. I feel I am treated like a decent human being here, and I don't take that for granted.

reviews.advice: Understand the customers and the products your Salesforce is selling rather than swooping in at the end to make it seem like you were involved in closing the deal.
reviews.cons: If you have the wrong account mix or there is no ELA closing for your accounts, you can find it really difficult to make your numbers. Quota is based on assumptions that are often wrong. You will have multiple managers that are mainly interested in forecasting and will often push you towards how they want you to forecast in order to appease their superiors, regardless of whether you feel the numbers are accurate.

reviews.advice: Ensure that teams have the necessary resources, including personnel, tools, and time, to accomplish their tasks successfully. Address concerns related to workload by either redistributing tasks or providing additional support.
reviews.cons:
High Workload and Pressure: IBM, being a large and globally recognized company, can have high expectations and a fast-paced work environment. Some employees may feel overwhelmed by the workload and pressure.

Limited Work-Life Balance: In certain roles or during demanding projects, employees might find it challenging to maintain a healthy work-life balance. Long working hours and tight deadlines may contribute to this issue.

Bureaucracy: Large organizations often have established bureaucratic processes, which could lead to delays in decision-making and project execution. Navigating through these processes might be cumbersome for some employees.

Limited Managerial Support: Your experience of feeling overworked without sufficient support from management is a common concern in various workplaces. In a large company, communication channels can sometimes be complex, and individual experiences may differ based on teams and managers.

Emphasis on Metrics: Some employees may feel that the company places a strong emphasis on metrics and performance indicators, which could potentially impact the work environment and stress levels.

Limited Flexibility: Depending on the role and team, some employees might find that the company has a more structured and less flexible approach to work arrangements.

Communication Challenges: In a large organization, communication can sometimes be a challenge. Important information might not always be effectively communicated across teams, leading to misunderstandings or a lack of clarity.
reviews.pros: Professional Growth and Learning: IBM places a strong emphasis on continuous learning and development. As a Technical Owner, you may have access to training programs, certifications, and opportunities for professional growth to stay updated with the latest technologies and industry trends.

reviews.advice: Management knows how they can improve the employee experience at IBM, because we've told how, in survey after survey. They are not interested in employee feedback unless it aligns with what they were planning to do already.
reviews.cons: IBM used to be famous for putting its employees first. When I joined, I was told about how good the benefits were, and how IBM was a "family." In the past few years, that philosophy has been discarded. Every few months upper management makes sweeping policy changes, with no employee input, that significantly hurt US employees. When employees react en masse with concern, alarm, and constructive feedback, they ignore or gaslight us, or commit the strawman fallacy by mischaracterizing employees' concerns and then dismissing them. For example, in November 2023 (right after the employee engagement survey concluded), the did away with 401k matching, replacing it with a novel financial vehicle called an "RBA" with much lower yields, and tried to spin it as a good thing for us. Based on publicly available information, I'm estimating that this will probably save IBM at least $100M over the next decade in US benefits payouts. It also means IBM holds our retirement money, rather than the employee. IBM simply does not care about retaining talent right now -- if you are a senior or well-paid employee in the US, they see you as an expense, and they're showing you the door.
reviews.pros: IBM has a low bar for hiring engineers, so if you're having trouble finding an SWE job at GAFA you can probably get one at IBM (once the job market opens up again).
reviews.summary: IBM no longer cares about its talent

Every earnings call Charlie drones on about becoming a "more nimble, less market sensitive" company, while the company's operating model remains the same. The company is disorganized and bureaucratic, making it hard to get things done without many layers of approval. This may be changing for the better with the recent layoffs, but time will tell.

In addition, the company can be highly political. Promotions or the ability to move into certain groups are often based on having an MBA, or tenure length, rather than the ability and motivation to actually get things done. There are Directors and VPs who are absolutely coasting, while a handful of hard-working individuals pull all the weight.

Compensation is often below market, and Senior management celebrates this. On an internal company call, when discussing compensation within the company, Rob Falzon made the hilarious statement of "we don't want our employees to be mercenaries (hired soldiers)" - implying that Prudential employees should be okay with being under-compensated, because Pru makes up for it with such a great "culture." The problem with this, of course, aside from being plagiarized from a Goldman Sachs CEO, is that culture doesn't pay bills. reviews.advice:
For AbbVie's management, it's crucial to address the recent turnover in leadership positions and strive for more stability within the organization. This can help reduce the micromanagement culture and create a more conducive work environment for employees. Additionally, management should review and potentially revise the incentive compensation structure to ensure it accurately reflects the growth potential of tier 1 brands and provides fair rewards for sales performance.

Furthermore, management should take proactive steps to improve communication and collaboration between sales and marketing teams, ensuring that both departments work together effectively to achieve sales targets. Addressing the concerns raised by employees regarding profit-sharing programs and the absence of an employee stock purchase program can also help boost morale and retain top talent within the organization.

Lastly, management should prioritize providing adequate support and resources to sales representatives, acknowledging their efforts in promoting AbbVie's top-tier Immunology products and ensuring they feel valued and motivated in their roles. By addressing these issues, AbbVie's management can work towards fostering a more positive and productive work environment for all employees.
reviews.cons:
AbbVie is grappling with recent challenges, particularly revolving around a notable turnover in key leadership positions. Within the past year, new leaders, including the President of Immunology, Vice President of Rheumatology, and Sales Director of Rheumatology, have assumed their roles. This influx of new leadership has fostered a micromanagement culture and destabilized the organization's structure. Despite AbbVie's esteemed reputation, the company has consistently fallen short of its Rhuematology sales targets for consecutive quarters. Regrettably, this has led to an unfair distribution of blame, with sales representatives shouldering unwarranted responsibility. The elimination of profit-sharing programs, coupled with the absence of an employee stock purchase program, has resulted in significant pay cuts for sales representatives, further exacerbating employee dissatisfaction. Moreover, the flawed incentive compensation structure, which disproportionately emphasizes territory history over growth potential, has failed to deliver on promises of high earnings.

In addition to these internal challenges, AbbVie is grappling with the aftermath of HUMIRA's loss of exclusivity. This has prompted the company to urgently position its newer products as superior alternatives for rheumatoid arthritis patients who have ceased HUMIRA treatment. This strategic pivot emphasizes the pressing need for AbbVie to adapt swiftly to evolving market dynamics and effectively promote its newer offerings to maintain its competitive edge in the industry.
reviews.pros: Working at AbbVie offers several advantages, such as access to top-tier Immunology and Rheumatology products with preferred coverage. AbbVie also prioritizes providing ample resources and support to its employees, customers, and patients, fostering a supportive and conducive environment for all stakeholders.

reviews.cons: More of a sales job than anything
reviews.pros: Good place to start right out of college

reviews.cons: Hierarchy and visibility carry great import

reviews.advice: Do 6-month evaluations with serious consideration for interior promotions before out-side-in hiring. Then hire only at the bottom level (entry). Let tech. decide when/who to promote for tech. because business holds the wallet, but doesn't necessarily know what's best.
reviews.cons: The Company is huge, and at times it may take more than a little time to get recognized for your abilities and the growth you've had. There's a reason there is a "only way up is out" reputation exists for some enterprise companies...
reviews.pros: They have fantastic pay for the position you're in, and they teach you interesting and engaging utility of modern technology mixed with legacy fundamentals. I've learned quite a bit while AmEx while getting paid more than fairly - I'd recommend a stretch here to whomever may be reading this!

reviews.advice:
Please speak for your employees and don't take a shrug of shoulders or a NO as the answer. If you know it is not fair/right, then don't give up on that. Make it known, drive it up the chain of command. 
Also way to much focus and emphasis on the ABC mafia!!!!! Such a small group that receives all the benefits makes no sense as to why this is a part of the workplace. Even our intro greet on our calls has to be inclusive, cannot use sir or ma'am because it will offend someone. Well, what if all this nonsense offends my views or feelings as they like to say. Well, since I'm not a part of that group, I have no say in it!! Stop all the Disney treatment and act more like your name says "American"!!!! I don't have any issues with that group, but I do have issues with how companies have dealt with it. We are all human!! Thats what matters.
reviews.cons: There's not a lot of room for growth unless you know people. Even a great performer only has upward growth but is still in sales and not higher up in the chain of command. Working virtually means that even if the systems issues you may encounter are because of Amex equipment, you will get written up or warned about it. The virtual employees receive a desktop PC rather than a laptop, like the hybrid employees. This makes your PC dependent on VPN connectivity or an Aruba device, which is not efficient. All the work apps are accessed via another virtual portal, which is inefficient.
reviews.pros: Semi-good benefits: Pay for school upfront if you don't qualify for pell grants or can be concurrent with it.

reviews.advice: American Express, at least specifically the FIU department, needs to enhance their on the job training to include all job functions, or at least have in person classes/calibration meetings so that everyone is on the same page. Instead of announcing business changes appropriately so that everyone is aware of them, they send out mass emails which get lost among the hundreds of other emails you receive every day.
reviews.cons:

-Department does not provide helpful training tools nor do they provide an easy to use procedure manual
reviews.pros:

-Office location is pristine
-Remote options

reviews.advice: Actually do something after listening to your employees? Executive leadership has explicitly acknowledged that they expected their actions to result in lower survey results. Why are you pushing on ahead? Listen to your directors and their reports when they tell you something isn’t good…
reviews.cons: Collapsing under its own weight and arbitrary processes. No drive to innovate. Executive leadership is fostering a toxic culture encouraging people to come in while sick while continuously piling work onto teams struggling to get by. Wages are stagnant.
reviews.pros: Direct leadership is great, and there are decent learning opportunities. Your direct leaders will usually have your back and go to bat for you as best they can. Peers are wonderful as well.

reviews.advice: Foster a better understanding that friendship and professionalism are both fantastic, but that they should not be happening at the same time. Award the good performers, demote the poor performers, but be friendly and professional with everyone.
reviews.cons: If you do not get along with your Sueprvisor, this position can quickly turn into a nightmare. I love my team, but I've seen a number of toxic leaders that quiet fire their employees over the smallest disagreements. It may be shallow, but you must play to the ego of those in charge, like many jobs.

jobTitle.text: Travel and Lifestyle Customer Service Specialist

reviews.pros: With a good supervisor, this can be one of the healthiest jobs in the world. Time off, difficult but manageable workloads, a fair PIP with multiple levels that are very fair.

reviews.cons: The work can sometimes demand long hours which may impact work-life balance. There can also be slow movement in terms of career progression due to the size and structure of the organization.
reviews.pros: American Express offers a collaborative work culture with robust support for professional development. It boasts a respected brand that adds significant value to your resume. The company also provides excellent benefits and opportunities to engage with innovative projects.
reviews.summary: Supportive Environment and Strong Brand with Room for Improvement in Work-Life Balance

reviews.advice: Skim through team leaders and hold them accountable for what is expected from them to maximize each team’s success. Team leaders should be accessible during teams scheduled business hours, however a lot of them seem to be too busy or do not know how to work systems correctly. Team leaders should be required to complete certain hours on the phones to fully understand how systems are used and to be able to assist the frontline agents.
reviews.cons:
Middle management can be hit or miss. Some are extremely knowledgeable and truly care about their team and each individual’s success. Others seem to lost their interest on their position on being a leader or do not have the experience to perform a leadership position.
Sometimes being part of such a huge company you can feel like you’re just a body to complete the work. However managers do offer opportunities to have one on one meetings or are always available when meetings are requested.
reviews.pros:
Endless opportunities to progress on your career. The company has so many opportunities and internal job openings that once you’re in, there’s need to change the company even if you want completely change your career path. Temporary work assignments offer a great way to get a feel of what you like to do before committing fully for a new position. 
Compensation for your time is good. Base pay is hourly and quarterly bonuses and annual raises are based on metrics and each employees performance. 
Benefits they offer are hard to beat including generous maternity leave, annual paid time off and financial assistance for school.
Military spouse dream career!

reviews.advice: Read a book (any book) on how to manage a sales team. The methods currently in place might have worked in the 19th century, but fear is not a good motivator for the modern sales professional.
reviews.cons: While the company, as a whole, might win awards for being a great place to work, the SME division is terrible if you enjoy sales. Constant gas-lighting the entire sales team and they now issue “infractions” and dock your pay $5,000 if you get too many infractions. It is a culture of fear and capped commissions.
reviews.pros: Benefits, 401-K & 6% match, great brand

reviews.advice:
- recognize the cost of being in office and offer commute plans

- look at payscales and start looking at.how this will effect talent. If more local opportunities arise for workers they will start leaving in droves. We all.commute 1 hour plus into the office and the wear is showing.

reviews.summary: Good culture, but needs to think more about employee pay and travel

reviews.advice: Pay people more. Promote from within. Spread out decision making to the SMEs/experts. Stop share buybacks and give raises to employees (not shareholders)!!

Management is wildly different between organizations. Upper management tends to leave every 1-3 years, so stability suffers.
reviews.pros: Virtual work available. Diverse corporate culture. Benefits and training better than most.
reviews.summary: Ambiguous Promotion Requirements, but Overall Good

reviews.advice: Best CEO in 30 years.  He really listens to employees and takes action.  Brought back bonus to Band 30 and below when I asked.
reviews.cons: No Cafeteria at this location
reviews.pros: Very flexible.  Ability to move across different depts.  Great benefits and wonderful people and leaders.

reviews.advice: Spend more time on the development of your sales teams, not only for the greater good of your consumers but also for the company. Management teams in Sunrise, FL were strictly focused on checking boxes and doing what they needed to do to keep their jobs. Additionally, please be more honest in the interview when asked direct questions about the department. Much of the information conveyed in the initial interview is simply not true and leaves new employees feeling misled upon the completion of onboarding.
reviews.cons: Awful company culture within the sales department. The resources you are provided heavily depends on the relationships you build with the veterans of the sales floor. If you are not in a position to network, your longevity is nonexistent. You are not provided enough training to be successful when hitting the floor. Additionally, the goals and expectations of the sales force are nearly impossible to meet due to compliance issues and a poor implementation process. Management is very hands-off and indirectly promotes a sink-or-swim environment where you are left on your own.
reviews.pros: 40 hours a week, hybrid schedule, free food.

reviews.cons: Inconsistent pay for different people in the same role. Upper management C-Suite need to stop pushing in office and focus on improving technology resources.
reviews.pros: Decent pay for starting roles. The company pushes for growth but they limit salary increases to internal employees. Work culture seems positive and I'm fortunate to work with a professional and friendly team. However, there is elitism amongst certain band levels.
reviews.summary: Positive experience with potential to become better

reviews.advice: Management should start creating shared goals so teams/departments will more willingly work with one another. Right now, it's always a constant struggle of getting other team's attention since they tend to ignore you unless it's clear what benefit they can get from you.

reviews.advice: In my experience, all tthe managers maintained professionalism, guidence and appropriate redirection if necessary.
reviews.cons: The hours can be really tough. Even though the stores are only open 7am-10pm, there's a lot of opening and closing duties, so you can be there as early as 5am and as late as 11pm for closings.
reviews.pros:
I worked for theem in the 80s, they were my first job while in highschool. In 2021, I made a big life change and needed a job. I needed a flexible schedule and thought "why not Publix?"
In order to get the interview & hired, make them your number one priority, they're not big on being a "second job." They usually only hire part time positions, but if you show up, put in the work, show respect and professionalism to EVERYONE in the work place, it will be acknowledged in both from management and co-workers. In my experience, management and co-workers were extremly helpful and patient while I learned an industry I hadn't been in for 40 years.
Starting pay isn't great, but the longer you're there, the more hours and modest raises will be offered. There is plenty of oppurtunity to trensfer from one department to another, same applies to different stores.
Customer service is very important, but you;ll need to be mindfull about "going too far" for customers.
Corporate guidlines are stricktly followed, Duties will include everything from cleaning floors and bathrooms, to the specific functions of the specialty departments.
I was there almost three years and only left for family reasons.
It's definately a company worth investing time in.

reviews.advice: I was rated exceeds expectations on my yearly evaluation, and the "raise" I got didn't even cover the increase in the price of the groceries. If your most valuable asset is your people, you should make sure your wages allow them to be fed and housed.
reviews.cons:
*Managers are rotated every other year or so. While this can be good if you have a bad manager, it also means you can't count on having a good manager forever.
* Anytime you introduce an element of "corporate," regardless of the company, you're gonna get sweeping, generalizing decisions that don't make sense for your situation. It also makes it hard to build rapport with good managers and if you care about your department, it gets very draining to continually have to prove yourself to new people.
*PTO is also your sick time, so budget accordingly and hope you don't get a string of bad luck. 
*Part-timers only get benefits if they hit 1000 hours worked in a year, and when I was in the customer service department, I was only getting about 990.
*I've been there 3 years so the stocks must be based on that 1000 hours too.
* Work Culture is good on the surface, but don't look too deep because I'm not sure they actually believe what they want the public to think they believe. Actions speak louder than words.
reviews.pros:
*3 weeks PTO
*benefits have expanded to include part-timers
*monthly free merchandise coupon, good for trying some new stuff
*I hear talk of stocks being given to you for time worked
*Overall, probably the best corporate retail I've worked for

reviews.advice: Stop forcing employees to suffer through work they aren’t good at when you can put them to work doing something they excel in.
reviews.cons: The customers are mentally abusive and disrespectful and workers aren’t allowed to do anything but say “Sorry” then walk away. Doing work that isn’t exactly your best will stunt your growth in the department even if you’re better at every other part of the job. Managers don’t tell you if you’re going something poorly because they expect you to know everything the second training is over even though training covers almost nothing compared to the actual work. If you perform poorly at a task that you dislike but have a coworker who performs well and enjoys the task then it would make sense to ask your manager for a different task that you don’t dislike as much or something you can preform better doing, that doesn’t work at Publix. Not liking a task is going to get you stuck doing it more even if you aren’t good at it. Over all I would say its a good idea to work here if your fine with some extraordinarily aggravating work but with good pay.
reviews.pros: Good pay, easy work, flexible hours depending on position.

reviews.advice: Do better, act like you actually care, clear communication, act like adults this isn't high school stop playing favorites
reviews.cons: In the deli one of the many things that are wrong include not ordering deli soap, bleach and waterproof aprons. Another thing is because we don't have a lot of people to cover brakes you have to cut your brakes short and then be told to stop cutting breaks and take you're full break. Another thing is after associates having a few conversations about how buses don't run Sundays after 11:00-11:44 at the latest still being expected to stay almost getting stranded (something I've seen happen to another associate). another issue with the deli being told not to get stuff off the shelves but then when stuff isn't ordered like tomatoes lettuce cucumbers etc being complained at by the customers and then told to go get it off the shelves anyways after being told you'll get fired if you do. The lack of direct and clear communication throughout the store including the deli. The unprofessional petty and spiteful behavior of the adults that work there (managers and employees). Being told to leave on Fridays even though you're scheduled to work because you're overtime. The lack of communication when it comes to your schedule being changed. The fact that consistently for 3 weeks out of every month I am put on below 39/40 hours and then that last week have me on 40 hours so I don't get overtime or full-time status. The clear lacking in care of anyone's situation by saying "we're all going through it right now" or some variation thereof whenever I or other associates speak about troubles and the hindrances outside of our control that we face. The inconsistency in the scheduling IE: 1:00 1:45 1:15 2:00 2:15 2:45 3:00 3:15 3:30 3:45 3:50. Not getting my break on time I was told not too long ago all breaks need to happen for 7:00 but because of the lack of personnel consistently I always almost always have my break before or just right after 7:00 and then having to hurry back and be out by 11:30 the latest. Having to clean morning shifts dishes on top of the dishes that I have to clean for night shift when its my turn to do dishes. The floors make our feet hurt they messed up the renovations, it's less space in the entire deli all around. Sink in the kitchen is coming off the wall it's been like that for a while (Something I've seen happen to other associates including me to some degree) They don't want you to have a second job tell you they have a position and hours available then after you quit second job say to you "you have to show us how you work/you're work ethic" essentially to get what they were supposed to be offering.
reviews.pros: Finally offer full benefits and the stock options
reviews.summary: Almost no one /most who work in Deli don't like working in Deli you're not helping

reviews.advice: Your Managers are great people. Please continue to build them up.
reviews.cons: Publix can be a little old school, conservative, and stuffy. This is includes their payscale. I took a pay cut when I got hired as a contractor and then another pay cut when I got hired as a FTE. I did get a raise but it really wasn't what I was expecting. When I resigned for a higher paying job... They did offer me something to stay but it would not be until 3 months later.
reviews.pros: Publix treats their employees with respect and courtesy. They have good benefits, including tuition reimbursement and a stock program. They do screen their employees well, so no true bad apples. If you don't get along with someone.. you are the problem.
