reviews.advice:
Enable full-time remote work for employees based in Florida and extend the opportunity to work remotely to all states, irrespective of the presence of physical stores. This expansion is warranted by the absence of compelling reasons to restrict remote work to specific states.

Pay your employees more.
reviews.cons:
The absence of a rationale behind the prohibition on remote work for all employees remains perplexing. Specifically, while employees residing outside the state of Florida enjoy the flexibility of remote work, those within the state are inexplicably deprived of this option no matter how long they've been an employee. Consequently, individuals situated in areas such as Miami or the Keys are compelled to endure arduous commutes spanning 5-6 hours to the office twice weekly. Despite the passage of several months, no reason has been provided for this policy, suggesting its indefensibility.

The work environment fosters a culture characterized by intense competition, rapid pace, and toxicity. Employees frequently find themselves compelled to extend their work hours unnecessarily, without clear justification.

The company's approach to work lacks progressiveness, often appearing to move in a regressive direction. Development processes seem to lag, employing antiquated technologies and methodologies that contribute to sluggish progress and outdated practices.

Salaries are lower than the standard.
reviews.pros: One upside is gaining various skills to bolster your resume, although it might be tiring for some. But nothing else really here.

reviews.advice: What can I say…it is what it is
reviews.cons: However there is no short cuts. A degree is meaningless. Previous experience outside of grocery is meaningless. As long as you realize it’s a grocery business and that’s all it ever will be you’re fine. But they don’t really care if you have advanced skills or experience. Warren Buffet could work here and he’d just be a clerk and have to grind his way up with every other non-degreed schlub. They don’t need people who can do intermarket analysis, trend analysis, advanced business knowledge…they just need people who can stack boxes. That never changes. Once in management you’re still a stacker with a few additional responsibilities. It’s the same all the way up. Our store mgr still works boxes just like any other clerk.
reviews.pros:
This review is based on the retail side of the business. Corporate may be different but it is in Florida and I don’t live there.

This is a great company if you’re young, have no intention of going to college, have no marketable skills and want to work your way up over many years. Manager pay is on par with degreed positions. An asst dept mgr makes 60k, dept mgr 90k, ast store mgr 100k, and store mgr 150k.

reviews.advice:
In my time at Cisco I was a part of 3 different and distinct business units.  I enjoyed working for each of them and found that I was able to contribute value in every role I held.  What was painfully obvious to me was that the company is (or was) going through a bit of an identity crisis.  Consumer vs no consumer.  Social media vs no social media.  AWS like cloud offering vs Cisco cloud offering.

My advice to the leadership team is this.  We (Cisco for life) are *Cisco*.  *We* develop the standard for networking, infrastructure and cloud.  *We* are the industry leaders in our segment.  *We* stand a cut above and make no apologies for it.  Own being Cisco.  We don't need to compete with Apple, Facebook, Google, or Amazon.  *We* don't chase our competitors.  They chase us.
reviews.cons:
Cisco can be a machine.  There isn't an overt demand for all of your time (even the time outside of work) but more of a subtle, slight encouragement to always be on.  If you are not careful, you will live, sleep and eat Cisco 24x7.  Don't get me wrong, this is 100% a choice and if you are aware of this subtlety in the culture it is very easy to set appropriate boundaries that will be respected by the company and leadership team.

If you don't like where you are in Cisco or what you are working on, give it 6 months because you will be reorg'd.  While it is sometimes necessary to realign the company to meet competitive threats or market demands, reorganizing the company once a year is excessive and tends to create a distrusting environment for the rank and file which makes being a leader in the organize challenging.  There is a loss of momentum and motivation that occurs a few months before and a few months after reorgs so this leaves the company being effective at delivery and execution only about 70% of the time.

While Cisco attracts some bright, motivated people the truth of the matter is you are either cut out for the company and its culture or you're not.  If you aren't it will be painfully obvious to you and those around you.  Sadly as a leader it is hard to cut dead weight from the team and the only really accepted way is via layoffs, which is why the company reorgs once a year despite the company line about the reorgs.

employerResponses.response: Thank you for such a sincere review. We appreciate your feedback and hope you are pleased to see many of our "We Are Cisco" initiatives. Indeed, it can feel like Cisco frequently changes because it is part of our innovative culture. We thank you for your time with us and wish you the best.

reviews.pros:
I decided to wait almost a year after leaving the company before posting a review.  The primary reason being is that when you decide to leave an organization it is usually because there is something there that isn't aligning with you or what you want anymore however, the grass is not always greener someplace else.  This has been my experience.  In fact, the appreciation I have for the company has grown so much in my time away that I would really like to return.

The company truly believes on promoting within and as an employee you are encouraged to grow your career within the organization and learn new skills by taking different positions.  Benefits are excellent.  Cisco is the industry leader for networking and now cloud.  It is sometimes easy to forget that on the daily grind but you are working for the company that everyone looks to for network and infrastructure standards.  Culture within the business units managing product lines give you a lot of freedom to be innovative and creative in your approach to your role.  In most cases you are given a fair amount of autonomy and control over how you do your job provided that it aligns with the strategic objectives.  Benefits, 401k match, RSUs and ESPP are amazing.  And while the salaries aren't the top of the industry, they are above market and pretty competitive.

I was one of the apprentices for the Technical Consulting Engineer role. During the first two months as an Apprentice, Cisco has an organization and specialized team that prepares you for the role of a Technical Consulting Engineer, and to be honest they do a great job at it. 

Then you are placed into a team within the 5 specialized areas in TAC: Service Provider, Enterprise, Security, Datacenter, and Collaboration. Each of these areas have specific teams and you start to train in those specific technologies and slowly start taking cases of increasing difficulty on the mentorship of more senior engineer. My experience was good, however an individual's experience will depend upon the team that they arrive at.

The truth is It's a shock to come to realize you are being slowly brainwashed because the training is exactly like military basic training: long exhausting 12-13 hour days, few meal/beverage breaks, exist on few hours sleep, nightly required homework, bathroom breaks discouraged, frequent tests written and drills requiring 80 grade FAA and 90 grade overall average Delta AL passing grade, 7 weeks training 6 days a week. 3. One week of vacation is not enough time off for years 1-5 when we should be utilizing the travel benefits offered to share with our clients. reviews.advice: Delta needs to realize that it is a technology company. It is an airline but it is, without question, a technology company and should recognize employees can work remotely. We kept the airline running during COVID.
reviews.cons:
Delta is dead-set against remote work and too much outsourcing. In my case, I was employed for 15 years in my last stint, accompanied by 4+ from a prior run (20 total years). 
Pre-COVID, I had requested permission to move out of state to accommodate my special needs child's education. The state we were moving had the top rated school of its type in the US. I was given approval by my manager and director as well as HR so, I picked up everything and moved so that my child could get what they needed.
After COVID, my entire management team took a retirement package and a new group came in. I was advised that I would be required to work in the office 3 out of 5 days. I pointed out that I received approval and, without that I would never have moved. That did not matter as my new Director just flat didn't care. I reached out to my team's HR rep and he feigned ignorance of the situation, even though I had the emails. I contacted my prior manager and director, who verified but it did not matter. At that point, I was scrutinized and forced out. This, after 15 straight years of exemplary service with the reviews to back that up. I was an exceptional employee, nominated three times for the prestigious "Chairman's Club" (I have the pins to show). It did not matter.
So, after believing this was the last employer I ever had, I decided it was better to retire and take whatever benefits I could get and find my next "last employer".

I loved my work and my employer but it was obvious to me that Delta just didn't care. I was abandoned after 15 (20) years, working 70+ hours a week because I loved what I did but my family will always come first.

reviews.cons:
You'll be treated like the number you are. Don't let the corporate facade of happy people in happy places get you. You'll be a number who reports to another number who reports to another number and you'll all just be numbers together on a spreadsheet. 

When you're an outlier number.. you'll always have to explain why and you'll always be asked why you can't do more. 

These corporations do not care about you & they never will. They will tell you they do, they will throw parties, they will throw you money.. but in the end, when you no longer serve them.. you're out. 

If you work for another corporation writing estimates.. don't expense grass to be greener over here. If you're looking to get into a job for the first time.. I'd recommend you run. Go follow your passion instead. Don't make yourself comfortable with the salary & the benefits of any corporate job. You'll be stuck & next thing you know you've had an unhappy 25 years serving someone else.

-Great name and strong diversified businesses at the Group level (even though heavily skewed to personal lines, but this is changing)
-#2 player in the US surety market and #1 global surety
-Strong book of business and lots of talented people in the organization
-Strong training program and invests heavily in their younger talent
-Decent benefits, but overly generous maternity leave (16 weeks / 4 months paid).
-U.S. centric work culture and work ethics - challenging the status quo is welcomed and if there is something that is broken, management empowers people to fix it. Big on team culture - one of the best I've seen.

reviews.advice: Revamp your entire tech team procedures. You have maybe 100 techs supporting 10's of thousands of employees. Stress is not conducive to a good work environment. I'm so glad to be out of that place.
reviews.cons:
You start your day behind the 8-ball. The queue is already 3 digits deep and you have metrics to maintain. You can't get up to use the rest room or grab a drink if you need a minute to recompose yourself after a difficult call. You do that on your scheduled break times. It's call after call after call,

The building is massive so you have to sprint in order to get a snack or a drink AND use the restroom in the 15 minute time allotment. Your half hour lunch hardly feels like a break. And when you've busted your hump all month or all year, the appreciate they show is occasional pizza. It's very similar to unalive by a thousand cuts. It was such a high paced high stress position that permanent damage was done to my heart. I had to leave for my health. The pressure of the calls, the pressure of maintaining your metrics and your boss never going to bat for you if there's a dispute with a call really makes for a horrible job.

reviews.advice: Any advice falls on deaf ears, honestly. I would suggest listening to your people that way you may have less turn over.
reviews.cons:
One of my pro's was the flexible schedule, being able to work a half day of your choice was always a nice thought. However, your metrics and KPI are heavily dependent on you completing your work within a WEEK's timeframe. So, if you were overworked and had way too many claims, you most likely wouldn't want to take this half-day you worked hard for all week. 
High Turn over rate makes your job 100000x more difficult. You are punished for doing your job - if you have fewer claims, because you know how to close and manage your desktop - you will get a ridiculous amount of the remaining claims. This includes when other adjusters quit or leave the department. 
Your success definitely depends on your manager - a lot of things have to be "manager approved" and if your manager is lazy and/or behind on their work - your KPI will suffer. 
Also, training is definitely lacking and they'll tell you "ask your manager" a LOT in training. If you have a manager that doesn't want to help, you'll never feel like you know what you're doing. During my time, I had two different managers. One was horrible, and my work suffered. The other was actually helpful and cared about the team, and we succeeded. 
They'll tell you that there's a lot of opportunity for growth and movement in the company. There is for the people that are bad at their job. For example, someone on my team was close to getting fired because of their work. Instead of that, they somehow found a better position for them....with MORE pay. However, I was 'exceeding expectations" and it was like pulling teeth trying to move. A reason I ended up leaving was because I felt like they wanted to keep me in claims forever.

reviews.advice: Listen to your employees at every level. A happy workforce is a productive workforce, and a productive workforce makes for better quality work. The response to this has been unilaterally negative, and the silence from senior leaders had been deafening. My trust in management has been destroyed, and I am unsure if it will ever be restored.

reviews.advice: Figure out what the position is, what its core responsibilities are and what style of management for inventory is needed to provide best service at lowest cost.  Take better notes on conversations so that day-over-day reversals become rare, and when reversals are pointed out, stop gaslighting your teams.  Eliminate the sources of your culture of passive aggression and mean girl cliques -- it harms the team, even if it gets you information.
reviews.cons:
Training is a mess and often relies on peers over management
management is frequently at odds with itself over strategy, even down to the specifics of giving opposing directions to the same task
Best practices can vary day over day, making it impossible to truly understand directions. When questioning for clarity, "navigating the grey area" is used as a hammer
Role is talked about as a mainly buying and inventory management role, but in reality is an Item Analyst position with additional tasks in development, training, budget, data entry, and item and vendor management.
Overtime is expected to make up for the chronic understaffing of the department, but overtime is never discussed as a "must"
There are no real core or first come responsibilities, making prioritization difficult at best and an easy opening for management correction for not prioritizing "their way"
Agents are tasked with managing all their work independently, while also receiving minimal instruction, poor communication and frequent criticism for how task is being managed
Management reports there is an "open door policy" but are in 8am to 6pm meeting blocks most days. 
Management reports being open to change and new ideas but consistently refuses to accept or pursue them
Managerial level work is frequently put to non-managerial level associates, without special project designation or increased pay. These higher level tasks are always in addition to work load. The ability to make everything work determines whether or not an employee is eligible for promotion, further increasing workload and unspoken expectations of overtime.

Besides emails they use multiple applications to assign tasks, view reports etc which would be fine if when you looked at each of them you got the same information, but you don't. There is a lot of pressure as an Operations ASM to get Markdowns complete for example. Those reports are sometimes 48 hours behind so when you are asked for updates your DM is looking at numbers severely different from what you have accomplished in the week and you wont know if you "hit your numbers" until after your assigned hours are depleted and you will have to reassign hours but still run the business and not add any hours so something will suffer. 
In their off-price model, they say they never know what they will be sending on the trucks each week. They have an estimate however, they do not give you enough hours to process that estimate and you do not know what you are getting often times until the day the truck is supposed to get there. We were the last stop on the route which means the truck would leave 2 days prior to us receiving it, we still would not get the information until the truck arrived in some cases. The company would tell us that we would get a truck 2 days per week and all of a sudden there would be 4 trucks the next week, we set our schedules 3 weeks in advance so there simply was no possible way to get those pallets processed without stress and scrambling to get more hours approved and have associates accept those extra hours. Very unorganized and overwhelming

Have no loyalty if you really want to work there and enjoy the flight benefits - they are wonderful!

reviews.advice:
Listen to your field leaders. Make store teams feel valued not just by the DMs and RMs, but by the company overall. The last few videos and memos from our new CEO feel disconnected as if we at Chico’s FAS are a bug to be squashed. 

Chico’s stores utilizing the old store architecture need a refresh to compete with other brands and increase sales. It’s hard to sell high end when the store looks low end.

Dress code needs to allow for employees self expression.
reviews.cons:
Employees used to feel valued and heard by home office, until the company was acquired by Knitwell. Now, it’s all about the push of sales at any cost. 

The pay is low, especially for internal promotes. The company has a scale that is different for internal promoted versus someone hired outside the company. 

The discount is great when you hear it, but items even at the MADE discount are still incredibly high. The company should look into a deeper discount or even perks or contests where employees can win free product. 

Employees in the field no longer matter. There is no more work/life balance as stores were told they had to be open for Easter.

Diversity is few and far between. If you are a female with blonde hair, you will fit right in.

Benefits package is awful. Very low PTO, 4 weeks is the standard of pto in retail, but at Chico’s it is three until after 5 years. Also, unable to take PTO and bereavement leave consecutively in the event of a death out of state, where you would be needed to a settle family affairs.

Most stores have been open for years with no updates, not even a coat of paint. Stores are expected to operate like a high end boutique while the fitting room carpet is twenty years old.

reviews.pros:
The company culture fosters a sense of belonging and collaboration that is truly commendable. Here are a few reasons why I wholeheartedly give Best Buy a five-star rating:

Supportive Leadership: The leadership team at Best Buy is genuinely invested in the success and well-being of their employees. They provide clear guidance, mentorship, and support every step of the way.

Opportunities for Growth: Best Buy offers ample opportunities for career advancement and professional development. Whether it's through internal promotions, training programs, or educational assistance, the company encourages employees to reach their full potential.

Inclusive Environment: Diversity and inclusion are not just buzzwords at Best Buy; they are fundamental values embraced throughout the organization. I've always felt respected and valued for my unique contributions, regardless of my background or identity.

Work-Life Balance: Best Buy understands the importance of maintaining a healthy work-life balance. Flexible scheduling options, remote work opportunities (when applicable), and generous time-off policies ensure that employees can prioritize their personal lives without sacrificing their professional responsibilities.

Positive Atmosphere: The atmosphere at Best Buy is incredibly positive and uplifting. Whether it's celebrating successes, overcoming challenges together, or simply enjoying camaraderie with coworkers, there's always a sense of positivity and teamwork in the air.

Overall, my experience working at Best Buy has been nothing short of exceptional. I am grateful to be part of such a dynamic and supportive team, and I would highly recommend Best Buy to anyone seeking a rewarding career with a company that truly cares about its employees' success and happiness.

Set goals for your supervisors (you do this) but actually follow up with them when they miss. When productivity or carry over goals are missed the excuses is ALWAYS ‘high’ or ‘low’ volume.

In reality, one shift in a department carries that department while another clowns off and nothing is ever done about it. 

Do something about dirt bag supervisors. One Sup in particular yells at their coworkers and employees and is also the reason they all have to work 50 hour weeks. NOTHING is done about it.

Qualcomm has always been a beacon of innovation, attracting incredibly talented individuals and offering a wealth of supportive and groundbreaking projects. The environment used to be one where hard work and creativity were recognized and rewarded, contributing to a vibrant and productive culture.

Lately, however, the atmosphere has shifted. The rise in office politics has made it increasingly difficult for individual achievements to shine through. Remote work, while flexible, has introduced challenges in maintaining a healthy work-life balance, with late-night calls and meetings becoming the norm. This has made it tough to disconnect and recharge, impacting personal time and overall well-being.

Moreover, there’s a growing trend towards relocating projects to the India team and layoffs for cost-saving reasons. While understanding the financial aspects of business decisions, this move raises concerns about the long-term implications on quality and team dynamics.

reviews.cons:
Abbott embodies everything wrong with corporate culture today. From the outset, it was evident that this company operates within a toxic framework of misogyny, sexism, unfairness, ageism, and deceit. 

Firstly, it became clear that women at the corporate level were consistently marginalized and overlooked for promotions, despite their qualifications and hard work. The culture reeked of outdated, patriarchal attitudes that undermined the capabilities of female employees. It was appalling to witness such overt discrimination in this day and age.

Additionally, the pervasive sexism extended to everyday interactions. Male colleagues routinely spoke over their female counterparts in meetings, dismissing their ideas or attributing their success to male colleagues. The atmosphere was stifling for any woman seeking to advance or even be respected within the company.

The unfairness didn't end there. Ageism was rampant, with older employees sidelined and their contributions undervalued. The company's management seemed to prefer young, less experienced individuals, contributing to a toxic cycle of age discrimination that stifled diversity of thought and experience.

Moreover, Abbott is a haven of deceit. From misleading promises during recruitment to false performance evaluations, it became apparent that honesty was a foreign concept within the organization. Not surprising considering their major baby formula recall. Many employees, myself included, fell victim to a corporate facade that concealed the company's true intentions and operational methods.

In conclusion, Abbott not only fails its employees but also perpetuates harmful stereotypes and discriminatory practices. I strongly advise anyone considering a position at Abbott to think twice and seek employment elsewhere, in a company that values integrity, fairness, and respect for all individuals.

reviews.cons:
High Pressure: Sales roles at Oracle can be high-pressure environments, with aggressive sales targets and quotas to meet. This pressure to perform can lead to stress and burnout for some individuals.

Complex Sales Process: Selling Oracle products and services often involves navigating complex sales cycles and dealing with various stakeholders within client organizations. This complexity can make the sales process challenging and time-consuming.

Market Saturation: Oracle faces stiff competition in the technology market from other major players like Microsoft, AWS, Salesforce, SAP, & GCP. Competing in a saturated market can make it difficult to stand out and win new business, which in turn leads up to getting let go.
reviews.pros:
Compensation: Oracle typically offers competitive salaries and benefits, including commissions and bonuses for sales roles. High performers can earn significant income.

Training and Development: Oracle invests in training and development programs for its employees, especially those in sales roles. You may have access to resources and opportunities to enhance your skills and knowledge in sales techniques, technology, and products.

Career Growth: With its size and global presence, Oracle offers opportunities for career advancement. Successful sales professionals may have the chance to move up the ranks, take on leadership roles, or transition into other areas within the company.

Brand Reputation: Oracle is a well-established and respected company in the technology industry. Working for a reputable brand like Oracle can enhance your credibility and open doors for future career opportunities.

This is mind-boggling and leads to a massive brain drain throughout the year. One reason for this is because bonuses and raises are not a thing; you do not have a performance review and there are no career milestones to work towards (leading to, effectively, a dead-end job). Finally, most operation teams are seriously overworked. This is caused by people leaving (probably to seek more pay) and management "temporarily" giving their workload to someone else on the team while they "find a replacement." This never happens; I know some teams that shrank from 10 to 6 analysts and stayed like that for years. And no, we do not get more pay with these increased workloads (trust me, I've asked)

reviews.advice: Pay ALL your employees going rates and give them COLA, if not step increases. Oracle has too many chiefs who dream up strategies but take very poor care of the few employees left who implement them.
reviews.cons: In the 15+ years I was there, most of the time we had headcount and salary freezes. I started as a trainee, but despite more than qualifying was never given promised non-trainee status and $25k raise because of constant freezes. Getting re-hired for an open position took eight months because of freezes. To get a promotion I had to leave the company for a few years. The team I came back to never saw raises, not even COLA, and our team was paid noticeably under professional averages. I had some great managers, very admirable, who also weren’t getting raises. Constant posturing and direction changes for Wall Street but not much substance support. Frequent layoffs so no one felt secure. Toward the end of my tenure they removed support for a large percentage of paying customers who didn’t want to move to the Cloud (often for very good reasons). Oracle will take all of your time if you let it - it’s up to you to draw life boundaries and hope your manager will support you. It used to be a much more diverse place, but once the post-1990’s layoffs started it’s become whiter and more male.
reviews.pros: Smart, interesting colleagues. Opportunity to learn about excellent but very complex products. Great resume entry. Good insurance and stock buys options. reviews.cons:
1. Bonus Compensation is weak. There is only one annual bonus of $7,500. Most other firms have quarterly bonuses which are larger. Since TIAA doesn't have high expectation for sales there isn't opportunity to make large bonuses. Other firms are more sales oriented so you could make more money if you want to make sales. I am leaving the firm next month because of this main reason.

2. External movement is harder than competing firms. TIAA has a 18 month policy to be eligible to leave the National Contact Center Department. Most other firms allow for you to move outside the department after 12 months. I have been in the department for 12 months. My goal is to be in the Wealth Management Department. This is part of my reason for leaving next month.
reviews.pros:
1. Management is very good. TIAA doesn't pressure you to sell anything. TIAA cares about their employees and participants. Great coaching and training. There is opportunity to shadow other departments. 

2. Great work life balance. TIAA has flexible shifts from 8 am to 8 pm in 8 hours segments. You can temporarily change your shift or request partial PTO. No work required after you leave the office. 

3. Opportunity for lateral movement within 18 months in department. There are constantly new opening for positions within the department for Premier, Brokerage, National Support Line, Chat, and Mentoring.

reviews.advice: Disservice to impose 18-month restriction -- if there is a business need and someone has shown the necessary skills (metrics) as a high performer and has prior experience it makes no sense to penalize that person. This policy contradicts diversity and inclusion because good people that want to work and make a positive impact for TIAA leave for other employers instead of waiting the 18 months.
reviews.cons: Start off in an entry level call center (inbound phone) role regardless of your prior experience. You must STAY in this low paying role for 18 months before you are eligible to apply out of the phones for a real job.

reviews.advice: Rethink the archaic stack ranking system and look inwards to see current practices, then maybe you can start changing banking for good
reviews.cons:
I've got to be honest, working at Capital One has been a mixed bag. On one hand, the mission to change banking for good caught my attention and got me excited. On the other, the reality of their stack ranking system has been a tough pill to swallow. Even when you're doing everything right—meeting deadlines, delivering quality work—it feels like it doesn't matter unless you're in favor with the ranking system and your managers favorite. 

What really gets to me is seeing how everyone can be working hard to bring the bank forward, that would make their performance review “strong” but because of this system, some associates are still forced to the bottom or hit with a PIP. I’ve seen this not just in one part of the bank but I’ve experienced this in retail and commercial bank, and this has been happening more on commercial as attrition is at an all time high, managers play favorites and show little support to their team. It's disheartening, especially knowing that big names like Google, Microsoft, and GE have already moved past such outdated practices.

The constant manager turnover doesn't help, making it feel like you're always trying to prove yourself all over again. It's a lot, and it contradicts the whole "changing banking for good" message.

We really need to rethink this approach. If we're serious about making a difference in banking, it should start with how we're treated and evaluated. It's about time we supported the people putting in the work day in and day out.
reviews.pros: You will meet some amazing, talented and kind hearted people in this organization
reviews.summary: Time for a change at Capital One

reviews.advice: Stop hiring corporate careerists. But, only applying that to the ground floor isn't enough. It starts at the top. Also, Stack Ranking which I didn't even get the chance to mention, only adds to the toxic behavior and politics that's rampant throughout the company.
reviews.cons:
Blatant sycophant behavior would take place in front of my manager and director during stand-ups. Team members who were on the more genuine side would be quite uncomfortable. Meanwhile, the leaders would either turn their head, or enable them if they felt it was coming from an Associate who was savvy politically or had rising popularity within the department. (What was advantageous for the career climb was more important than substance.)

If you're mainly looking to apply yourself creatively or strategically you'll be disappointed. At times, I found that my manager (who was quite patronizing despite demonstrating limited ability) struggled to understand high-level brand concepts. It seemed like most of the department was designed not to build that unconventional 'What's in your Wallet' advertising you see in mass media (that's done by external ad agencies, btw)—but instead, are there simply to maintain the corporate brand's status quo. 

As a result, there's a lot of hive mind. And deviation from that poses the risk of coming off as threatening to management, who's mind is too far gone from the concept of any sort of individual imagination.
reviews.pros: A good brand to have on your resume. You'll get the chance to see how a Fortune 100 brand builds their marketing. Good pay and benefits. Work life balance is great.

reviews.advice: Revamp your performance review process.  It's currently horrible and does NOT lead to good work/life balance as the review tries to take everything everyone does into consideration, not just what their job description covers.  This includes adding things that have nothing to do with the company (like volunteer work) to reviews as people try to outdo each other.
reviews.cons:
Their twice a year performance review process is horrible for outsiders joining. You will be compared against everyone with the same role in your org and they don't account for how long you've been at the company. 12% of employees in each role must be put in the poor performance bucket every review period. 
Despite the claim of a good work/life balance, I have not seen that in the tech teams at Capital One, particularly at the team lead and above positions. It's somewhat of a cutthroat environment in my opinion for the reviews. They've also become hostile to fully remote positions.

reviews.advice:
Improve the talent management process so high performers are not arbitrarily treated as underperforming 

Enable employees to apply their talents where they can succeed and to move to another role if they are in a role that makes no sense

If you are going to lay off employees, own it instead of hiding behind strategic changes or performance issues
reviews.cons:
Astonishingly bad talent management, often putting people into roles that they are not qualified for such as placing non technical people in technical roles

Unpredictable performance levels that often have little to do with actual performance

The misuse of talent tied to the bizarre performance ranking system combine to force top talent into situations where they cannot succeed and are penalized financially and in their career progression 

Once someone is caught in this position and get a negative review, they are not able to rotate out until they do succeed, which traps employees in a rigid no-win situation when a new assignment would resolve the issue

All of the above combine into a method of putting employees onto a PIP and then laying them off without saying that it is a layoff, adding in legalese that puts the onus on the employee for choosing not to take reasonable steps to improve using the PIP

The PIP is treated as an acknowledgement of poor performance and a choice not to improve rather than what it is, an opportunity to get severance and escape a bad situation

reviews.advice: Company culture has fallen off a cliff within the last year. Ditch stack ranking, it creates perverse incentives and makes the work environment unenjoyable and draining.
reviews.cons:
Capital One practices stack ranking. This was somewhat relaxed during the pandemic, but the low performance bucket was as high as 15-20% at 2023 mid year. They seem to have historically used this as a mechanism to lay people off without having the negative press that accompanies it. Read other reviews to get a sense of what kind of behavior this incentivizes and what sort of culture it creates. If you join as a new employee you will be at a disadvantage compared to those who have been there for a while/have connections within their organization. Even if it does not immediately worry you, I have seen driven, talented engineers driven out of the company because eventually someone in their upper management disliked them.

There's definitely a fake nice culture, people will be friendly but knives come out behind closed doors during performance calibrations.

A big source of the company's revenue (credit card interest) comes from people trapping themselves in debt. It doesn't feel great to contribute to that.

reviews.cons:
Here is the reality of being a machine learning engineer at C1, despite all the social media marketing: you are rebuilding a tool that readily exists in commercial and open-source projects, which no one else uses within the company, except the MLEs who are building it, in order to justify continuing to build it.

At the end of the day, you are reproducing an overengineered solution, which is also (in-part) intended to remove the need for your role (and data scientists). Modeling experience is largely non-existent since your time is best spent reinventing the wheel,

Furthermore, you are also going to end up in effectively the only MLE org within the company, which also has one of the worst happiness and management cultures within all of Capital One. Prepare to spend everyday working with mostly arrogant and unpleasant (to put it mildly) managers, who lack tech experience in many instances, while privately commiserating with coworkers in Slack. If you have experience elsewhere, you will be amazed to see such joyless teams.

The whole RTO process is stupid. They don't care anymore for the work you do, they care about you coming in for x amount of hours. You can literally sit and do nothing for 2 days a week, be lazy and watch YouTube, and Capital One will be happy that you're in the office.
The performance review ladder is garbage, there's literally no room for growth. The bar keeps getting raised every year, and it's gotten to the point of doing an insane amount of work, and then your leaders saying "That's great, but you can do more" - I literally don't have the capacity to sell my soul.
I used to recommend this place for friends to work at, but after 2023, not anymore.

reviews.advice: Start taking care of the stores and associates we have before expanding and continuing to open more stores. In 4 and 1/2 years as a store manager with DG I've seen very little to no positive change in day to day operations and PLEASE STOP micro-managing EVERYTHING. If the majority of company communication transpires through text messaging and conference calls then shouldn't the company compensate store managers in some fashion for their cellphone costs ?
reviews.cons: How can a company truly justify cramming half a million dollars worth of merchandise into a building less than 10,000 Sq. FT. In size and continue sending more and more every week without having issues with where to put all of it. Send what's needed for the store, not what the warehouse has an over abundance of. Update systems to control freight flow through POS and rate of sale. Work/life balance is completely non-existent working for DG. I currently operate my store with myself, an ASM, and 1 full-time LSA because we can't get applicants or they can't pass the background check for hiring especially in smaller communities. Trucks show up whenever they like so scheduling deliveries is a waste of time. You're expected to drop everything and get that truck taken care of regardless of what's happening in your building. We talk alot about shrink and safety concerns for our associates and customers but continue to overstock stores with merchandise that can't be properly displayed in the spaces provided.

It was a complete disaster. Should’ve been shut down. But I worked open to close and over night all night and had the store looking pristine. Set realistic expectations for the employees you have. I loved my store and colleagues and unfortunately seeing my own managers and higher ups suffer physical ailments from the amount of stress they were under made me lose hope in anything improving. Listen to the people manning your stores, we do know how to improve the things you swear we know nothing about. Who else would be an expert besides those interacting with customers and working the sales floor? The lack of respect for employees is quite disappointing considering I met many people who did a tremendous amount of work and received no recognition for their effort. Sacrificing time with our families, non existing social lives, no energy left at the end of the work week to do much else. There's no empathy, no soul to this company. Just money, work, numbers.
reviews.cons: Company regularly cuts hours for entire store if sales are not on par with what they want. Lots of turnover. Many issues with working conditions. Unrealistic expectations for employees. reviews.advice: Some key advice for management is to stop playing favorites and handing key accounts/books of business to certain people while disregarding the rest of the team. Hold everyone to the same standards, some people are held to strict call standards where as others are not. The favoritism has to end, selective accountability also needs to stop. And lastly, be more accurate when explaining to a new hire what the OTE actually is. Stop the micromanagement.
reviews.cons:
My time on the ADR team at Arrow has been overshadowed by issues of inconsistent Mid-Market account distribution, leading to demoralizing favoritism. Despite C-level praise, raises remain elusive, forcing many to juggle two jobs. The absence of a hybrid schedule for ADRs, unlike C-levels, adds financial strain due to gas prices. With low base pay and unequal commission opportunities, transparent policies and proactive leadership action are essential for a fair and collaborative work environment.

1. Favoritism: Discrepancies in account distribution lead to some enjoying lucrative opportunities while others struggle without making commissions.
2. Selective Accountability: Varying standards for call metrics create a sense of inequality among team members.
3. OTE Discrepancy: The disparity between promised and actual earnings is a widespread concern.
4. Resistance to Feedback: Efforts to provide constructive feedback are met with resistance.
Addressing these issues, particularly favoritism, and implementing transparent policies are crucial steps towards creating a more equitable and supportive work environment.
