reviews.cons: Working in financial services is hard! It’s fast paced as an environment, that’s either your thing or it’s not. Main con is honestly seeing all the things people say about this company that are so far from true and lowkey wild (starting to drive me crazy) financial advising is hard-no your not trying to sell ur friends and family, that’s dumb (why would that be a fortune 100 companies marketing strategy like what??) and literally is not what is taught in the office, yes this role is tough, if it wasn’t everyone would do it cause you make good money, make impact, and have a lot of freedom, but that takes time to build. Pls people get off Reddit-and have some critical thinking skills.
reviews.pros: I have loved my experience at NM, people genuinely want to see you succeed, there is great growth and development opportunities. In the OC offices you will see people will stay for a long time because they genuinely like and believe in the company which is really cool. A lot of support for training development and licensing from CA L&H to securities licensing, even for staff roles. It’s impressive being around really smart people who work really hard, pushes you to be better. Great office culture promotes growth from within and will also work with people to place/move them to roles that would better suit their skill sets. Really great atmosphere to really become financially literate as well. There is so much helpful development to learn the ins and outs of finance.

reviews.cons:
Nothing is set up to make it smooth from start to finish.
Entirely too many websites and applications.
Unnecessarily complicated.
Have a quick question....there are no quick or easy answers.
Phone wait times of 20 to 90 minutes at times...if they even answer...if you don't get hung up on..if they don't let them department go early with no warning and if all repa aren't in a department wide meeting.
Even at it's best....it's awful.
Tech support...flip a coin.
Online support? Ha. You can spend 20 minutes online trying to find the answer so you don't have to call....and you have to end up calling anyway.
Easy to screw up an application...they don't try and prevent it.
Want an answer before you proceed? Good luck. The NM way is...make it hard to do it right...reject when it's wrong...then tell the AFR...you did it wrong. You should have done it this other way....but we won't tell you beforehand.... we'll tell you afterwards.
reviews.pros: Rare situations when things work exactly how they're supposed to, then is good.
reviews.summary: This company DOES...NOT...CARE. Irrelevant how much of your time it wastes

reviews.cons: Lot of red tape, resistance to change. Pretty ordinary engineering craft. Goals are always created conservative. Heavy meeting culture. Lot of roles in the organization lack accountability. Because they have engineering manager roles at much early stage in the ladder which pushes people into people leadership, it sets lot of teams for failures. These candidates hardly may have spent 3-4 years in hands-on development before they became managers and are living life in people leadership. They can hardly offer good technical leadership.
reviews.pros: Strong financials, Good track record of paying bonuses to employee beyond target for several years. Good opportunities to learn if you are a junior employee or if you are planning to stay in the company for a very longtime. Company values Subject Matter Experts who knows the internals of the company and platforms lot more than skill and industry knowledge. So you will thrive if you plan to to live longer here.
reviews.summary: A decent place if you are not a remote employee

reviews.advice: Management very good overall.  Perhaps more focus on communication and relationships, but overall they care about what they do and want everyone to succeed.
reviews.cons: You need to have the right kind of personality, you get told no a lot, really have to be strong and independent to make it happen. Management makes success sound a lot easier than it really is.
reviews.pros: Lots of good learning opportunities, meet a lot of great people, high income potential.
reviews.summary: Great opportunity if you're willing to do the work.

reviews.advice: Work with the City of Milwaukee and try to resolve some of the concerns employees have about the commute. It became apparent how unsavory commutes are when you are forced to spend an hour or more in traffic dealing with other drivers and hazards.
reviews.cons: The focus is on returning everyone to downtown location where public transportation options are limited and parking is expensive and not guaranteed. Work from home took a stellar effort by employees to make it work, and productivity increased. In return, the company wants to severely limit that option and require return to office despite there being no real necessity for them to physically be there.
reviews.pros: Wonderful coworkers, real ability to influence changes and improvements. Company has a fantastic moral direction.
reviews.summary: Trying to return to the old days

reviews.cons: You will get out of this career what you put into it. They have a proven track on how to be successful, but you have to follow it.
reviews.pros: The best company in the comprehensive planning space to be with. Has the greatest financial strength & an open architecture on the insurance & investment side of the contract.

reviews.advice: NM used to do the right thing but many leaders who have been with the company less than 5 years are only there for themselves.  Stopped hiring remote workers.   No advancement is you are remote.
reviews.cons: Incompetent middle line leadership who think they know everything but don’t. Leaders only out for themselves.
reviews.pros: What the company does really impacts people’s lives for good

reviews.cons: You will get out of this career what you put into it. They have a proven track on how to be successful, but you have to follow it.
reviews.pros: The best company in the comprehensive planning space to be with. Has the greatest financial strength & an open architecture on the insurance & investment side of the contract.

reviews.advice: Respect the staff.
reviews.cons: Separate rules from home office. Incentives and benefits vary by the person in charge of your location. Leadership is a hit or miss. Favoritism is a big problem.
reviews.pros: You can work closely with those in the office and help with growth.

reviews.advice: let business be business and stop pursuing the current trends of liberal politics and social agendas
reviews.cons: going more woke, continuing to be more liberal and promoting liberal policies and agendas
reviews.pros: large company with lots of support for training and technology

reviews.cons: It really is not a place for someone that does not have a large network of professionals. Working there without a network is almost pointless
reviews.pros: It was a nice environment and the training is interesting

reviews.cons: The salary is in the lower half of the industry spectrum for change management. It is also locked in and no one gets more than a 2-3% raise max in the same role.
reviews.pros: NM really does take care of their people with abundant opportunities for internal growth, budgets for professional in improvement, and lots of margin for family or personal needs. Generous bonus and decent healthcare
reviews.summary: Lots of workplace perks, lower salary

reviews.cons: The only downside I can share is that while you are expected to be an "employee" of Northwestern mutual (even though you contract yourself through this company) there are costs to running the business. The office takes some of what you make and also expects you to pay for things like your computer, the rental of your office, parking, etc. making it hard to enjoy a work/life balance.
reviews.pros: Great place for the entrepreneurial spirit. Sense of community, motivation, and friendly competition while everyone is willing to help when needed. No maximum on potential income to be made. Very good benefits available to everyone that works here. A place you can be yourself and really put in the work to grow as an advisor and person.

reviews.cons: Can get stressful at times when the workload increases
reviews.pros: Pay is good for the level of experience and day-to-day duties

reviews.cons: This has gotten a lot better, but there was a point when I was getting different answers from different Home Office employees within the same departments. I didn't always feel confident that I had the right answer, which was difficult especially when the questions I had came from clients.
reviews.pros: I work directly for a WMA, and he & our team are great - which makes a huge impact on my perspective. If we have any questions, our Home Office is there to assist and for the most part, they have been helpful.
reviews.summary: Good company to work for, room for improvement though

reviews.cons: Most work feels meaningless since it gets deprioritized and rarely built
reviews.pros: People are great. Very helpful. Work/life balance is usually right.
reviews.summary: Good people in a slow-moving company

reviews.cons: None at this time currently
reviews.pros:
Ability to advance
No micromanagement
Great coworkers 
Helpful and positive managers

reviews.advice: Management should continue to stay visible, approachable and transparent. Lead through example and provide mentorship opportunities as the experience can be priceless.
reviews.cons: A very large company - over 30,000 employees. Typically larger companies are harder to navigate.
reviews.pros: I have been with the company for over 25 years and have had great leaders who support my career through mentorship, professional development and just being transparent on what is expected. There are so many different paths you can take at this company; as a result, so many opportunities available if interested. Management is always looking for "tomorrows' leaders" and supports this through development programs. I can't say enough about my experience at Travelers.
reviews.summary: Travelers is a great place to work!

reviews.advice: Look inward and hold business areas equally accountable for execution of defined objectives.  Even profit centers can find efficiencies and can contribute to profitable growth
reviews.cons: Significant hierarchical bias internally that severely limits employee satisfaction and business success; patriarchal approach to recognizing accomplishments; lack of accountability for Underwriting group creates downstream issues with all partner business areas (operations, audit, risk control) Tremendous culture of groupthink and bias not only against Operations employees but also within Operations ranks; Individual employee value is diminished due to political objectives; significant absence of servant leadership despite constant rhetoric.  Yes I have chosen to stay for 20 years due to life circumstances but the company is swiftly losing good employees and is limiting their opportunities for growth by considering Underwriting to be untouchable and beyond reproach and not valuing the significant contributions of Operations functions.  Constant speeches about partnership and collective voice and appreciation for contributions which are surface without follow through in compensation or meaningful recognition; Press releases regarding billions of dollars of profit with biased compensation to UW and minimal allocation to Operations; constant focus on efficiencies without looking at the biggest drain on corporate resource which is the ineffectiveness and lack of adherence of underwriting to established job requirements.  If you are in Underwriting it’s a fantastic experience - do the bare minimum, make excuses and never get fired.  Other business areas not so much.
reviews.pros: Stable employment, great benefits, some (not all) very strong leaders, sound underwriting and marketing business decisions that promote company growth; commitment to diversity for major protected classes

reviews.advice: Underwriters are not machines and not inclined to quote marginal business or lines that don't make sense because it's the nature of the position.  The company expects us to quote non-stop.  We are looked at in terms of the quote ratio and not as individuals on the front line of protecting the company.  Open up more jobs in the satellite offices (non-home office and business center).
reviews.cons: Difficult to move around in UW if not part of UPDP training. These folks definitely are given priority. Satellite offices have half to two thirds less job postings available than business centers or home office locations. Very opaque bonus system compared to competitors. Extreme open seating office enviro. Primary metric is quote ratio so the expectation is to quote crappy business just priced very high to not write or quote lines you don't have a chance of writing bc we can't offer a total acct solution.
reviews.pros: The best UW company out there. So many resources to learn. Their Industry Leads invest alot in developing info for UW decision making. Smaller satellite hubs have mgmt that is more flexilbe vs home office or business center hubs. Good benefits and pension plan available.
reviews.summary: We are just a number but a number with decent benefits and pay.

reviews.advice: Other than additional flexibility with the office policy without having to go through HR (who does seem to approve a fair amount of accommodations) I don't have any recommendations at this time. Maybe having an office buddy with the same in office days to have more of a sense of belonging-- no one has been mean or rude or anything less than pleasant but there's still a feeling of lacking true belonging when I'm in my home office-- traveling to see my team every 10-ish weeks I have a completely different experience.
reviews.cons: The only downside I've seen so far is Travelers' office policy. I have a hybrid arrangement. My business partners are located in a different state and my teammates are in additional other states so I come into the office 3 days a week to talk to them with headphones in via a computer screen. The other two days are the same except I'm at home and don't have headphones. The role was hybrid and I agreed to the work arrangement and I don't mind upholding it, but it just doesn't make a lot of sense. It almost feels more lonely going into an office where there's literally no one who I work with or who is going to use the niche product I'm building. I can exchange pleasantries but not really develop deeper working relationships.
reviews.pros:
I have highly qualified and capable coworkers- I'd put the developers on my team at the same level as the big Tech companies.
Competitive benefits that match or exceed what I have seen for similar experience and skills in my geographical area.
Investment in coaches to ensure that skills are maintained and grown, the coaches that I have interacted with are part of the reason that I accepted a position at Travelers and why I've had great early success and feel I'm on a solid trajectory.

reviews.advice: Travelers switched from a 5 scale to a 3 scale in rating employees almost a decade ago. Management has said almost verbatim, as well as subtly, employees need to walk on water to exceed expectations. Unless the second coming works in a cube somewhere, management doesn't believe employees exceed expectations which does not bode well for morale.
reviews.cons: All appearances the C Suite grows, likely getting large bonuses for the few while the work is done on the backs of the many. CEO sends an email early 2024, banner year, but didn't hit some metrics so bonuses stagnant, shrinking as more are eligible. Merit increases also down, not keeping up with inflation or even the rate increases on Travelers issued policies. Transparency would be showing the C Suite's bonus are down or sacrificed for the working class.
reviews.pros: Good benefits to take care of you and your family. Decent amount of PTO, however behind many other industry peers of equal size and impact.

reviews.cons: If I were to suggest any improvements to working at Travelers, it would be to develop more efficient internal approval processes and/or project timelines. Things move a bit slower than I'd like, but that is also the nature of the corporate world. When things are on a such a large stage, they need to be done right!
reviews.pros: Coming from a much smaller employer prior to Travelers, I remember how nervous I was to dive head first into the corporate world. I was so pleasantly surprised with Travelers. From the moment I started, I knew I could bring my authentic self into work each day. My voice was heard, my ideas were amplified, my personal story was honored and my career journey was fully encouraged. I have grown so much throughout my 5 years, both professionally and personally. I have had such supportive leadership here. Each time I have brought professional development opportunities to them, I have received full support to pursue them. The benefits have been a blessing to me and my family. If anyone was looking into working at Travelers, I would tell them to go for it! There are so many different career paths - something for everyone.
reviews.summary: 5 years in, many more to go!

reviews.advice: Take off the rose colored glasses and find out why the best and brightest candidates are not looking at insurance as a long term career.   Be more flexible and willing to embrace new ideas for accomplishing the same goals.
reviews.cons:
They seem to have difficulty hiring experienced employees due to their insistence on having them work in an office. Many of the newest hires quit after they get some experience and move on to a better paying job where they can work remotely. They have done a poor job, in my opinion, with planning for the future as it relates to staffing—-many employees are getting close to retirement, and claim management doesn’t seem to appeal much to the 
Gen Z’ers. It seems like you are always having to do extra work for a vacancy or because a new, inexperienced worker is training or job shadowing and not capable of handling a workload. It’s also a company where you are rewarded for hard work and long hours with more assignments and longer hours. It used to be a company that seemed to pay more than the competition, but I’m not sure that is the case any longer.
reviews.pros: Best things: Stable company, layoffs are rare, good amount of PTO.

reviews.cons: Behind the curve for auditing platform, scattered resources (difficult to locate), high turnover, expectation of balance between quality and quantity is unreasonable (Reviewers are more power hungry vs. helpful), high level management/officers seem very disconnected from low level employee reality, company is more concerned with their outward image than their employees
reviews.pros: Decent benefits, great training for all auditors (beginners & experienced), helpful direct management

reviews.advice: EMPATHY. Learn this. Not everyone can afford to pay 400 dollars up front for licensing. Sometimes people need to work from home, and they shouldn't be punished for it. Honestly, do better.
reviews.cons: EMPATHY: Direct manager lack empathy. For example. You are sick and need to work from home. Many managers will make you stay the next week and extra day in office. Becoming an adjuster can cost $400+ out of pocket until they reimburse you. Older managers are very out of touch. Insurance discount for employees is horrible. Travelers does not consider cost of living with raises. home day and Internet goes out? Forced to go to office, even if you only have one car for your family.
reviews.pros: Great pay and a hard but rewarding job. Benefits and PTO is pretty good plus a pension. Training is good and you do have opportunities at this company.

reviews.advice: New employees need a better training program.  Learning buy computer tutorials is not training.  A learning environment centered around discussions, handling mock claims, better coverage trainers would be helpful.  Being thrown into handling a claim you do not know how to work is not good for the organization or employee.
reviews.cons: Dated computer system, poor leadership, poor training, schedule is not flexible even though they tell you it is.
reviews.pros: Great benefits, nice co-workers, decent starting wage.

reviews.advice: Listen to your adjusters. They’re your bread and butter. If you knew how many people want out, you’d be panicking.
reviews.cons: Being an outside rep in the Houston office was a mess. The territory system was all kinds of jacked up. One employee was all over the Houston territory which stretched from south of Waco to Galveston. Claim load makes no sense because it isn’t proportional despite territories not really mattering like they should. I was working well over 40 hours a week and still felt behind. This job destroyed my work/life balance and I’m still trying to put it together several months after leaving.
reviews.pros: Competitive pay, decent benefits, generally supportive co-workers.

reviews.advice: I know corporate doesn't really listen to management, it would be great if each hub had more local control. Below VP management has to tow the line for auto product's bizarre program implementation instructions that normally appear to be half thought out. The people grading national reviews should be graded on their quality just as everyone else is, many FTM jobs would probably open up.
reviews.cons: Quota, Program organization, Auto Product Department. The one role appraiser title has turned in to one person audit it all rather than celebrating the core knowledge needed for vehicle systems.
reviews.pros: Friendliness of management, nice coworkers. Very flexible when it comes to family life.

reviews.cons: Compensation is not comparable with the market - about a $20K-$40K range for same AE position with other carriers.
reviews.pros: Worked on the Claims side and now in Underwriting. Culture between Claim and Underwriting is night and day. In Underwriting I am treated as an adult with a great team and flexible work/life balance. From the Director to upper Management everyone is supportive and makes me feel valued. Love the "work hard, play hard" mentality.

reviews.advice: Understand that times have changed. The pandemic has proven that things can work outside of the normal brick and morter location and working remotely works better for some people.
reviews.cons:
The lack of flexibility with the return to office policy is constricting. Desk "hoteling" is a little strange in a post pandemic environment.
Old school thought process for management can hinder projects on occasion.
reviews.pros:
I've just hit my ten year mark with the company. I've been able to do a lot within my multiple roles including travelling, representing the company facing new clients, being the face of training for multiple new hire classes, and help to onboard new facilitators. 

I say all of this to make the point that the opportunities are there...if you are willing to work for them. State your goals and find your path early and management will help you get there.

Pay is fair and competitive, PTO is plentiful, other benefits are available and easy to access.
reviews.summary: Great company for growth...if you're willing to work for it.

reviews.advice: NA
reviews.cons: No recognization for the work
reviews.pros: Lot of flexibility and work life balance

reviews.cons:
-Parking can be pricey.
-Departments can be slow to email responses.
reviews.pros:
-Everyone here is very friendly. 
-There are plenty of people to reach out to if you need help. The workstations are high quality. 
-Most are offered a 3 days in office 2 days from home work schedule
-Flexible work schedule

reviews.cons: Corporate structure. Too many meetings
reviews.pros: Flexibility, diversity, benefits and good management

reviews.advice: Meh
reviews.cons:
Everyone is very friendly here but it feels like a high school. If I have to hear the word “collaboration” one more time….  This might be for some people but it wasn’t for me. Also why enforce being in the office 3x for? Anyway… be prepared to hear how lucky you are to work at travelers for the rest of your time here. From an underwriting standpoint, referrals can become tedious and don’t even get me started on quarterly file audits. Toooo much stress on new business numbers and agency calls rather than how your entire book looks. Also, what is the point of spending so much on salesforce when NO ONE is going to use it or finds it useful? This company definitely rewards loyalty over anything else. It doesn't matter how well you did this year or last year. Are you going to be here for the next 10 years? 
All in all, travelers was a good experience.  I learned a lot. Maybe I'll apply back for an RUO position in the future so I can decline everything that comes my way. Btw I heard they started checking badge swipes. We stan a company who micro manages employees…..... not
reviews.pros: Travelers is definitely top in the industry for development and growth and no doubt one of the best places for an early underwriter career. They also baby you a LOT. I could probably not do anything for the next 5 years and they wouldnt care lol. Your experience also varies wildly by your LOB and manager. Travelers also has superior CRM and underwriting systems and now salesforce. Upper management is all filled with highly knowledgeable people and I’m happy I was able to learn from them.

reviews.advice: Continue to be engaged and focused on your teams
reviews.cons: People stay a long time at Travelers so sometimes moving to another position can take longer than you would like.
reviews.pros: Opportunities for growth, company culture, work/life balance, financially stable, care about their people (including agents, vendors and customers), focused on training & self development

reviews.cons: Good environment to work in
reviews.pros: Leadership needs some more training

reviews.advice:
Value your employees. We have a major problem with retention of talented employees because they quickly learn that they are not valued here.

Also, please make sure that the people chosen to run your software projects understand that constantly adding "new features" is not helpful if the code doesn't actually work.
reviews.cons:
No opportunity for growth. Annual raises are less than inflation and promotions are unlikely, regardless of effort put in.

Benefits are garbage. Low-deductible plan costs too much to make financial sense, and the medium deductible plan is like not having insurance at all for a significant part of the year. Even after going through the deductible, it's hard to get insurance to cover anything.

Full Return to Office where your coworkers get you sick + No sick leave (must use PTO) + Insurance that won't pay for your doctor visits and medication when you're sick. Quite the combination.

Lead on my current project is not a software engineer, and it shows. Most of the work I did last year was fixing his very avoidable mistakes.

Vesting period for employer contributions to 401(k) is 3 years, with no partial vesting. So unless you get lucky with a position that will keep you happy for three years, you get nothing.
reviews.pros:
Laid-back workplace
Good job security (notwithstanding layoffs in California)
reviews.summary: Stable employment, but much to be desired.

reviews.advice:
1. The bureaucracy beast has gotten very out of hand, cut it back. Save your businesses and take some risk before you have some really bad quarters.
2. Burnout is a very big problem at NG. Insane deadlines, poor planning, constant executive briefings, and all the meetings-about-meetings need to stop.
reviews.cons:
NG senior leadership has been clearing house in the upper ranks and implementing lots of new unhelpful policies that make it very hard to get things done. Lots of upset customers. Reams of charts.
Teams and Managers are very overworked and burning out hard with RTO and all the other policy changes.
Bonus Plan is measley and annual increases are standard 2-4% per year.
reviews.pros: Good Pay, 9/80 work schedule. Great coworkers, very smart people. Interesting and meaningful work. Awesome front line managers in my dept.

reviews.advice: Take company culture seriously or employee turnover will keep increasing. It's very simple - hire good people and fire the toxic ones.
reviews.cons: Second team I joined was terrible and gave me lasting work trauma. Team lead didn't know how to manage people and was set in his ways (i.e. stuck with processes he was comfortable with, even though they were unproductive). Senior SWE I worked with was a toxic micromanager (even though he wasn't even a manager lol) that did whatever he could to kiss up to the team lead, even if that meant throwing us younger SWEs under the bus. Unfortunately leadership didn't take this problem seriously and when a fellow SWE and the senior SWE got into a conflict, leadership simply decided to move fellow SWE to a new team instead of resolving the root of the problem, which was the senior SWE. Other fellow SWEs eventually left the team (I'm sure you can probably guess why) and I was left alone with all the work and the ever-toxic senior SWE. Eventually found out that turnover rate on this team was extremely high, go figure, and I quit the job. I come to work to do my job and get paid, not play office politics and deal with toxic people. We all have other things going on in our lives and the last thing we should have to worry about is toxicity in the workplace.
reviews.pros: First team I joined was great. Team was nice and helpful and my manager was very empathetic and understanding.
reviews.summary: What's the key to a happy and productive work life? THE PEOPLE.

reviews.advice:
Ensure all employees are treated fairly and respectfully. Maintain composure even if you disagree with their views, as losing your temper can hinder open communication and have a negative impact. Address individuals with persistent misconduct promptly; it’s unjust to those who work diligently and strive to fulfill their responsibilities.

Pay employees fairly, if they are taking on more responsibilities they should be fairly compensated!
reviews.cons:
NGC at BWI may not be ideal for employment. Success hinges on managerial belief and support, which has recently been lacking, especially in addressing personnel issues. The company often ignores misconduct, failing to take corrective measures depending on the individual. Favoritism and bias are prevalent in handling grievances. Seek employment with a company that values equality and ensures management and HR effectively address issues and support you.
Having more responsibilities doesn’t necessarily mean earning higher pay. Often, individuals take on highly stressful roles or managerial positions with additional program facing duties without receiving extra compensation, which is very backwards.
reviews.pros: Depends on the program you support but generally speaking flexibility is good.
reviews.summary: Find a better place to work

reviews.advice: Pay attention to your smaller, more remote teams. They care nothing about the company edicts. They do as they please because nobody's looking.
reviews.cons:
Less than competent low-level management, for a technical company there is a high level of fear when it comes to embracing newer technologies.
Management positions and tasks are handed to people that the company feels most comfortable with. There is many an MBA leading technical teams, inserting their incorrect technical knowledge , which often slows down or derails projects; but hey, what can you do they're in charge. 
Those who have been around for a while are put in leadership positions, even though their technologically out of touch, I remember recently explaining how headphone jacks have changed and why the customers headsets would not work with the machines we've installed.

Too old school: 
Instead of using modern software, multi-million dollar projects are tracked in Excel. 
Everything is documented to an extensive degree, to the point that documentation takes months and implementation can take half of that. That may work for this company, but if you leave and go elsewhere like Microsoft or Google they will laugh out of an interview with such slow throughput.
In summary, they are like flip phone makers that sell their wares to senior citizens; not cutting action but have a fan base, but when that fan base dies....
reviews.pros: Great starter company to spring board off of using their name.

reviews.advice: Northrop Grumman has miles of modernization to achieve. Between balanced classified and unclassified tasking, and revolutionized communication habits, a lot needs to be done to make this work place represent the painting of industry excellence it projects. Hire more people who know how to talk to people. Prioritize this site. Stop giving Baltimore all the "real work" and neglecting the site. Really foster growth relationships with your employees, not just 15 minute conversations. There is such a severe allergy to "micromanaging" at this company that it seems like no management or even basic communication is performed.
reviews.cons:
Coworkers are unsocialized and unprofessional
Tasking is extremely slow
Communication is extremely poor
advertises flexible work environment but reality is largely not the case
No paper towel in the women's bathrooms but there is in the men's bathrooms
There is such a severe allergy to "micromanaging" at this company that it seems like no management or even basic communication is performed.
reviews.pros:
Competitive pay, and okay benefits
Work life balance is excellent due to 9/80 schedule and classified nature of majority of the work

reviews.advice: While we have some of the smartest, nicest senior management who truly care about their workforce, the lower level managers (not all, of course) tend to overwork the junior level engineers or the super dedicated worker who cannot say "no" in hopes of getting a promotion.
reviews.cons:
Sr. Principal/Staff level engineering positions are very competitive and hard to get here...more so than in other locations like Virginia or even Huntsville, so unless you came in at that level from another office or just by sheer luck such positions became available, you may have to work years before you move past the Principal level.

Also, bereavement benefit is shockingly dismal. I had a colleague whose mother passed away and all she got was a few days.
reviews.pros:
Overall, the company culture is great. Younger, friendly workforce. Most look like they were plucked right out of college. You also get to work with some really smart, seasoned Subject Matter Experts here, so the opportunity to learn here is almost unlimited!

Great diversity and inclusion/Employee Resource Groups you could join if you are Latino, Veteran, Disabled, etc. Competitive salary, medical (Anthem Blue Cross High/Med/Low deductible plans only), standard Vision/Dental/Legal/HSA/FSA/401(K) plans, company-paid S/T disability, basic Life Insurance/AD&D Insurance, EAP

There are several offices within just Chandler, Mesa and Gilbert (and multiple business division) so you have opportunity to move between offices/divisions. Hybrid work is allowed; complete remote is no longer allowed unless you get special approval.
reviews.summary: Great senior management and company culture, cool project opportunities, but...

reviews.advice: Pay closer attention to your managers.
reviews.cons: You are set up to fail. Worst manager and job. The program manager is verbally abusive, stuck in the past, swears profusely, rejects innovation, and goes out of their way to assert their dominance. reviews.advice: Start caring about your employees. Start solving the issues that need solved instead of buying office furniture and repainting walls. reviews.cons: Too many cons. Management is poor. They constantly change planners and leads. Can't hold onto engineers. They play favorites.  Some cells get better treatment.  They ignore problems and concerns regarding builds. They expect you to do everything and work Saturdays. A customer wanted x amount of valves in 2 days,  a ridiculous quantity,  day shift lead told us she expected us to drop dead to push them out. Workers are treated poorly. There is a huge rift between day and night shift. It's honestly not worth the pay to work here especially if you have family and kids. Let's also not forget how their computers are not up to par. So when you gace issues. They drag their feet to fix it, forgetting you need the computer to do your job, and if you have to call IT, take some Tylenol or excedrin before because you'll spend 2 hrs talking to someone overseas who barely speaks English, and doesn't understand what your asking no matter how you dumb it down.

reviews.advice:
If upper management only has 9 direct reports, why do some of those people have 22 direct reports?  That's not flat management; that's hypocrisy.
Turnover isn't an accident. Other teams at Honeywell have the same kind of challenges and manage to address employee needs and instead of losing a few of them every year.
reviews.cons:
The amount of turnover should speak for itself. Most teams have lost half their members in the last two or three years. One reason for that is that if you work here you will have to compete with up to 20-25 other direct reports for your boss's help.

Don't believe the terms in your offer letter- those 13 days of company holidays? Last year managers told us "don't plan for December vacations" despite above-average Q4 performance. Salary might seem ok but raises never track inflation. Work life balance is notoriously bad- a whiteboard here has the quote "death is not a reason not to close your story", and after my spouse had a panic attack my leader said "well we all have work-life issues like that we have to deal with".

There's a reason Anthem is hiring a lot right now. Customer schedules are at risk and leadership would rather throw more water in the bucket than plug the holes in it. If Anthem were a great team more Honeywell employees would want to switch teams.
reviews.pros:
This is specific to Anthem- you might also see "Next Gen avionics" in the job description.
You'll be working in a modern environment. No 30-year old cubicles, you're not using obscure tooling like PVCS that you'd be ashamed to put on your resume.
Anthem is a huge priority for Honeywell and gets a lot of attention.
reviews.summary: Watch out for the Anthem Program

reviews.cons:
All depends on if you are in it for only you or looking at a larger picture. There are many, in every company, who have negative statements about their workplaces. If you know that you are going to work for a large global company and think it will be like working at a small family business, wake up.
Honeywell is there to make money for their shareholders and that can create a fast paced, hard core, very direct environment that not everyone can live/ work in.
Be honest with yourself and know what you are getting into, no matter where you decide to work. After all, it is your decision to accept any/ all job offers and the associated pay/ benefits.

Would say that over the past 5-10 years HR has put us in a very "woke" system that is broken. This is one piece that does need attention or you will run the folks with the IP away.

Our current Exec Leadership is evolving, however, while very focused on growth, they are listening and engaging.

Our benefits packages are better than most. While we are middle of the pack in some areas, we do lead in several.

Our Employee Resource Groups create a space for everyone to feel like they belong. They offer ways for community engagement and personal betterment.

Very innovative company, almost too a fault. We are highly invested in R&D which can mean you sometimes forget about all the great NPI we have made.

Amazing team of employees and friends.
reviews.summary: Good Company - Just be ready for change

reviews.advice: Continue hiring and onboarding training. Take surveys of recent new hires and show actionable results to hiring managers to build even better relationships between HR and employees, which I understand at times is stressed and confrontational.

reviews.pros: Talent Acquisition was very direct and interested in getting all the correct information for me to review prior to accepting. Initial acceptance onboarding has a designated path for completion. Access to the sites are strictly controlled for a safe and secure feeling.

reviews.advice: I recommend a review of all training training modules with the goal of providing a consistent user experience: think HUE applied to all training.
reviews.cons: As with many companies, the onboarding process is inconsistent. In particular some training modules are great while others clearly haven't been updated in a while.
reviews.pros: Benefits and salary are good to very good on a regional basis; Lots of talented people who are very cooperative. Lots of growth and room for advancement, depending on which group are are in. The AI assistant is surprisingly helpful and not at all irritating!

reviews.advice: Innovation is more than a buzz word that can be mandated through program plans.
reviews.cons:
- Honeywell says Innovation is a top priority but somewhere the message gets lost in middle management, and therefore many new products still use code written in the 90s and archaic software tools
- Export control processes have gotten Draconian and un-collaborative. Hope you enjoy typing a business justification for virtually every external email. Many teams have to been told to stop using Excel's real time co-authoring for anything.
- Managers care more about analyzing KPI's and CDR's than understanding the work of entry-level employees that make those KPI's and CDR's happen.
- Program budgets on civil aviation can be disorganized and chaotic. You may work mandatory overtime and then be told to stop working on all customer projects in the same quarter.
- Work-life balance depends heavily on the teams. Sometimes managers barely know what each employee is working on each week, but I've also seen teams where weekend meetings were normal
- Direct managers may be remote, and can sometimes be too hands-off. Good luck getting your manager to appropriately address a dysfunctional team when you've never physically met them and only talk once a month.
reviews.pros:
- None of my bosses have micromanaged details like hours worked or emails responses
- Good opportunities for lateral movement, so many people stay at Honeywell for years
- Some of the Phoenix area sites have made significant improvements in the last five years with ping pong tables, employee events with food provided, and many newer employee clubs
- Most engineers are friendly and I've rarely met toxic or egotistical lower-level employees.

reviews.advice: Keep on keeping on.
reviews.cons:
Not many cons to state.

- They wasted an entire week of my time flying me to Miami, FL to do an orientation where I the "facilitators" were all sarcastic, threatening, and made inappropriate remarks about discriminatory things the whole week (such as saying, "SDI/State Disability is only for women who need to go on maternity leave, not for someone experiencing a health issue that requires time off. There was someone else who commented, "Why would you train a 'camel'?")
- Last reason: Some director caught on to all this. I sat at the office every day while the lead multiple times on the phone told me about my restroom issues, amongst other nonsensical things. There were within the permanent Teams chat history messages from the lead and supervisor about all this nonsense and toxic culture. He decided it was best to lay me off and provide me a $19-20,000 severance. They ended up not providing any stub or remittance for the severance, and only paid $11,000.
The maximum tax rate when yearly income cannot be calculated is 22% for Federal/State here. I was not paid my full severance.
(Therefore, their NDA and anti-liability clause of the severance agreement does not apply).

Guess what? That means there is no arbitration or mediation. If they have an issue, they would have to go through small claims to get their fake severance back, and the judge and clerk would laugh at the paperwork and throw it out before it even goes through.

Thanks for the $11K. I'm going to be leaving this here for future "candidates".

There are very limited opportunities for career advancement and promotions. Management drags its feet on the issues that impact employee experience including diversity and inclusion, addressing employee feedback, and hybrid/remote work. Instead of exemplifying the Cheniere value of being “nimble”, most of upper management hangs onto their traditional way of doing things. This includes doing little to address the lack of gender and racial diversity in management (and tokenizing diverse individuals at any opportunity) and requiring employees to work 10+ years before being promoted to senior roles, unless, of course, you are buddy buddy with the C-Suite. As a result of this poor workplace culture there has been a rapid drain in top talent since the pandemic. Only once employees announce their decision to leave do you see any sort of interest or response to address their concerns. If you are willing to keep your head down and ignore the good ol’ boy mentality you can get experience for a few years and move on like most. Leadership likes to mask this as “Well we like seeing your faces and feeling like a team here, but we are ‘flexible’ to let you work from home as needed.” - this is not the case. Actions speak louder than words, and behind the scenes it is clear that leadership and management actively discourage any type of WFH despite their “flexibility” claim. Cheniere is bleeding employees because of this. Former employees are jumping ship to go work for competitors with actually flexible work schedules and higher pay; filling job positions is difficult due to the rigid in-office requirement; and current employees are begging for some kind of hybrid schedule. Yet leadership is unyielding to the changing industry standards, and they compensate this rigidity by allowing employees to wear jeans daily and regurgitating the same talking points back to their loyal but desperate workforce - “Attrition rate is not as high as you think. We actually have been filling positions quickly. Cheniere is a family, and we like seeing your faces. WFH is an option on an as-needed basis.” The company’s unwillingness to adapt will cost them a lot of talent - good talent at that. Their pride in their “small yet mighty” workforce will lead to an overworked, undervalued, burnt out mess of a “family.” That, coupled with a healthy dose of “Good Ol Boy” mentality, aversion to internal hiring, little opportunity to promote, micromanagement, and company kool-aid fueled delusion about the state of their workforce, leads me to not recommend this company if you value your work/life balance or advancing your career.

reviews.cons:
Cons include an absolute no WFH policy which was compounded by rampant scheduling of non-critical mtgs well after traditional work hours (I found this disrespectful of employees' non-work obligations, and ultimately this was my reason for leaving). Acquisition/onboarding processes seemed very seat-of-the-pants for a company that does this often. Seemed to be a culture that valued efficiency via aggressive slashing of established processes and headcount, without first understanding the impact. Had more than a few occasions where processes were abruptly cancelled, only to be rebuilt from scratch a few months down the road when their absence made their value more apparent. Also, the company in general did not appear to value investment in data/analytic tools. 

In sum, it's a company that seems to value staying lean and aggressively cutting loose anything w/o obvious and immediate value. Nothing inherently wrong with this approach, but not taking the time to assess value up front created plenty of inefficiency when the same processes had to be recreated from scratch months down the road.

reviews.advice: Drop the obsession with sales. You're damaging customer relationships and making yourself look like "Just another corporation."
reviews.cons:
If you work at a store worth their salt they will work you to the bone. Especially in a large or high-volume store there is so much to do, so much to clean. A morning shift person will have the absolutely insanity of a morning rush, but an evening person should be expected to handle evening rushes with a limited staff as WELL as get the place spotless in what I believe is not a reasonable time. We could get the place clean by 10:45, all right--if we broke the health and corporate rules about when to tear things down. And of course if that was ever found out we were in deep. And if we went over 10:45 we were also in trouble. Management sometimes has some very unrealistic ideas about what the job actually entails and what rules and boundaries should go with that.

The pay in my state starts near minimum wage. The ceiling for a barista is $10/hr, which you hit when you've been there about five years. But tips help, and some high-volume affluent stores will have tips up to $4/hr.

There's also a tendency to have fanatical management. Other "kindly" corporations like Whole Foods have this too--the managers drink the Kool-Aid and worship the company. I once spoke with my manager because my schedule was being changed with less than 24 hours notice, and that was against state law. She got this crazed look in her eye and spat "Starbucks law goes above state law!" But that's only a tendency. There are some pretty cool managers out there. Mine was insane.

The customers are spoiled rotten so they also get kind of unreasonable about their Starbucks. They will stand there and demand that you make a drink five times because there's still foam on that latte and they said NO foam, not LIGHT foam. This is a business model of Starbucks': everyone is special, and we will bend the rules for everybody. And I've had people scream at me and call me a (b) and promise me that they would make me lose my job. I've also had stuff thrown at me. But, that's also just customer service.

These last few years Starbucks has been obsessed with selling, too. There's a lot of pressure on the staff to make sure people go home with $15 bags of coffee and sub-par espresso machines. It's hard to maintain the relationships they want us to maintain while trying to sell stuff.

Overall, if you can put up with the customers and the physical demand, and if benefits are more important than income, do it. It's rewarding in its own way. Wear insoles.

employerResponses.response: Thank you for taking the time to provide feedback. Starbucks’ culture and success are driven by our partners and their achievements. We are also committed to upholding a culture where inclusion, diversity, equity, and accessibility are valued and respected. Partners truly are the core of our company, and we strive to ask for input, consider feedback and communicate transparently around company-wide decisions.  It is our intent to ensure that everyone feels supported and cared for, and we will share this with our teams to ensure we continue to improve in this area.

reviews.pros:
The benefits are out of sight. I was offered Starbucks stock after my first year, as well as 401k through Fidelity, and a superb Blue Cross Blue Shield health insurance plan. You can cover your whole family with that plan, and it can include domestic partners. I got a pound of free coffee every week and free coffee all day (although I think that was specific to my store, which bent the rules). There's also an Employee Assistance Hotline which you can call if you're having issues in your personal life. And HR is really responsive--they won't see you as a troublemaker if you're legitimately having an issue. They will handle it.

Also, sexual orientation and gender identity are included in their anti-discrimination policy. None of the gay or lesbian people on my staff got crap for it, even though about half the staff was quietly conservative Christian and Republican.

If you're a people person, you develop relationships with the regulars and it's fun to make their day. I felt it was pretty rewarding to make drinks. I loved the artistic side of it. And again, the free coffee...just awesome. 

They're also usually pretty flexible about scheduling, so it's ideal for if you're working two jobs or are a student. I worked with people in their 50's who had their own careers, but worked part-time at Starbucks for the health insurance. 

The vacation time system is also pretty sweet. I worked with a guy who was there for 10 years and took like a month vacation to his home country.  

The staffs can be really tight...or they can be really vicious. But a spirit of teamwork is definitely encouraged. And exemplary work is recognized.

In an 8-hour shift you get three breaks: one 30-minute clock-out lunch, and two 10-minute on the clock breaks.

You'll also occasionally get those amazing customers and you live for seeing them. We had four customers who every year each put 100 bucks in our tip jar around Christmas. Sometimes those people can make your day with the things they say and do.

reviews.advice: Ask yourself those questions
reviews.cons:
I have been working for a year at Netflix.

I've seen what was supposed to be very mature people, sharing absolutely almost no contact that anyone would qualify as "human".
Sure, that sounds hyperbolic, let me develop (and maybe cherry-pick a little).

Have you heard about our culture? The one about giving candid feedback? - I have seen people complaining of behavior they literally demonstrated themselves in the following days.
But I have also seen these feedbacks resulting in tears both in the eyes of HR persons or fellow engineers. How human does that sound?

Have you heard about our culture? The one about not tolerating brilliant jerks? I have nonetheless seen angriness and frustration, expressed in private, public and meeting. People rejecting new ideas by default, like, any ideas they wouldn't have worked themselves on for days wouldn't count. Even if those ideas are from the best examples in the industry or academics. How many publications/contributions have you seen from Netflix to computer science in general? How does it compare against any other company of that size in the Bay Area? Can you imagine either the real insecurity (x)or the lack of innovation that could lead to this situation?

Except for a few managers, directors or VPs feeling free enough to behave at work in the same way than how they live, almost every engineer I have been interacting with, have shared as little as possible about their private life.
The rare exceptions of interpersonal exchange ends up around some sort of competitive behavior: Who is the most geeky, sportive, owns the fastest car/biggest house/visited the strangest place.

I've heard workaholic people complaining about ambitious peers who were over-managing, over-working to get even more work to do after. I feel like we're past workaholism at this point.

Maybe there are a lot of shy people! Maybe there is a culture of fear, not only of being fired, but also a fear of interacting with people going to be fired.
Maybe it's all in my head, maybe people giving 5 stars to their experience here don't care the human aspect of a company. And maybe they're right.

What about your crush, your fears, your desires for the future, your appetite for life? I've been blessed to work in enough large companies to know that the behavior that I'm seeing in Netflix is not a healthy one. I've also been lucky enough to work in other industries more socializing than tech and I can tell that Netflix has a lot to do on that side, and off-sites or team meeting won't solve that problem.

I am afraid about the tragic, but inevitable consequences of the ways people operate in this company: I guess that the day the worst will happen, it will be addressed in an impersonal memo by Reed; followed-up by 1 or 2 reminders during offsites. Possibly commented by HR in a Q&A document. And move on. This company seems as reactive in its management of people as it is proactive in its business operations.

I still work at Netflix though, not only for the paycheck, but because I hope. I hope it will change. The needed change can't happen from a candid feedback, a Q&A, or  only from inside.
Change has to come from everyone, including people who take time to read comments like this one. Netflix has so many good people and offers such a great service.

As a curious Netflix employee reading this review: think about your past, isn't there a big human thing that you would love to feel again in your current company that you've felt in the past?

As a candidate: think about what would be a good question to ask to that HR partner once your package is almost here to be offered to you, think about that comment you make at the end of an interview when you're being asked by an engineer: "Do you have any question for me?"
What Netflix needs is an inception, something that anyone and everyone would think about after leaving the call or the room they were sharing with you.
Ask yourself, and then the others, the question you should ask if you think you want to spend a good amount of your life and energy in the place you're applying for.

- Will I learn and contribute to the knowledge of other's? Even outside the company?
- Will I see emotional responses from my peers? Will that be for other reasons than being fired or bluntly criticized?
- Will I find a friendly environment that will nurture my appetite for life?
- What is the amount of emotional interaction (celebrating, sharing, playing) to expect from a company whose service is the best to "entertain"?
- Do androids dream of electric sheep?

reviews.advice: Is there a point?
reviews.cons: In a nutshell, your Netflix experience boils down to your direct manager. Managers are almighty dictators reinforcing a pervasive culture of fear at Netflix. I was originally hired by a different leader with whom I had the opportunity to connect and vet. But everything changed when I joined, my manager was someone I hadn't had a single conversation with during the hiring process. If your manager is an empathetic leader invested in your experience and growth, then read no further. But if your manager is anything like mine - a recently promoted IC with absolutely no training/experience in leadership, expect to be overly micromanaged. Expect to be humiliated and treated disrespectfully in the name of candidness over kindness. In a one-on-one conversation, my manager snapped at me when I was about to speak (I wasn't interrupting) and asked me to repeat what they just said. Expect to not have any communication for weeks on end and receive feedback out of the blue that takes you by complete surprise. Expect to have the culture memo weaponized against you. Expect to not have any allies - any attempts to move to a different team that could be a better fit will be thwarted by internal politics. Seeking help from HRBP is as futile as denying climate change. At this point my only hope is a major re-org, but I wouldn't wish this manager on anybody. Having worked in the industry for over a decade at different sized companies, I've had all kinds of managers. This is the first time I feel psychologically unsafe.

reviews.advice: 360 reviews that impact performance ratings. Engagement survey is a good start but can be more targeted to quality of management (people vs. project management). Hire external expertise and trust them to do the job. Allow them to learn and pull elements of DBS but don't force them to if they are producing results. Hire people who know the function > internal people with historical knowledge. Both are important but already over weighted to the latter. Regularly ask your teams simple question, "How can I be a better manager," then listen and put it in your performance review.
reviews.cons: Overly process driven - Feels like you cannot cross the street without jumping through a dozen hoops. Feels like process > best answer. Progress is SLOW! Risk averse - Being empirical based is great, but being overly analytical stifles innovation. Allergic to outside expertise - Focus on hiring from within + Internal methodology is strong in some areas, but it's treated like the gospel and external expertise is devalued and underappreciated. Creates lack of trust and confidence. Hierarchal - Employees seem hesitant to speak out of line to challenge senior leadership. Many people seem in it for the long run (protect jobs > best result). Bad Decision Making - Constant feeling that senior executives don't really know what their doing (excluding delivering production related results), but won't trust those who do to steer the ship, Make short term decisions despite functional best practices. Diversity and Inclusion - Old fashioned and slow moving; Good intentioned white men who were great at sales still run the company - they try their best but unclear of the best steps to take; hesitant to make bold moves or trust those who know. Unknown and disconnected - Working here won't scratch your ego around big brand names. Decentralized nature is wasting tons of resources and synergies. Sparks of change beginning to shine but issues above will slow and stifle.
