reviews.advice: The further you get from the foundational vision of creating great products and ensuring customer success, and instead recruit big company people focused on ego and self-promotion and growing a fiefdom, the more Salesforce starts to become just another Oracle or SAP or Microsoft. My sense is, that's what the board wants. If so, so be it. There will be another innovative and passionate startup to disrupt salesforce some day soon.
reviews.cons:
After my long tenure and many Dreamforce conferences, I'm nearly fried. To say the culture is fast paced and the focus is always changing is an understatement. The reason Salesforce always seems on top, and chasing the latest trend, and in the press, is because employees are expected to run harder, carry more, cheer loudly, and pivot constantly. It's the world's biggest startup in behavior. But at the same time, with the recent influx of top career sales leaders from Oracle and what appears to be a board-level mandate for doubling revenue, employees are being asked to do even more with even less, fill higher quotas with smaller territories, less help, and the big company bureaucracy is rearing it's ugly head. 

Worse still is the politics. When you hire a bunch of smart, aggressive people, and put them in an environment of outsized expectations, throw in a bunch of re-orgs and changing management,  and sprinkle with uncertainty and constantly changing priorities, you inevitably get people back stabbing each other and throwing others under the bus to appear smarter and more worthy of promotion. 

The few at the top will get very, very rich. The rest will lose the sense of personal ownership and start to wonder why they've given up health and family
reviews.pros:
I've spent over 8 years with Salesforce in various management and individual contributor roles, all customer or partner facing. Some of the pros:
- vibrant, fast paced culture 
- smart, fun, aggressive colleagues
- management is focused on latest tech trends and staying or becoming a leader for many of them
- by and large, customers and partners are very positive about the technology
- good benefits and perqs
- hip urban culture at HQ
- a chart-your-own-course mentality that rewards those who aggressively seek out the job they want and pursue it, or sometimes even create it
reviews.summary: Still a lot of opportunity to learn, connect, and chart your own course, but Big Company culture is encroaching.

reviews.advice: Not gonna bother because it won’t matter any way
reviews.cons:
I came into Salesforce like every rep, excited and eager to get my “MBA” in sales. Working here you’ll have to be prepared to give up everything just to stay afloat. In the first year you will most likely be given a terrible territory and what you do with it will decide your future here. Things you will need to juggle effortlessly or will lead you down the road of being let go are:

- Activity- lots of calls. People who fib numbers here are celebrated by leadership but frowned upon by reps
- Opp rigor- the amount of fields you will need to update are mind numbing
- Pipeline- with a terrible territory be prepared to pipe aspirational pipeline that will be highly scrutinized
- Prep meetings- there are endless prep meetings before calls. Due to schedules each person involved will require a prep meeting, leaving your day with little time for anything else.
- Team selling- be prepared to sell with folks much junior than you and not held to as high of standards. If the deal falls through, it’s on you. There are a few coprimes that are skilled sales reps
- Your “brand”- It’s important to maintain appearances, even on bad days. Your brand is determined by how involved you are in diversity, volunteer work, and leading the team, which requires tenure.
-Manager 1:1’s- these are a trap to look out for. Salesforce preaches trust as one of it pillars, but beware that everything said in those meetings will be used against you when they have soured on you
- Time management- working a 12 hr day is table stakes. There are endless distractions you will need to navigate and make hard decisions on “brand”/ appearance maintenance vs selling

The work/life balance is very heavy on the work side. The exec team repeatedly say their biggest regrets are not spending enough time with family. This will never change if they don’t take it serious. There is a lot you can learn here but at the expense of your self confidence as some managers make you feel worthless when your awful territory isn’t performing. If that isn’t enough to make you steer clear, the pay is very low and less than 20% of reps hit their annual numbers

The “Ohana” culture is a mirage. There is nothing remotely familial about the culture. It is an ultra competitive pressure cooker. I just had such higher hopes for my experience left disappointed...
reviews.pros:
- Benefits are top notch
- Perks in the tower and holiday party are impressive
- Sales tactics and strategies are great for growth even as an experienced rep
- You’ll meet very talented sales rep with a wide variance of styles
-ESPP
- generous maternity/paternity leave. Although this will affect your likelihood of be promoted

reviews.advice: Keep up the good work! Can't wait to see what's next, and hope to continue growing my career here.
reviews.cons:
- You can feel "left-behind" here at times, so it's crucial to stay organized to keep up with the pace, especially early on. 
- Work-life balance (self-induced): it's easy to become attached to your work and your accounts, and it trickle over into your personal life after hours, or on weekends. 
- Difficult quota to hit, but that's for a reason. if this were easy I suppose they would let anyone in. 

Can't think of anything else. It's hard to find things wrong with Salesforce, in fact this section took me a lot longer to provide the bullet points above then the pros section.
reviews.pros:
The 1-1-1 Model here (google it) and a tangible benefit that results of it is 7 full days of VTO (volunteer time off) to be used responsibly at your discretion. Matching gifts to a non-profit of your choice. 

- Benefits here overall are incredible
- ESPP is attractive
- Time off is generous
- comp package works in your favor- i.e. hard work does in fact = revenue. 
- equipment is all up-to-date and excellent (iPhone as work phone, and MacBook as laptop)
- Training that consists of bootcamp in San Francisco, and further training at a local hub. Ongoing trailheads and updates also keep you on your toes. 
- Fast-paced environment 
- Great culture 
- Talented professionals 
- Collaborative environment across different segments 
- Brand recognition 
- Smooth employee processes in the background (payroll, time logged, benefit tracking, incentive tracking, employee profile, etc). 
- Continuous acquisitions of companies continues to strengthen our products and offerings. 
- Snacks, events, and happy hours
- Flexibility and autonomy given to consult with your clients 
- Networking opportunities here are endless

reviews.advice: Go back to the real "Ohana" culture by getting back to roots and having more team cross training for products.  Managers seem to busy trying to make their numbers that they only give real time to reps that have money on the line.  Do a better job at onboarding and training properly so that new AM's feel confident about what they're evangelizing to the customer.
reviews.cons: They've just lost their true "Ohana" spirit because they're so focused on trying to keep positive growth. You hear people preach about "Ohana" and being team focused which it can be but overall there's all kinds of internal politics which take away from the Ohana meaning. Also a big lack of real onboarding and training is leaving a lot of employees to figure things out and spending too much time researching an answer and getting momentum. This can also be caused by oversold as well as frustrated customers due to Account Managers being rotated on them every fiscal year.
reviews.pros: Good company.. Solid tech and all the acquisitions allow you to work with a customer on many levels and provide solutions for business problems.
reviews.summary: Great company but lost it's real "Ohana" spirit

reviews.advice: Listen to your customers and invest in the ones that want to partner with you.  SFDC got too big, too fast and the people suffering now are the customers.  Not all accounts benefit from transactional, hard-sell mentality.  Cut down on the level of inspection on your employees so they have the time to do their job of strategically consulting their customers, and ultimately driving revenue.
reviews.cons: The cuts ran too deep- all Strategic AEs now cover 3-4 accounts and it's impossible to be strategic with our customers. There is so much admin work, so much micro-management, and so much activity inspection that it's nearly impossible to do your actual job of selling. The performance culture creates an environment of hunting and "hard closing" rather than strategic consulting and driving value. Our customers are angry that they are being treated like transactions, and have a constantly revolving door or reps because the turnover is so high. I'd avoid working here in Sales if at all possible.
reviews.pros: Aggressive base salary and OTE, and nice benefits

reviews.advice:
Treat everyone fairly. To many managers play favorites. 

Provide clearly guidelines for promotions. 

Take more ownership over things that are out of AEs hands and stop shifting blame onto us.
reviews.cons:
The pay doesn't feel competitive, my base salary to much lower than my peers. 

Territories keep shrinking.

Our org hasn't received part of commission checks in Q1, we're on a pooled model so we get half from a team target. For some reason someone thought its ok to just give us a draw for 3 months. 

Used to be a fun place to work, but culture has changed a lot over the past couple of years. 

A lot of turn over and layoffs.
reviews.pros:
Looks good on a resume. 
You'll learn a lot within the SaaS space
Brand recognition makes selling easier
Many different departments you can work in.

reviews.advice: Salesforce Leaders, keep up the great work!
reviews.cons: There is nothing we cannot resolve.
reviews.pros:
Salesforce is truly exceptional. Over my 13+ years here, I've found it to be more than just a workplace—it's a community, a culture, and a second family. The environment nurtures growth and fosters a healthy balance between work and personal values, including the freedom to practice one's faith openly, supported by an inclusive and understanding team.

What sets Salesforce apart is its dynamic nature; every day brings forth new challenges and opportunities for innovation, ensuring that boredom is never a concern. It's not just a company; it's a journey, one that I am deeply committed to, and I can confidently say that I envision retiring right here. Thank you, Salesforce, for providing such a fulfilling professional home.

reviews.advice: Please provide more awareness around mental health and assistance to those who maybe struggling.
reviews.cons: The only con I can speak to is many of us came in towards the tail end of the pandemic as remote team members and when they did the huge layoff and shifted to bringing people back in the office it was an issue for many. Even the CEO admitted that remote hires didn't get the level of support and training we needed to succeed as many who came in prior and were ingrained in the company culture/environment.
reviews.pros: The people you work with are best of the best. The culture is amazing when it comes to helping each other succeed and winning as a group.

reviews.advice: Monitor closely the behavior and actions of your VPs and Senior Directors. Otherwise, it is perhaps too late to avoid being an office-politics based company.  With your managers indulging in nepotism, racism and ethnic-affinity, you will be unable to succeed as a business.
reviews.cons: High level of office politics especially at the managerial level. The company is transforming into a federal government job with the people managers (including VPs and Senior Directors) playing office politics in order to hide their insecurities. Moreover, they are openly practicing nepotism, preferring their favorites over an individual's skills, talents, hard work and results. The career growth opportunities are extremely limited unless your manager has an ethnic or racial soft spot for you.
reviews.pros: Lot of 'talk' about values, at least they exist on paper. VTO opportunities are comparable to the other big technology companies.

reviews.advice: Walk the talk.  Think about ideal customer experience.  What can you do to reduce churn and enable long term employee success.
reviews.cons: Ultra high account churn. Questionable leadership ethics, one-size fits all / top down management. Metrics and quotas wont map to reality. You need to be very careful to pick the right opportunity, the right business unit, the right leaders to work for, and of course all at the right time. Salesforce is not committed (in my observation) to employee success. You need to hit all metrics or you are out - regardless of reality on the ground.
reviews.pros: Amazing employees, market leading products, Salesforce's brand enables you ability to access and engage with leaders at the top customers in the industry.
reviews.summary: Great company but... they don't walk the talk

reviews.cons:
Restricted stock grants are not a guaranteed part of employee compensation and are awarded sparingly based on merit.

Promotions are not solely dependent on an individual's merit. It is also based on business justification and need. For me and most I know of, this has been a non-issue, but it could delay a promotion that is otherwise warranted.
reviews.pros:
Salesforce's company culture is excellent. In the engineering group in particular, it is very team focused with an emphasis on psychological safety and zero blame.

Internal career growth opportunities are prevalent.

Compensation and benefits are strong.

Most engineering teams are able to travel 2-4 times a year to meet up in person as many are still fully remote; this in particular is huge for team building and not feeling so isolated.

Salesforce does a great job at rewarding its high performers. Don't mistake that to mean that employees are overworked or expected to work outside normal hours. For roles higher up the ranks with more responsibilities, this can sometimes happen here and there, but it is overall discouraged. Recognition programs are also quite prevalent.

For engineering career paths, moving to a managerial role is not required (or encouraged unless you desire it) and you can go very far as an individual contributor.
reviews.summary: Excellent Culture, Career Growth Opportunities, and Benefits

reviews.advice: Be better people. Stop the favoritism. Give EVERYONE the same opportunities. I'm so tired of seeing the same people get congratulated on their achievements that they were hand-selected for. It's total BS.
reviews.cons: Marc Benioff is a joke. He's smart in some areas but completely oblivous to what is actually equal. Trust is NOT a core value, but they sure like to talk about it a lot. Salesforce core values are a joke. There is NO equality here. It's all about favoritism and who you know. They love to go around the room and say "how are you feeling today?"....<---no one cares. My manager talks about my colleagues all of the time in our 1:1 meetings. I honestly don't even know how she's a manager. She loves to brag about herself and how she got here, and most people have more years of experience than her. I hate it here. Everyone hates it. I can't wait to just see all of their best employees leave at the same time.
reviews.pros: The snacks are pretty good and they don't care if you just grocery shop. Literally, people putting like ten things in their backpack at the end of the day.
reviews.summary: This has turned into the WORST company I've ever worked at.

reviews.cons:
*Career Pathing - Could be better, Leveling seems off/not a complete rhyme or reason (e.g. managers report to managers, directors report to other directors). For our specific team, acquisition people often come in mis-leveled, I was told that lateral movements were celebrated... I haven't seen it in action much in Professional Services, but I see growth/moves more within Sales.
*Sales is king, if you are part of ProfServ (Professional Services/delivery) you are definitely on the bottom rung--a great org to be part of for sure--but the focus and support is NOT on you like it is if you are working for a Big4 or major consulting firm.
reviews.pros:
*Awesome Benefits (6-months maternity leave, unlimited PTO, home office wifi reimbursement for remote employees, $100 wellness reimbursement monthly, $5K education credit)
*Great Tools (mac computer, home office setup, slack, google office suite)
*Very Self Service (from onboarding to when questions come up--it's a very self service organization-the onus is on you to go and find the information/logging tickets when needed)
*Awesome Focus on Community - VTO-volunteer hours and sincere focus on giving back throughout the year!
*Remote work - great opportunities to work remotely and your schedule is respected, only challenge is sometimes wishing to be in a location that has an office (because the offices are so cool!) and there can be FOMO when it comes time for major meetings.
reviews.summary: Great Company, Awesome Benefits, Innovative, Career Pathing Can Be Better

reviews.advice: Fix the culture. We had it right only a short time ago. Ever since "high performance culture" came about, you stopped caring about your people (specifically in tech). And I think people are less motivated to care about the customer when you don't care about your own employees.
reviews.cons:
There's way too much office politics. The culture degraded over the years unfortunately. Wouldn't recommend working here for longer than a year or two.

Expect to work weekends at least once a month.
Expect "finger pointing" culture to be obnoxiously apparent in all parts of the company
Expect to have nearly 80 hour work weeks occasionally.
Expect not office politics to seriously affect your work. People are "friendly" until you have to get them to do something. Then the gloves are off and it becomes rather uncomfortable and toxic.
Expect to work with some untalented and unmotivated people. Lately, Salesforce has been opting for cheaper labor and it shows. The talent pool at Salesforce has gotten progressively worse.

Stay away from Service Cloud, and Marketing Cloud! You've been warned.

employerResponses.response: Thank you for your review. Our goal is to create a workplace where everyone can be successful. What you describe goes counter to that. Please know that leadership often reads these comments and your feedback will be shared with the right people. I advise you to have an open and honest conversation with your manager by leveraging a regular 1:1 to address your concerns. Thank you again for your feedback, and we hope that we can continue to improve for you.

jobTitle.text: SMTS - Senior Member of Technical Staff

reviews.pros:
You will learn a lot here. There's decent growth if you play the politics right. Moving between teams is seamless and without any hard feelings. 

From what I've seen, compensation is slightly below the market, but is still pretty good. Although, they claim to be some percentage above market average.

reviews.advice: Try to unify diverse work environments across different parts of the company
reviews.cons: Navigating the diverse work culture of Salesforce company can pose challenges in finding one's place. Varying backgrounds, perspectives, and communication styles require adaptability and empathy. Building connections amidst this diversity demands patience and openness, but ultimately enriches the workplace experience with new insights and collaborations.
reviews.pros: Salesforce is an exceptional workplace that fosters growth and innovation. The supportive culture encourages collaboration and creativity, making every day fulfilling. Leadership values employee well-being, offering excellent benefits and opportunities for advancement. Plus, the mission-driven ethos inspires pride in contributing to meaningful technological advancements.
reviews.summary: Salesforce is where Innovation Meets Fulfillment

reviews.advice: The managers I've had in customer success and content roles genuinely care about their reports. I recommend they continue to model work-life balance by taking days off, taking extended PTO, and really demonstrating that it's ok to unplug from work and not check in while they're away.
reviews.cons: It's a huge, international company, so if you don't like having to work within the structures and occasional red tape that come along with having a large and cautious legal team and top-down org chart, this might not be for you. Sometimes you might feel like a cog in the machine, but I think that's par for the course in huge tech companies.
reviews.pros:
- Good managers. I've benefited from many great managers in my ~10 years at Salesforce. 
- Great teammates. Perhaps even more consistently great are the people I've worked with on teams. 
- Inclusive workplace. Our Employee Resource Groups are many and active. Super easy to get plugged in.
- Innovative. Salesforce is always thinking ahead, trying new things, and encourages employees to do the same. 
- Fun and flexible. I'm a remote employee now, but still enjoy visiting the nearest office for the exciting things happening there every day.
reviews.summary: Great team, leaders, pay, and work

reviews.advice:
Advice would be to be honest with yourself about what metrics are actually attainable and not keep people held down in role. You continue to encourage people to fake it til they make it and even then you most likely won't even make it. 

Make promotion realistic and actually develop salespeople instead of encouraging empty stat padding
reviews.cons:
- Faking numbers (the entire org relies on fudging numbers to hit their metrics, which is often called "playing the game")
- No autonomy (Your success is directly correlated to if your AEs like you as well as if your patch is good)
- No path to promotion and zero room for growth (Constant hiring freezes and metrics are always evolving to unrealistic numbers. Best way to be promoted here is to leave and then come back)
- Leadership is unable to help and you do not learn much while in this role
reviews.pros:
- Great Benefits and Perks ($100 Wellness a month, 401k match, ESPP)
- Great Coworkers
- Very nice office with tons of free food and drinks
- The work is relatively easy and not too stressful of days
- High base with automatic commission
- Great brand and good for resume
reviews.summary: Great Perks and Good Pay,  but no opportunity for Career Growth

reviews.advice: Marc needs to get back to control of the company
reviews.cons: I worked for Salesforce for over 10 years(almost all of those years were in leadership). I drank the kool aid for awhile but have to say the last two years the quality of leadership and management sticking to Salesforce core values was truly lacking. Even the human resource department (employee success) changed on their processes. Used to a leader would have to document conversations with an associate on work performance, then go to a coaching plan and if an associate was not showing improvement then going to a performance improvement plan. The leader had to provide documentation and include employee success in all of those steps. I know of several folks that their leader never had conversations about performance(flat out lying and leadership up the chain)at all then all of sudden forced out by by forcing a PEP – Prompt Exit Package with 2 months severance. When the associates went to Employee Success their response is well we trust that what they have said is true (no documentation needed emails between the manaager and employee of anything in the past). A lot of these folks had great performance, RSUs, etc before. Salesforce did this quietly during the layoffs. These folks received just 2 months whenever folks who were really already on PIPS received the full 6 months of severance because of layoffs. Its sad to see this company does not truly follow on the first value of TRUST and has leaders that are unethical

employerResponses.response:
Hi there — thank you for sharing your feedback, and for your contributions to Salesforce over the past decade. 

As you know, our core values are absolutely critical to who we are, and we’re disappointed to hear that your experience felt counter to that. This is certainly not the type of culture that we strive to create for our employees and their leaders. If you’re comfortable doing so, we encourage you to escalate your concerns to our anonymous reporting platform, EthicsPoint, at salesforce.ethicspoint.com, where you can provide further information for us to investigate. (You do not need to be a current employee to submit.)

Thank you again for your feedback, and for helping us to become a better workplace for all.

reviews.pros: great benefits and time off

reviews.cons: the company is getting sold
reviews.pros: i like the company culture
reviews.summary: a good place in a bad time

reviews.advice: You are executives as one of the largest companies in the world!  Set the example from the top so that the working environment is fair for everyone and not just those at the top or those like by the leaders of the cliques.
reviews.cons: Worst management I have ever worked with. Skills and competencies take a back seat to the rumor mill and the popularity contests that is this company. Management learns of some rumors and without getting any facts at all strips aways responsibilities based on your social score. There could be no merit whatsoever to the rumors being spread about you and yet management will not address the concerns with the employee and will still manipulate the workload based off the merits which hold no truth. It is toxic. Management is allowed to single employees out and make backhanded comments toward employees they do not care for.
reviews.pros: The company has flexible working hours and remote working options.

reviews.advice:
Ensure that teams are operating efficiently and working collaboratively with all departments that are necessary to make a production come together. 

Encourage different divisions of the company to collaborate to allow employees to be cross-trained in different areas of the company. 

Focus more on the west coast employees and make sure that there are events for them to participate in.
reviews.cons:
While there are a lot of upsides, there are several areas where I feel like the company could improve.

I've seen several teams (e.g. creative, production, marketing, digital) that either haven't been properly trained on how to effectively work with legal, finance, etc. or choose to ignore the training they've received. They often either avoid working with those teams altogether or loop them in last minute for them to put an agreement together, pay out talent, crew, etc. and it creates significant issues for the company in terms of how we're viewed by talent and their representatives as well as for employee morale and overall satisfaction. I've also seen this result in significant money being wasted as we often are paying (or overpaying) for services and/or associated late fees that wouldn't be needed had those teams been looped in early on.

There aren't many events for the west coast employees as it seems like most of the events are geared for the east coast offices, although occasionally we do have some decent events pop up.

We don't receive the week between Christmas and New Years off, like many entertainment companies do.
reviews.pros:
I've been at Paramount for nearly three years and so far it's been a great place to work. Paramount is a great name to put on your resume and I've truly received support with my career growth. Also, the benefits have been great! I've never had an issue with my health insurance, they provide unlimited PTO (which I've never had a problem getting approved and have used 3-4 weeks every year) and a 5% 401K match. 

Like most companies it's understaffed and employees are overworked, but that's to be expected almost anywhere. There are times where I'm working back to back 60-80 hour weeks, but there are also times where it's slower and I'm able to have a fairly light week. 

My team has been nothing but supportive for my career growth as well as personal growth. They've given me projects that have allowed me to expand my knowledge and learn from leaders on my team and throughout the Paramount legal department. While I initially started out in a more supporting role on projects, over time I became a leader and took full ownership of all projects I was assigned (whether from my team or sent directly from the client groups I serve). My team has also been incredibly accommodating for any personal time I need, usually allowing me to fully unplug (assuming I work with someone to cover my projects in advance of taking leave), whether that's for a vacation or medical/family emergency.
reviews.summary: Great place to work, but nothing's perfect

reviews.advice:
START OVER FROM SCRATCH.

Desperately in need of new leadership at the corporate level and at each division. Most of the company is run by long-time Viacom execs who still think it's the late 90's/early 00's, when cable was healthy and MTV and Comedy Central were relevant.

Need younger, fresher, more diverse leadership with fresher content and marketing ideas.  NOT "GOOD BURGER" SEQUELS, "MEAN GIRL" REMAKES AND 7 DIFFERENT YELLOWSTONE SERIES.

reviews.advice: Stop being so cliquey and hire people
reviews.cons:

reviews.advice: Our leaders are remarkably charismatic and hard-working, and they care deeply about their business and the team members who contribute to its success. There is a lot of untapped potential that might be realized if they continue to gradually open themselves to new ideas and ways of thinking about how work can be changed to better serve both organizations and the people working in them. So much of what is already being done here works incredibly well, and with some tweaking, the culture could be taken to the next level.
reviews.cons: A reality of working at this company, for better or worse, is that it's very old-school in terms of work culture. With few exceptions, remote work (either fully or in a hybrid capacity) has not been embraced following the COVID shutdown, and most (not all) upper management is wary of providing employees with too much flexibility out of a concern that work will not be completed. Additionally, leadership is (as is very common among old-school leaders) often highly resistant to change that, while painful, might be necessary to improve processes or the employee experience. I hesitate to describe this culture as a pure con, since I experience it as more of a workstyle preference which either will or will not fit well for each individual. My personal preferred work culture would be one that is more in-line with contemporary research and understanding of what drives and rewards employee motivation, and that wholeheartedly adopts new workplace practices that are becoming selling points at a growing number of other organizations. With that being said, there's a lot of heart here, and I have truly learned and grown a lot as a result of performing my role as a member of this company. In spite of the things I would change about the culture, there are many practices and outlooks that I will carry from here with me whenever I do choose to move on to another organization in the future.
reviews.pros: Over my time working at Southern Telecom, I have found it to be an overwhelmingly positive work environment with enjoyable coworkers, stimulating tasks/projects, and generally strong rapport. People invest themselves in what they do, and most interactions that I observe between team members of various departments are productive and pleasant. I can honestly say that I generally enjoy being at work, which is largely due to the good relationship that I have with my direct supervisor, but is also due to the good relationships I have with my colleagues and to the stimulating work environment. The office is also bright and fairly open, which helps to prevent feelings of dreariness/grogginess, even on darker or rainy days.

The lack of consideration for personal time and family commitments was apparent, as they expected employees to plan their lives around work, even sacrificing weekends. The manager's constant loud eating and phone conversations in another language made it challenging to concentrate and work peacefully. In conclusion, the corporate accounting department's approach to management and work-life balance left much to be desired. The excessive working hours, micromanagement, and disregard for personal time were major downsides that affected the overall work experience. reviews.cons:
Understand that Paccar's three trucking division nameplates (Kenworth, Peterbilt, and DAF) fiercely compete with each other, and each division has its own cultural norms and IT departments - none of whom seem to want to play well together or show any genuine concern for the other. This is a huge risk for you as a BA because, for example, one division favors a COTS package and wants to implement it, but the other divsion does not, and yet at the end of the day Paccar is supposed to be one company right? Well, not exactly. So securing funding for your projects will be difficult because the trucking divisions have separate budgets and priorities as well.

North America Paccar (Kenworth and Peterbilt) is a few years behind its European nameplate (DAF) in terms of after-sales technologies and processes.

Paccar in general (regardless of nameplate) is about five years behind its competitors (e.g., Volvo, Freightliner, etc.) for after-sales.

Wonky expense and travel booking system (Concur)

Wonky support ticketing system (Cherwell)

Poor, minimal onboarding experience - other than a few meet & greets set up by your manager, you'll be on your own.

Azure DevOps boards are a mess; incredible amount of project overlap between roadmap initiatives, their requirements, and the user stories.

Must wait 6 months before being approved (IF you're approved, it's not automatic) to WFH, not to exceed two days per week. (But managers often ignore the policy, and are inconsistent when using the benefit, so you'll frequently be "surprised" when your manager decides to WFH without telling you ahead of time.)

ZERO TRUST - your badge is timestamped when you come and go from the building. Doesn't matter that you're salaried, you better have your butt in your seat for 8+ hours per day -- it doesn't matter that you worked overtime last week or last Saturday, there is no "balancing things out" allowed.

Wonky performance management and training system ("Success Factors") - you're required to set goals, assess yourself, track your progress, etc. It's just too much...

reviews.advice: Value experienced staff.  Retrain existing 'first'.  Make programs to proactively up skill existing staff
reviews.cons:
Every 12-18 months, the company undergoes a "reorganization" aimed at redirecting priorities and reducing costs. While skills and performance are cited, these reorgs disproportionately target higher-paid, veteran employees. The real intent is to cut costs not really care about their veteran employees.

I was with the company for 25 years before being released due to a recent reorg. My department lost funding and could not maintain my salary - one of the highest due to my tenure. No other departments could take on my compensation either.

This pattern indicates a strategy of replacing experienced, skilled employees with entry-level hires purely to cut costs. While legal, it systematically pushes out veteran expertise. Employees should be aware that loyalty and performance may not protect against being cut solely due to higher salaries.

The company could be more transparent about the financial motivations behind these reorgs. And it risks losing critical institutional knowledge and skills. While some cost-cutting may be necessary, there are likely better ways to achieve savings while valuing and retaining essential experience.

PTO is generous for someone who does not typically take time off, there is also included bereavement and maternity options available. While not exactly a typical office job, the call center life is a fairly easy day job for those who enjoy staying completely engaged during the entire work day. Subject matter is easy to learn for someone who retains knowledge or material well - or takes good notes to refer to; systems are in place to help employees research and determine accurate answers to assist customers in need.

reviews.cons:
Training was solid, but there are aspects/concepts that were never touched on. There have been days when I've felt like I was unprepared for something that popped up.

Be warned, it is very hard to change shifts. The wait-list is close to a year, so if you want a certain time, make sure you get it on the first try.

Callers can very rude - but unless they get particularly nasty, you just kind of have to eat it.

The programs/systems we use for the job are incredibly unreliable. One vital system is literally from decades ago and generally cannot be trusted to work two hours in a row, let alone two days.

While you can move within the company, you do have to have been in your current position for about a year or so. So, again, if you don't like where you are, you just have to bear it for a while.

This isn't so much towards the position itself as it is for U.S. Bank as a whole. I've had numerous callers come in and ask for something I/the bank cannot give them - and when I ask who told them that, they will almost always say "the branch". I don't know how branch bankers are trained, but there is a big disconnect. It causes confusion for the customer and headaches for phone reps.

Benefits are nice.

Callers can also be cool; it means a lot to help them out or give them info. If you're good with people/customers, you can really thrive here.

reviews.advice:
Please listen and talk to your employees more and not just the middle managers.

Skip levels and reviews should go both ways. Leaders should be asking employees to rate their managers on availability, effectiveness, and the impact they are making within their teams. You have some amazing managers but you also have a lot that are poor and have no business leading people. 

Communicate layoffs clearly and do not continue with the silent layoffs. This may seem like the right approach but it creates confusion and concerns in our teams and productivity loss as a result. The approach does not motivate us to be better or work harder. You don't want to become the 3M of banking or worse Wells Fargo.

Talk between departments, before doing layoffs that impact another group (ex. recent UX research reorg as well as layoffs in TOS and Content). You are already spreading some of these groups way too thin. Engage that group to realize the overall impact of your cost savings move. These changes not only impact the working teams but also our customers as a result. The communication here has been poor and is not getting any better. 

Hire additional FTEs in Development and Testing, these Development Managers are overloaded and not as effective as they would be with proper FTE support under them. I'm on board with utilizing offshore but again you have to have enough FTEs here to support the process. 

Look at collocating teams again if you are going to push RTO, coming into the office should mean in-person interactions not just with your co-workers but with the team you work on or support. 

Optimize the Workday job search so we can find jobs again by grade level. There is nothing worse than wasting your time and getting results from a lower grade or a lateral move.
reviews.cons:
CEO received a huge pay bump in 2024 but most of us were told we didn't meet our goals. As a result, our yearly merit increase is less than half that of inflation, and bonuses were reduced. I think Andy is a great CEO but I'm curious how we cannot meet our goals but Andy still gets his raise. 

Leadership often appears to make decisions without knowing the whole story. Communication is also very poor and tone-deaf at times.

Leaders give off this ivory tower vibe anytime people complain about RTO. They openly ignore how the financial impact on us, is much greater than on them. Due to their high salaries; parking and gas prices being way up don't have the same impact on their bottom line.

Leaders often spend money on lunches, breakfasts, shoes, travel to India and so there is little budget left at the team/group level. This kills morale for those, especially people driving into offices. 

The bank has done a very poor job with RTO, the spaces are not inviting, leaders and managers often are not there (still living in a remote city) and the general response is "Deal with it, this is how it was before". Again very tone-deaf of leaders to talk this way.

Even with these Cons, I do like working for the bank, thanks to my amazing coworkers and in my case my manager.

There's an inflexible VP that grants autonomy then promptly undermines managers by second guessing them on every decision.
If you want to spend your time trying to figure out how to think and solve problems 1 way, the VP's way, then the team I was on is for you.
The company claims it has your back then if you aren't one of The Chose Ones (LGBTQIA+, minority, etc.) they tell you "That's your problem".
I worked with adults that never left HS. Drama runs rampant. You have to worry about feelings first and job second.
They gaslight you on virtues and have different standards for you relative to your peers. The rules apply to you but when you ask for equal treatment/application then you're "A Problem" or "That isn't the purpose of the conversation". You have to see it from the POV of others but you're unreasonable to ask they see it from yours. Annual calibrations are an opportunity for folks you don't work with to air old grievances as if they're still relevant. Do not expect others to acknowledge your growth and development.
Return to office was a total joke. I would come in 3 times per week and never see 1/2 the department because they were the chums of the VP. Don't expect a high quality of work. I encountered folks w/degrees that couldn't understand multiplication. Many folks are illiterate in basic skills such as navigating spreadsheets. There are plenty of emotionally fragile people that suffer breakdowns and need a week off to recover being told "I struggle with your late, incomplete and incorrect work. We are jointly accountable (per our Core Values). The next time there is a quality issue then it will be escalated."
Finally, be prepared for others to "collaborate" which really means to steal your work and present it as their own.

reviews.advice: These restrictive policies significantly detract from the overall employee experience. Addressing these issues would undoubtedly improve morale and foster a more supportive and inclusive workplace culture
reviews.cons:
Firstly, the company's bonus policy is a significant letdown. Despite employees dedicating themselves throughout the year, bonuses are only rewarded if you're still with the company next year on the exact date they disburse them (Mid / Late April of next year). This approach essentially penalizes those who have contributed to the company's success but have moved on before the bonus payout. It's disheartening to see your hard work go unrecognized simply because of timing.

Moreover, the vacation policy is equally disappointing. Regardless of whether you've worked until the last working day of the month, If you leave the company, you will not get the unpaid vacation days. You would only accumulate the vacation days if you pass the calendar month. This rigid approach fails to acknowledge employees' dedication and their right to enjoy earned time off, creating unnecessary stress and dissatisfaction.

Additionally, the lack of 401k match during the first year of employment adds to the list of grievances. While understanding that some benefits may have vesting periods, the absence of 401k match for the initial year makes it harder for employees to secure their financial futures. It sends a message that the company prioritizes its bottom line over investing in its employees' long-term financial well-being.
reviews.pros: I worked at Macy's for a significant period, and while there were some positives, several concerning policies significantly diminished the overall experience.

reviews.cons: The onboarding and training process is very poorly designed. It's not effective at teaching unless you're able to sit at a computer for hours watching videos, reading policies, and actually absorb information in that way. There's very little actual hands on learning as an option, and almost all of the things I learned and actually prepared were learned on my own. My experience is that leadership does not adequately communicate expectations nor do they expressly communicate them. Policies are difficult to track down in written form after completing orientation. I was unable to find a written dress code after looking for months. PTO or sick time is not available to employees until one year of employment. I was hired and primarily working during the winter months when people commonly get sick. I got sick with the flu, covid, and an upper respiratory infection within a 6 week time period. Only my covid absences were considered excused, and even if I had a doctor's note, Macy's as a company doesn't accept doctor's notes as a reasonable accommodation for any absence relating to illness. I had complained about harassment to my People Leader and I was dismissed repeatedly. After repeat complaints of harassment I was ultimately let go due to my "repeated" absences which were illness related or emergency related (Emergency Room visits, blown out tire on car) Do not work for this company if you value work/life balance because this company celebrates people coming to work ill and rewards you for pushing yourself beyond what is healthy to the human body and mind.

reviews.cons:
Monotonous Work: The day-to-day tasks at Macy's can feel repetitive and uninspiring. Whether it's stocking shelves, assisting customers, or processing transactions, there's little variation in duties, which can lead to boredom and burnout.
Ineffective Management: Management at Macy's leaves much to be desired. Communication is often lacking, and decisions seem to be made arbitrarily without much consideration for employee input or feedback.
Stressful Sales Targets: Meeting sales targets at Macy's can be stressful, especially when factors beyond your control, such as foot traffic or inventory availability, impact your performance. The pressure to meet quotas can detract from the overall job satisfaction.
reviews.pros:
Decent Team Environment: While there are moments of camaraderie among colleagues, the overall team environment at Macy's feels average. There's a sense of collaboration, but it often lacks the depth and genuine connection found in more tightly-knit teams.
Limited Growth Opportunities: Macy's does offer some avenues for career advancement, but they feel constrained and somewhat bureaucratic. Promotions seem to be based more on tenure than merit, which can be frustrating for ambitious employees looking to progress.
Employee Discounts: The employee discount at Macy's is a standard benefit, nothing exceptional. While it's nice to have, it's not a game-changer in terms of compensation or job satisfaction.
Diversity Efforts: Macy's makes efforts to promote diversity and inclusion, but they often feel superficial. There's a checkbox mentality rather than a genuine commitment to fostering a diverse and inclusive workplace.
Work-Life Balance: Maintaining a work-life balance at Macy's can be challenging, especially during peak seasons. While the company pays lip service to the importance of work-life balance, the reality is that employees often find themselves working long hours with little recognition or appreciation.

reviews.advice: No. I'm not going to tell YOU how to do your job. It is your responsibility to look into things or situations that needs improvement. You should know what they are IF you really do pay attention to your associates.
reviews.cons:
1) Minimum wage. You'll probably get a small raise later maybe a year or two. But it's not much of a raise, a couple cents. 
2) "Sales Associate" - You pretty much do everything. You ring on the register, do returns, check fitting rooms, put back clothes. There are some days when you're the only one working in one department and it's not busy at all, and you'd go to the fitting rooms to check. I swear everytime I leave the service desk to do that, a customer will always show up when I'm not there. Really?? When you get out of the fitting room you see them and you have to run to them before they get impatient and leave. 
3) Catty associates -  The full time associates that have been working there for ages (literally like 20 years or something) are very very protective and competitive over their sales goal. If there is a full time and a part time scheduled for one department (1 service desk with 2 registers maybe) you sure as hell bet that the full time will stay and hog the register while you have to put stuff back. My advice: Don't let them step all over you! They have goals to make, but so do you! If they ever tell you that they have to make their sales goal because they're full time, tell them that you do too! It's not always like this with every single associate. With the people I worked and got along with we took turns because we know how competitive ringing goes around. We helped each other out. I hope the same goes for you. 
4) Opening a credit - As a Macy's Retail Sales Associate, you are required to open credits - which is part of the job so it's fine. BUT the part that is not fine is when the managers constantly remind and tell you to open credits as they walk around the store and they see you. It's okay to tell me once or twice about it but it's NOT okay when you shove it down my throat. I know I have to get credits but you don't have to tell me like I'm deaf or disabled. Managers can sometimes make you feel like you're not trying your best with opening it, in other words, incompetent. It has great incentives, don't get me wrong. But please, ease on with the nagging. We're trying our best but not everyone wants to open one for reasons such as: bad credit, closed macys card to decrease payments/interest fee, not interested in opening one at all!
5) Department assignment - Be careful on which departments you pick up when you try to get hours. Other departments are the best but some are just so boring and dead. My only advice is to keep yourself busy even if it's something you don't want to do. At least you're doing something. 
6) For people who wants to gain retail experience and some cash, this is the place for you. BUT if you want to make this your career, there's no future here for you. Some associates (mostly full time) have been here for the longest time and this is the only job for them, so just understand when they get too competitive or catty with ringing people out - that's pretty much their life. 
7) Easily burn out! - Take a day off or two, you will need it.


Bottom line:
Every company/employer has its pros and cons, but don't be discouraged. A good work experience is great for future jobs. Remember, work is work. You can't be picky. Overall, Macy's is alright.
reviews.pros:
1) Flexible Scheduling - If you were scheduled a shift that you can't do (drops down 3 or 4 weeks of work schedule), you can advertise your shift but you have to do it right away so other associates that wants to pick-up hours can take that shift and you'll be clear of that shift. I say do it ASAP because if you do it later then nobody would want to pick up a last minute shift
2) Pick-up shifts - Okay listen carefully! Shifts drops down EVERY friday but the picking up is Saturday. The executive office will tell you that you're allowed to start picking up Sunday morning. From experience and other associates telling me, you can start picking up Saturday at 7am SHARP. Be ready at 6:59am. Open/available shifts comes from the office (due to big sale events, they need more than usual associates working) AND from full time associates. They get their schedule AND advertise/pick-up shifts on the same day. So they get to advertise their shifts early bird style. 
3) Part-time Options - There are 5 different types of part-time option: Option 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5. I'm not really familiar with Option 1 or 2. Option 5 gets 3-8 hours, Option 4 gets 12-20 hours, Option 1 and maybe 2 are full time which gets 32-38 hours. NOTE: The minimum to maximum hours for each option will be the scheduled shifts. The only way for you to get MORE hours is when you pick up later on. AND during the holidays of course. For example: As an option 5 you'll be scheduled 5 hours. When its time to pick up you, picked up, let's say, 9:45am-1:45pm (4 hours). So add that to your scheduled hours for that week, you have 9 hours. It's not a lot but thats why you gotta be a pro at picking up shifts. Holidays will do you good. 
4) Pay Frequency - Weekly!
5) Associates/Co-workers - You will meet friends along the way. You'll see the good and the bad. You'll see who you get along with, stick with them. And stay away from those ones with nasty attitude. 
6) Good for people starting out in retail. You will really learn a lot. 
7) More hours Opportunity - I'm not really sure if this falls under pros or cons but I'll mention this anyway. Sometimes the store will be short on associates (called out, left early, etc.) and the managers will ask their associates on the floor if they would like to stay until a certain time. I said I wasn't sure if this was good or bad only because some people like the extra hours AND some probably already worked a long day and they don't want to stay any longer for that day. Oh and some has plans after their shift. Sometimes though it gets annoying, people just wanna go home and rest you know. 
8) Associate Discount - it's okay. It has its perks

Limited Advancement Opportunities: Advancement opportunities within the company appeared limited for entry-level positions, and career growth might necessitate transitioning to different roles or companies.

Flexible Scheduling: The job offered a degree of flexibility in scheduling, making it easier to balance work with personal commitments and responsibilities.
Team Collaboration: The team-oriented environment fostered a sense of collaboration and support among colleagues.

If you're relatively new to the industry and are trying to put in 150% effort and try and get promoted - simply don't bother. Promotions are HEAVILY (read: exclusively) dependent on which department/team you end up on and your manager. You can get exceptional on every category on your quarterly performance review and still be passed up on promotion whether it be due to your manager not submitting you or "budget reasons". At the same time you're being denied despite consistent exceptional performance, you'll see other people from your team and department in more senior positions continue to be promoted without delay. All of this on top of the fact that promotions are strictly quarterly, so if you are passed up you are waiting at minimum 3 months just to be denied again for the same BS. Not to mention at the same time you might even be receiving numerous accolades from coworkers telling you how great your work has been, but this will not realize itself in title/compensation. reviews.advice:
Strongly review the entrepreneurial sales compensation model and run the numbers on missed opportunities where individual compensation outweighed company margins.  Are 7-figure sellers compensated fairly for their effort or cashing in on large accounts with repeatable business at the expense of compensation models that will reward folks growing smaller accounts and opportunities to use those funds for capital improvements?

Better measure the contributions of back-of-the-house to enabling customer satisfaction and service excellence.  Consider opportunities to reward and engage non-customer facing employees with similar opportunities afforded to sellers and services.  Enable ways for them to share in the organizational successes as opposed to a two-class system of employee.  Turn cost-centers into profit sharing enablers.
reviews.cons:
Executive leadership models the culture of customer focus and employee engagement on paper with a primary focus on financials and strategy that impact investor relations. High emphasis on quarterly metrics and the impact to the books.

Company is currently going through a transition of integrating the 10 acquisitions made in the last 5 years, along with a few legacy acquisitions, and aligning roles and responsibilities. There have been noticeable waves of workforce reductions and long tenured employees moving on. Additionally, company is working through modernizing their technology stack.

Stark division in perks between the customer facing sales and services team and the back of house administrative and operational teams. Entrepreneurial focused teams do well for themselves, incentivized to making decisions leveraging channel partner programs that benefit them sometimes at the expense of the overall organization. Teams that generate direct revenue seem to spend with abandon while cost centers focus on every penny.
reviews.pros:
Great people, great DEI focus and engagement, competitive pay, good benefits, Middle management and individual contributor culture is strong with customer focus and employee engagement. Pay for performance enables significant compensation in the sales and services organizations.
CEO Chris Leahy is incredibly authentic and inspiring in her company wide communications.

reviews.advice: PAY PEOPLE A LIVABLE WAGE
reviews.cons:
This place refuses to pay a livable wage to their employees. This mine site is over 60% contractor run. The contractors pay their employees a very reasonable wage. However, a "do not compete" has been put in place recently because Climax employees have been jumping ship to go work for these contractors in order to be able to afford to live in this area. What bothers me, is that these contractors are being brought in from all over the country to work in severe climates at over 2 miles above sea level. They are never given a chance to acclimate which leads to multiple incidents every month involving altitude sickness. 
We have this cute little "Agile" team, which is formed quarterly for retention brainstorming. They aren't allowed to discuss the real issues as to why our turnover rate is at about 100%. 
Annual raises are usually somewhere between 2%-3.5%, which isn't even close to keeping up with the rising cost of living, especially in a small mountain town where the primary industry is tourism.
Line of progression is completely made up. Every position has a checklist of things that need to be done before you can move to the next level. I've been in two different positions now where I have met these requirements and progression has halted. Expectations and standards are made up, and when you reach them, interpretations change.

jobTitle.text: Senior Specialist, High Net Worth Representative

reviews.pros: Co-workers generally friendly, support departments generally helpful

reviews.advice: Hey, management, if you don't have a clue about what you're doing, "fake it before you make it" might fool YOUR boss, but the rest of us will see right through it.  You might want to promote people who know what they're doing, instead of just people who look attractive, or coerce you into promoting them, or that you have taken a fancy to for reasons not obvious to the rest of us.
reviews.cons: If you're someone who is a subject matter expert, you won't necessarily get ahead. Promotions are based on who likes you (crazy, right?) and not whether you actually know your stuff or are productive. A lot of the work we do is window dressing to fool senior management into thinking what we do is important and of value to the company when in fact it is just busywork and CYA activities. We are complicit in this because we need to keep our jobs. So hang out and get paid, but be wary of staying too long; you'll lose your edge. Also, any talents you may have had from previous experience is considered inconsequential; they only care about what you've done for THIS company and will be pigeonholed accordingly in any internal interview/job search situations.
reviews.pros: If you're someone who is unambitious and succeeds just by being friendly, you will flourish here.
reviews.summary: It's not what you know... but who

reviews.cons:
A couple years ago this company felt like it was making progress to stepping into the modern times by understanding that style of work and life was changing. Now they have mandated that you must work in the office 3 days a week-most likely to increase to 5 again- which was a huge step back into the 1950s mindset and micro-managing. In a company where the majority of the day is spent in meetings-virtually, why must we drive to an office to do that? 
Having laid off up to 40% of a single department, all that work has been put on those that remain with an insulting pay increase that doesn’t cover a quarter of inflation let alone the increased cost of having to come into the office. 
In addition to the added work there is a complete shift in procedures that isn’t defined enough for project managers to successfully do their jobs or help their business partners understand it as well. The leadership responsible for answering the questions of employees don’t have the answers and only ever say “it’s still being worked on and developed”. Multiple employees don’t feel they know what they are suppose to be doing and there is no support from upper leadership. 
There is also no career path clearly defined and discussions with people leadership yield no clear objectives to work towards either for promotion.
reviews.pros: Coworkers that understand where your coming from because they have to deal with the same problems.

reviews.advice: Make coming in to the office optional for all non client-facing workers and leave it up to the discretion of managers/directors what special meetings (quarterly planning, team lunches etc) most employees will be expected to attend in person.
reviews.cons:
The return-to-office initiative is a farce for most non client-facing employees (those in marketing, technology etc). 

I used to love coming in to the office... when there was a point to it. Now we're forced to spend money & time in traffic to come in, sit in front of our computers, and have most of our meetings on communication apps anyway, since many of our team members are still remote. As ludicrous as it sounds, we're basically coming in to the office to work remotely (and having to put up with the noise of other people around us shouting into their mics for their remote meetings)

To add insult to injury, colleagues who were lucky enough to have moved away during Covid or who are on the "Green side" (and don't live near an office) have the privilege of being able to work from the comfort of their home. It's inequity and favoritism.
reviews.pros: Most people working at Schwab are genuinely very nice

reviews.advice: There isn't much they can do. They bit off more than can chew with the merger and it has greatly reduced their quality and care for their customers and employees in turn. I love what they stand for but that's a picture of the past now.
reviews.cons: No chance of internal promotion, Very unrealistic expectations, Extremely unorganized and going downhill fast due to hiring quantity over quality (a lot of young workers with not nearly enough supervision to add to this burden). Not enough pay for the stress you are put under (I was on phones and wasn't allowed to transfer out of the customer service umbrella without applying as if I wasn't already in the company and getting a job outside my department was slim because the role I had was one that no one wanted). They really deceive you with the idea that you will be able to work your way up within the company. They also screw you if you do their internship program as you are a contractor and not entitled to bonuses or insurance or any other benefit. In the future they don't even count that time as experience with the company. I wasted a whole year being an intern because they tell you it will help advance you when in fact it held me back in comparison to my peers and created a lasting bitterness for the company. Wasn't the worst job I've had but you couldn't pay me to go back.

reviews.cons:
Right now the amount of employees are drowning in call volume. Back to back phone calls all day. 

Even if you’re promoted to a specialty phone line you still get stuff into High Net worth. Essentially all day instead of doing your job you have people with millions yelling at you, and you have to bend over and take it. As long as the rich people are happy, leadership doesn’t care about you doing the job you strived for.

2023 proved to be the year that brokerage firms will do anything to kiss up to the rich clients, at the expense of their employees. 

8 hours of back to back to back phone calls. You get 2 15 minute breaks and a 30 minute lunch. If you break those rules, or if they force you to take a 10 am lunch, you’re in trouble. They value rich clients over employees. 

Also if someone is in the central or eastern time zone, don’t force them to work till 7pm.

reviews.advice:
Pay your workers more!!! Giving “raises” that don’t even cover half of inflation is not a raise. The best talent is quickly leaving because of this which is showing in work quality and customer service. 
Leadership needs to hold themself accountable for bad decision making, and give employees true answers as to what they are doing to meet workers demands for a better work environment. To constantly ask us for feedback but ignore our complaints is extremely insulting. Many of us have brought up major changes that need to be made to directors which was immediately dismissed because he personally “didn’t see the need for it” although many workers in the room gave justifications for our demands. Sad that Schwab used to be such a respected company and corporate greed is causing the company to slowly collapse.
reviews.cons: The Schwab work environment has gotten tense between employees and leadership because they quite obviously do not care about us. When the initial announcement of return to office was sent, employees were only sent an email stating we all had 3 months before 3 days/week (that we cannot pick) in office was required. No one (below management level) even knew that they were considering this idea and this major change was randomly dropped on us. Employees gave so much push back they delayed the return to office but leadership constantly ignores the issues that workers bring up. The company wasn’t even properly prepared for us to return (parking garage STILL not sone, mo supplies, etc) Workers bring up the same issues (work flexibility, pay increases, tech updates, etc) but leaders constantly respond with ‘we’re looking into it’ every time these topics are brought up. Most people are looking to jump ship asap. It’s very obvious that lower level employees are taking the hit of bad decisions from executive council without any accountability from higher ups.

Support Work-Life Balance: Implement policies and programs that support a healthy work-life balance, such as flexible working arrangements, to reduce burnout and improve employee satisfaction.
Continuous Training: Invest in continuous training and development programs to ensure consultants are up-to-date with the latest financial products, services, and regulatory changes, enhancing their effectiveness and compliance.
Performance Metrics: Develop a balanced set of performance metrics that not only include financial targets but also client satisfaction, retention, and compliance adherence, to encourage a more holistic approach to performance evaluation.

Regulatory Compliance: Financial consultants must constantly stay abreast of and comply with complex regulatory requirements, which can be time-consuming and restrict certain business practices.
Market Risks: The performance of financial consultants is often tied to market conditions, which can be unpredictable and affect job stability and performance evaluations.
reviews.pros:

Career Growth Opportunities: There are ample opportunities for professional development and career advancement within the company, thanks to its size and diversity of services.
Learning Environment: The role often offers a steep learning curve and exposure to a wide range of financial products and services, enhancing professional knowledge and expertise.
Client Interaction: Financial consultants at Charles Schwab have the opportunity to build long-lasting relationships with clients, helping them achieve their financial goals, which can be personally rewarding.

reviews.cons:
So many. 
- back to the subject of pay, like a lot of companies who expect not just to make a profit and keep up with inflation, but to make a higher profit, they expect *people* to put up with “merit” increases that do not keep up with inflation and are based on rigged performance reviews.
- In my area, there is little opportunity for upward mobility, especially if you don’t want to be a people manager. Getting a promotion is very difficult, and apparently doesn’t help your salary much. Part of the problem is that in my area of expertise, Mastercard is like twenty years behind, so unless our leadership catches up quick (not hopeful), there won’t be any new positions senior to what I have now. So as my uncle advised me twenty years ago, if you want to make what you’re worth, you have to switch jobs. 
- part of the reason for being so far behind I think is that they hire from within way too often. People float around from here to there, and are very impressed with how much they know about Mastercard, but meanwhile have no real experience in highly specialized areas. And they really like to tell people who do have years of actual experience how to do their job, and they get away with that and with actively interfering while not doing their own job. This is not a generalization based on one person. It’s been a pattern for a couple years across multiple teams and continues to this day
- hypocrisy. Supposedly decency is a part of “the Mastercard way” but, starting with the most egregious of several examples, an awful, high ranking person, who people complained about to HR, who oversaw at least two major initiatives that utterly failed, and who sowed so much chaos and dysfunction I’m not sure our department will recover anytime soon, was rewarded with a fellowship. As if that’s not bad enough, this was announced right after layoffs (very expensive layoffs based on severance figures) that were made over budget concerns. 
- these concerns have also contributed to an environment where continuing education is not deemed important. Also, programs that are critical to an organization that claims to be data driven are expected to either bring in revenue or show a direct correlation to it, even though their purpose is to reduce risk and provide critical functions for programs that do bring in revenue
- AI hype: our leadership is very confident in their knowledge of AI, but seems to be stuck in an echo chamber that excludes so many considerations I am hearing about everywhere else. I’m also not hearing much from talk here about the huge sustainability concerns around AI, it’s just full steam ahead, which does not match the internal and external claims of a commitment to sustainability
 - healthcare coverage is terrible, I’m paying way more that I ever have for less. The one consolation was a free telemedicine service. They switched providers though, without any regard for the quality of the new one. Surprise, it’s terrible. Is that decent?
- apparently my state has a loop hole that allows employers to get away with paying out fewer vacation days, so I am no longer given my full vacation balance at the beginning of the year, which means if (when) I leave, I’ll get paid off much less, if anything, compared to what I would have if I left at the same time last test last year. So they’re cutting back on benefits, and then there’s the meager pay increases, which means people’s actual compensation has *gone down*. Is that decent?

reviews.cons:
Working as a cashier at Sherwin-Williams, like any job, has its downsides. Here are some potential cons:

1. Repetitive Tasks: Cashiering can involve performing the same tasks repeatedly, which may lead to boredom or monotony over time.

2. Customer Service Challenges: Dealing with a variety of customers, including those who may be impatient, unhappy, or difficult to please, can be stressful and emotionally taxing.

3. Handling Cash: Managing cash transactions carries a risk of errors, discrepancies, and potential security concerns, which can be demanding and require careful attention to detail.

4. Physical Demands: Cashiers may need to stand for long periods, which can lead to fatigue and discomfort, particularly during busy hours.

5. Limited Career Advancement: Cashier positions may have limited opportunities for career growth within the company, making it challenging to advance professionally.

6. Work Schedule: Depending on the store's operating hours, cashier shifts may include evenings, weekends, and holidays, which can disrupt work-life balance and personal commitments.

7. Fast-Paced Environment: Sherwin-Williams stores can get busy, especially during peak times or when there are promotions or sales events, leading to high-pressure situations and a fast-paced work environment.

8. Training Requirements: Cashiers may need to undergo extensive training to learn about Sherwin-Williams products, policies, and procedures, which can be time-consuming and overwhelming for some individuals.

9. Limited Benefits: Depending on the specific employment arrangement, cashier positions at Sherwin-Williams may offer limited benefits such as healthcare coverage, retirement plans, or paid time off compared to other roles within the company.

10. Exposure to Chemicals: In some cases, cashiers may be exposed to paint fumes or other chemicals used in Sherwin-Williams products, which could pose health risks or discomfort for those with sensitivities.
reviews.pros:
Working as a cashier at Sherwin-Williams can offer several advantages:

1. **Industry Experience**: You'll gain valuable experience in the retail industry, particularly in the paint and coatings sector, which could be beneficial if you're considering a career in this field or related industries.

2. **Product Knowledge**: Interacting with customers and handling transactions will deepen your understanding of Sherwin-Williams' products, their applications, and their benefits, which can be useful professionally and personally.

3. **Customer Interaction Skills**: Working as a cashier provides ample opportunities to develop strong customer service skills, including communication, problem-solving, and conflict resolution, which are valuable in any career path.

4. **Teamwork**: You'll likely work alongside a team of colleagues, fostering collaboration and teamwork skills that are essential in almost any work environment.

5. **Flexible Hours**: Retail positions often offer flexible scheduling options, allowing you to balance work with other commitments such as education or family responsibilities.

6. **Employee Discounts**: Many retail positions, including Sherwin-Williams, offer employee discounts on products, which can save you money on items you may need for personal projects or home improvement.

7. **Career Development Opportunities**: Sherwin-Williams is a large company with opportunities for advancement. Starting as a cashier could lead to roles in management, sales, or other areas within the company if you demonstrate dedication and skills.

8. **Stable Employment**: Sherwin-Williams is a well-established company with a strong presence in the paint and coatings industry, offering stable employment and potential job security.

9. **Skill Enhancement**: Handling transactions, managing inventory, and using point-of-sale systems will enhance your numerical and organizational skills, which are valuable in various professions.

10. **Networking**: Working at Sherwin-Williams provides opportunities to network with professionals in the industry, potentially opening doors to future career opportunities or collaborations.

Overall, working as a cashier at Sherwin-Williams can provide a platform for personal and professional growth, offering valuable skills and experiences that can benefit you in various aspects of your life and career.
