reviews.pros:
They are quite flexible depending on the team.
Good work and life balance.
Relatively easy to move around the company.

reviews.advice: C-Suite leadership needs a complete overhaul. The only two options I see for any positive change are municipalization or major leadership changes.
reviews.cons: The C-Suite leadership has made this company a place of dread and depression. The have hired an ineffective “lean management” firm which is not practicing lean and has created organizational decay and morale to fall to an all time low - they are toxic, nobody likes them, yet they have license to continue creating problems within the company. The CEO is now referring to shareholders as “our owners” and asking employees to use the same term - this is demeaning and gross. The CEO and his leadership don’t care about employees, or the public we serve, but rather have an obsession to bring “relentless value to our owners”. Think about that every time you pay your high Xcel Energy bill. There is a core of sycophants in the leadership that are afraid to speakup, and rather collect a paycheck, the board of directors also seem aloof to the problems the CEO and the COO have caused in the company.
reviews.pros: Peers are smart but becoming burnt out and depressed.

reviews.advice: actually listen to GLINT employee survey results, listen to employees more and investors less.
reviews.cons: virtual meeting while in office, disconnected and questionable leadership
reviews.pros: people. benefits, work satisfaction, flexibility

reviews.cons: No issues in the few months I have worked here.
reviews.pros: I can tell my boss wants me to succeed.

reviews.cons: Recent reorganization has resulted in layoffs.
reviews.pros: Working in the energy industry is generally a reliable employment option and Xcel has a long history and likely long future in this sector.

reviews.advice: Bring back diversity.
reviews.cons: But in the past 6 months multiple layoffs including hearing "we aren't concerned about attrition" multiple times by executives means they want to trim as much as possible. So much bloat was put into third party consultants to build large scale projects while neglecting what goes into the employees has left the company with bare bones. Then we were told we had to go back to an office that is now partly empty and leaving groups isolated. There is FAR less diversity at the company as most of the people who were pushed out were not part of the traditional core type of person to work at Xcel. And now I just interact with the same person type just in different departments. Everyone seems to be overworked and now it seems that the contractors are in more pressure to prove that their products are worth it.
reviews.pros: When I started during the pandemic, the company was very committed to making everyone feel part of a group. I felt seen and heard by the company. But the benefits are good.

reviews.cons: They don’t really care about lower level employees
reviews.pros: They were pretty good with time off

reviews.cons:
High Deductible insurance plan means you generally pay more in premiums than the plan covers if you are relatively healthy
Very strict expense management in recent months that reduced or completely got rid of benefits such as bonuses 
Minimal Staffing for some departments which limits when and how you can use your PTO
Can be stressful due to state regulatory requirements
Interdepartmental communication issues can lead to roadblocks
Outsourcing many in-house departments which can hurt job security
Many leadership positions vacated in recent months on top of additional layoffs and outsourcing
Company is profit driven but due to state regulations that inhibit increased revenue, this means that the lever of action used to increase profit is almost always cost reduction
reviews.pros:
Direct supervisors were very kind and wanted you to achieve your full potential
Diverse Workplace, accepting of those from all walks of life
Mix of teamwork and individual responsibilities
Solid benefits that keep the employee's future in mind
Opportunity for advancement and strong on the job training
reviews.summary: Great People but Corporate is Corporate

reviews.cons: Severely cutting expenses with a complete halt on travel, and introducing a "Voluntary Retirement Plan" as a means to reduce staff. The possibility of cutting AIP is looming, and uncertainty prevails. A high-ranking executive in the C-Suite is departing (one of the best IMO), marking the fourth VP or higher to leave this year. Morale has hit rock bottom, and many individuals I interact with are actively exploring other options. It appears the sole focus is on pleasing shareholders, while our stated values of Safe, Connected, Committed, and Trustworthy seem to be mere rhetoric. I find myself questioning whether management genuinely upholds these values or if they are just empty words. Over the past few months, leadership has taken actions that has eroded the trust of employees, and it could potentially take years to rebuild. There was a time when I took pride in declaring that I worked for Xcel. Unfortunately, that sentiment no longer holds true for me.
reviews.pros: I work with some of the greatest people.
reviews.summary: Used to be a great company

reviews.advice: New CEO? Need executives who actually stick up for employees and not just the company’s shareholders.
reviews.cons: The CEO has a big internal PR problem. Employees  have lost trust in his leadership and his integrity.  Fine if you want more in-person collaboration, but didn’t need to go to three set days a week, especially when employees are already stressed due to cost containment efforts. The Hybrid changes were very tone deaf and demonstrated how disconnected executives are from people doing the work. Workloads are high and burnout is rampant. Good people are killings themselves trying to meet expectations and complete piles of work, all while sitting in 6-8 hours of meetings every day and pivoting constantly as priorities change. Operating lean doesn’t just mean cutting back on people; it also means reprioritizing and focusing on core work. Haven’t seemed to figure out how to do that successfully yet. XE1, One XE Way, rally rooms - all of these programs are ineffective and don’t yield meaningful, sustainable results.
reviews.pros: Great people. Interesting industry. Many opportunities for growth upwards and laterally if you are a good performer and are intentional about development.

reviews.advice: Give employees more heads-up if you are having a layoff so they can have more time to find employment elsewhere in a timely manner that is good for them and not just Xcel Energy.
reviews.cons: Says its a stable job industry that doesn't have layoffs but I was apart of a mass layoff November 2023. Company not doing well financially.
reviews.pros: The company had a lot of goals on clean energy and to reduce carbon emissions by 80% by 2050.

reviews.cons: No work life balance, lack of transparency, unrealistic work expectations, promote hybrid for the culture but yet you sit on teams all day, toxic leadership.
reviews.pros: They pay is pretty good.

reviews.cons: Change in work from home policy, it would have been nice if executives had decided 1-2 days in office was sufficient permanently, needs better parking options and company should reimburse for parking downtown.
reviews.pros: Great company culture, supervisors are competent and treat employees well, collaborative team environment, healthy work-life balance.

reviews.advice: Keep doing what you are doing - investing in our Supply Chain, adding sellers across the US, and maintaining a people centric culture.
reviews.cons: With any large organization, at times we can be a little slower to move - we are a big ship.
reviews.pros: I have now reached 20 years with Grainger. This is a place you can build a rewarding career - I started as a sole contributor and the organization continued to invest in my success to the point I have reached leader of leaders role. I also love working for and with winners - Grainger is the leader in our industry and we've widened that lead over last few years - check out how our stock has performed compared to our competitors.

reviews.advice: Allow you're sales team more flexibility to perform the duties you've hired them to do.
reviews.cons: The amount of "busy work" they expect from their account managers is a overwhelming. Prepare for an extra 10-20 hours a week of internal busy work or staying on top of anything that's been sent to sourcing. The sourcing department and quotes are a train wreck but is also crucial to be a successful account manager. Everything within the company is BIG brothered by corporate. Account Managers have little control over anything within their book of business. Anything that needs to be done or requested requires an in depth business case which must then be approved by the district or regional manager....even basic discounts on anything. They offer little control but hold Account Managers accountable for EVERYTHING. They are quick to put account managers on a PIP if they have a bad half. If you're willing to work a minimum of 60 hours a week to maintain a normal book of business, nothing extra, then Grainger is your place to work! If you want to move up, you're required to make it known to your manager and begin the "professional development" process, meaning you do your job and also start attending meetings and completing work for the new role you hope to obtain, ie free labor for Grainger.
reviews.pros: Great company if you're new to sales. They have a great training program that lasts roughly 7 months. It's a very good program that even the most seasoned sales rep can learn something from. Decent pay as long as you're successful and meet your numbers.
reviews.summary: Good if you're new to sales

reviews.advice: Focus more on sales and strategy with AM vs just call times and call blocks. The data doesn't translate outside if 10% of the floor.
reviews.cons:
-Full of busy work.
-Very micromanaged from a distance.
-Management can sometimes play favorites.
-Disconnect from upper management to the sales floor.
-Call time is more important than sales 
revenue. 


There is a lot to like about Grainger. The company is great overall. But I'd avoid the sales floor. Look into sales support or technical support. CSGs are very inconsistent from AM to AM. It's really luck of the draw. I see people who do nothing get elevated or rewarded and people who grind miss goals constantly. I see managers play favorites with friends while doing zero to help people who work hard. Not everyone though. There are some good leaders. But you never know what sort of accounts you end up with. You also have to carry the weight of other less profitable divisions in all aspects. So the pressure is 24/7.
reviews.pros:
-Nice facility
-flexible office/at home
-good benefits
-good training 
-Pay can be good if luck into a good CSG.
reviews.summary: Good intro sales role - Metrics over sales.

reviews.advice: This company could learn a lot from actually bringing in younger employees into these decisions for input, as well as updating the incredibly outdated logo, social media, and marketing as a whole. Recognize that burnout is real across the majority of the sales function currently.
reviews.cons:
First and foremost, this company is incredibly out of touch and lacks any sort of progressive mindset. Managers regularly are robotic and show no feeling or empathy towards things in your personal life. Grainger doesn't acknowledge Pride month, externally or internally. We also don't truly acknowledge MLK day - it is a full working day. If you get COVID, be prepared to burn PTO even though there is plenty of work that can be done at home as they do not have a policy in place to allow for extra days if you contract COVID. Even if you get it from a customer. 

Next - sales team specifics. The expectations of sales members are insane. The amount of metrics you are expected to hit across the board on both Salesforce and with your sales goals are exhausting. Burnout is prevalent across my entire team and among others on different teams throughout the sales org. So much luck plays into this job that is incredibly frustrating. You can take 10 steps forward with a few accounts, then 30 steps back after a national contract is lost (which is completely out of your hands). Evaluation needs to be done on how to make this more realistic for everyone across the board. Decisions being made seem to be largely made by boomers who are completely out of touch with the younger world. Opportunities for internal growth are rare.
reviews.pros: Great benefits. 21 days PTO. Uncapped bonus.
reviews.summary: Great potential, but out of touch and lacking in progressive values

reviews.advice: Be the advocate for your team that you should be, and speak up to upper management about their unrealistic metrics that are placed upon employees.
reviews.cons: Many departments (including HR) are outsourced and are poorly managed/controlled by upper management. Getting assistance from HR is a complete waste of time. Upper management is completely unrealistic on what it means to provide customer support. The company website is poorly managed by an outsourced company full of inaccuracies and constantly needs correcting, Current model of customer support encourages employees to give bad information to customers and to "pass off" customers to other employees instead of doing the job that is expected of them without any correction from management. Technical Product Support feels more like a "marketing tool" for investors rather than true support for the customer.
reviews.pros: Compensation is good. Some flexibility in schedule. Company has more remote opportunities than other companies in the same category. Most of the co-workers I have met are very helpful. The company provides lengthy job training but could be improved.
reviews.summary: Poor HR, Management Subpar, Benefits Are Ok At Best

reviews.advice:
My advice to management: Stay the course. Keep playing the long game, not quarterly games. Put the customer first, always. Make decisions to strengthen Grainger for generations to come.

The great companies focus on what matters most. Grainger does that today. With discipline, it can do so for generations to come.
reviews.cons:
Of course, no company is perfect. As they grow, some challenges emerge:

• Complexity inherent in a global enterprise
• Raising the skill level bar within the Grainger Technology Group (GTG) higher
• Streamlining platforms and architecture, it's bloated and disorganized (cut platforms relentlessly, the pain will be temporary)

But these are merely growing pains. The fundamentals are sound.
reviews.pros:
Grainger gets the big things right. The company provides tremendous value to customers, makes long-term bets, and cherishes its people. This is rare.

But with scale comes complexity. Logistics and bureaucracy creep in at a large enterprise like Grainger. Yet even at its size, Grainger has far less red tape than smaller companies I've seen.

The culture shines through in their actions:

• Working hard on worthwhile projects
• Giving people visibility into their impact
• Relentlessly delivering value to customers
• Treating every employee with respect
• Empowering people to achieve great things
reviews.summary: People focused company with long-term vision

reviews.advice:
Walk the talk.  Know what is really happening in your branches. 
 Make sure company values are being lived by local management.  Take complaints seriously and follow up with employees when problems are brought to your attention. Treat your associates as the important stakeholders that they are.  Don't boast to employees about company performance and multi-million dollar projects and then give no year-end bonus to hourly employees with no explanation.
reviews.cons:
I was so excited to join this company back in 2022. I had been a customer in other locations for many years and was impressed with their stated values and work environment when I interviewed. I quickly learned, however, that the company's stated values are meaningless at this branch. reviews.cons:
As a FSE, you are vastly underpaid at Baxter for your responsibilities working on critical care equipment. You are signing off on a instrument you service and sometimes that same device will be rolled back onto a patient within the hour. If something happens to that patient, the onus will be on you along with the company, though mostly you. Be prepared to be scrutinized over such patient incident while getting paid somewhere comparable to a cable man installer with far less liability. The responsibilities for this job just doesn't align with their starting salary structure, period. Shameful.

You have wait for someone to retire or leave for the chance of becoming a senior FSE. If there is another senior level in your area, you cannot be elevated to a senior as well. The company has put out this notion that this is not the case anymore but I've yet to see this very fact get disproven.

Guys in the field justify their lack of fair salaries by working longer hours, but even that over the past year the company is hammering back on overtime a great deal. And of course work/life balance comes into question whenever you're relying on some overtime to make a decent living.

Worst of all, the supervisor for the North east coast is novice at the leadership position as well as forgetful. Two bad combinations. Also doesn't expound and elaborate as others normally would when given out instructions, so you're sometimes left with an awkward silence over the phone thinking more is still left to be said. Would not recommend this leadership at the local level.

reviews.advice: Need more one on one training for management positions.  Realistic expectations for work load/ customer service vs payroll because there are never enough people on staff to accommodate the level of service expected and be able to keep the store stocked and cleaned as it should be.  Not having product fully stocked negatively effects sales but you can't get it done for having to hold every single customer's hand.  There HAS to be more people on staff, or else better scheduling for off hours stocking, and in some cases both.
reviews.cons: They want caviar customer service on a spam payroll budget.  The customers have been trained to expect personal shopper type customer service but there are never enough people on staff to accommodate that type of service.  So every customer acts like they are the only customer in the store and expects your attention immediately even when you are obviously already helping someone or answering one of the 4000 phone calls every day and are on the phone.  It's very stressful and frustrating.  The company also needs to invest in more thorough training, especially for management positions.  Working outside in the cold and rain are not great when you're not used to it.

reviews.advice: I think management needs to realize that the team members that work underneath them are typically working at TSC just to get by. This is not a company that you tend to stay at and make a career out of. Quit making enemies out of your staff by bad mouthing them behind their backs. It's not that personal, we are paid minimum wage and often not scheduled a lot. Essentially, you're getting what you pay for.
reviews.cons: The pay is minimum wage and hours can be scarce when fully staffed. Also in my experience, you may get someone in a management position that isn't necessarily great for morale. They seem to forget that they are dealing with employees who are paid the least and maybe aren't being scheduled as much as they like. When you're paid little, work less, and putting up with a grouch don't be surprised when employees walk out on you.
reviews.pros: TSC has an all-around good philosophy for meeting and helping customers that incorporates everyone on shift. Everyone is really encouraged to interact and help each other. 4. Base salary is $24,000 for 2 years and you get paid half your salary

reviews.advice:
Pay workers competitively - including compared to other parts of the company.
Acknowledge that the development of SMEs and Managers in roles is critical rather than constant reshuffling. In my 4 years of work with Entergy, I've had 5 managers.
Expedite hiring processes - the new Human Capital Management Initiative, Revision 2, is toxic and the result of leadership positions having jobs fabricated specifically for them. 
Reduce Corporate Oversight - or require them to actually help instead of shoving the burden of admin work off of the individual sites. 
Focus on performance & employee satisfaction, rather than the Appearance of Performance (Indicators). Performance Indicators are not a comprehensive metric of actual issues within the company, and it shows in the yearly employee satisfaction surveys.
Benchmark Entergy Non-Nuclear Training for Training funding - why does the side of the company that focuses on training have substandard training facilities/funding?
reviews.cons:
*(see above upward-mobility issues) Senior leadership often refuses to accept that retention/turnover is a major issue stressing out employees, and when they do they don't accept that they're a major part of the problem.

Many in senior leadership view remote-work as "taking a day off" and discourage it despite it being a company policy for many positions.

reviews.cons:
There are plenty of downsides to working there. I worked in the Buildings & Places division.

They claimed to have the work. All they had were tenant improvement projects instead of the large building projects they claimed to have. I was treated very poorly. I was given subpar work while my younger colleagues were given the massive building projects.

My colleagues were not good at designing their structures. They missed basic engineering concepts like how to anchor structures to wood. I had to correct a majority of their mistakes.

They did not have many typical details. This explains why they burn through budgets. The constant changing of staff means that budgets get blown because the new engineer must approve what the laid off engineer did.

They use outsourcing of structural engineers alot. When I was asked to review their work, it was not complete. They did not even have calculations prepared. They had no clue about building codes.

My unprofessional boss was a narcissist. He harassed me constantly. I was never notified of any issues for several months until he sprang a Performance Improvement Plan on me. I asked for evidence behind the PIP. My boss and HR refused to provide it to me. My boss took the side of the other person without even consulting me first. I was punished constantly. He gaslit me constantly. The only way I could keep track of what he said was to have a tape recorder on me at all times. How does someone improve if they do not know what they did wrong? My boss offered me no praise at all. My boss is the jealous type that fears what he does not understand or cannot tolerate.

After I was issued the PIP, my boss increased his petty and unjustified attacks against me. He stood over me and treated me like a criminal. He sent me instant messages every hour without giving me a chance to do my work. He called me up on Teams constantly. He asked me to give him deadlines for projects before I had a chance to review them. Then when I did not meet the deadlines, he would scold me like a child.

HR harassed me constantly and told me to keep quiet. They kept telling me they never laid off any employees they PIPped. That was a lie because I was laid off thanks to toxic employees.

My boss ordered me to ignore structural safety issues. I was asked to jeopardize my professional engineering licenses for the firm's profitability.

My boss asked me to only approve responses to comments of building plans. The problem with that is that the buildings have no complete lateral and gravity systems. This boss cared only about profit for the job, not whether these buildings were safe.

Company has unlimited PTO. Good luck trying to use it. After I was laid off, I got no money for unused vacation time.

My boss ordered me to charge my time to jobs that I did not do because he ordered the job codes locked out.

My boss got upset because I charged time to Overhead on videos that corporate made their employees watch. My boss never did this with any of the other employees.

They never ordered my business cards. They never ordered my headset so I could talk through Teams. I was given an unsafe one to use. It had exposed wires.

They never got all the software I needed to do my job. My boss harassed me for not having it. I never had it because he failed to sign off on the paper work.

This company is always laying people off by claiming they do not have the work yet they are hiring new people. They refused to let those people transfer to over departments. Many of the laid off people were over 40 and close to retirement.

The company is laying people off so they can hire lower salaried individuals.

The company had plenty of openings in other business sectors, yet I was not allowed to transfer into any of them because my boss laid me off. A day before that happened, he congratulated me for my transfer yet it never got approved. My boss lies so much it is like water running out of a fire hydrant. Even when it was on tape, this boss denied what he said. This boss even went on social media to delete the videos of him and his co-worker harassing me. Guess they do not want people to see the toxic work environment for themselves.

The firm had the audacity to make me sign a severance agreement asking me not to talk about the harassment they put me through. My boss almost tried to kill me due to the stress I had to endure.

Being an admired company is a complete joke because they treat their employees badly.

Recently, a long-term employee filed suit against them for cooking their books and illegal termination. That employee said the CEO loved having high turnover. This is a big fat recipe for a major disaster.

You need to run away from this company as fast as you can.

You will get basic cross-training across the register and kitchen, but might end up only on register or only in kitchen because management thinks you are best suited to work in that position.
UNRELIABLE INCOME
If you want more than 20 hours a week, you will have to be available from 3 AM to midnight, or be ready and willing to cover for people who call off sick. If you want to work reasonable hours, you will get between 10 and 25 hours a week.
FAST-PACED
Sometimes it will only be two people in the store- one at register and one in the kitchen. Many orders will come in and you will have to scramble to keep up, while doing dishes and keeping the warmers full. You won't get breaks unless you eat during slow periods, or if someone is kind enough to cover for you while you run to the restroom.
LAZY PEOPLE
Depending on who you're working with, you can either have someone who works alongside you, or someone who leaves to smoke or chat with customers. People do not follow the rules, but don't complain because management is too busy working themselves sick.
reviews.pros:
EASY WORK
Whether you're on register, in kitchen, or in cooler, the work is basic and simple. A 12 year old could do it.
DECENT PEOPLE
Most of the people keep to themselves and don't annoy you unless you annoy them. Management does answer questions about the job and most coworkers will show you how to do something if you're having trouble.
DECENT PAY
Illinois minimum wage is $14/hour, which makes it worth your time. You get time and a half pay on certain holidays.

reviews.advice:
I would like to address some observations and suggestions regarding our workforce management practices at Norfolk Southern. The recent 7% reduction in staff across non-union positions has prompted me to reflect on how we handle underperformance within the company.

It's my belief that we could potentially avoid significant layoffs if each manager takes a more proactive stance on addressing employee performance. Instead of relying mainly on mass layoffs, exploring alternative strategies like implementing performance improvement plans (PIPs) could prove to be a more constructive and fair approach. Timely interventions for struggling employees, combined with regular and comprehensive performance reviews, could contribute to a more positive and productive work environment.

Creating a culture of continuous feedback and performance management might help prevent future mass layoffs. Identifying and addressing performance issues early on can foster a workplace where employees feel supported in their growth and development.

I understand the challenges managers face when making tough decisions, but I believe a proactive and strategic approach to employee performance management will benefit both individuals and the overall success of Norfolk Southern. Your consideration of these suggestions is appreciated, and I look forward to seeing the positive impact they could have on our workforce.
reviews.cons:
In recent times, the balance between pros and cons at Norfolk Southern has tilted, with the disadvantages starting to outweigh the positives. The existing issues with upper management's disconnection from day-to-day operations and a less competitive compensation structure have become more pronounced, impacting the overall work experience. The limited growth opportunities at certain career levels and the challenges in navigating internal mobility have contributed to a sense of stagnation for employees. As a result, the current state of affairs at Norfolk Southern suggests a need for strategic improvements to address these concerns and ensure a more balanced and fulfilling work environment for its workforce. 

Furthermore, an additional concern that has become increasingly apparent is the management's tendency to retain employees who contribute very little to the overall productivity of the team. It appears that some managers are reluctant to address or let go of underperforming staff, creating a dynamic where unproductive employees continue to linger within the organization. This situation has become demoralizing for those of us who consistently contribute to the company's success, as it fosters an atmosphere of inequity and frustration. Addressing this issue and fostering a more performance-driven culture would significantly contribute to improving the overall morale and effectiveness of the workforce at Norfolk Southern.
reviews.pros: Working at Norfolk Southern has been a positive experience marked by several notable pros. One of the standout aspects is the commendable work/life balance the company promotes. This balance allows employees to excel in their professional roles while still enjoying personal time, fostering a healthy and sustainable work environment. The corporate office is equipped with excellent amenities, enhancing the overall workplace experience. From well-maintained facilities to thoughtful employee spaces, Norfolk Southern invests in creating a comfortable and enjoyable workspace for its staff.

reviews.advice:
1.	The fundamental issue with respect to the appearance of fairness in performance evaluation is based upon the fact that the translation of raw scores into normalized bell distribution scores is NOT INTUITIVE. CPAs, Attorneys, and non-mathematicians are not trained to understand the theory behind normalization. Our world is a tik & tie, concrete, raw-score world. In an extremely high performing culture like TTD, bolstered by this kind of paradigm, 100 tNPS, etc. scores will never feel fair when they equal a 77%tile normalization score. I recommend that all forms of normalization be discontinued. As a plan B, I recommend that Intuit relegate all normalization exercises to a back-office tool that helps the reporting team to a. determine what raw score will mark the difference between each rating group, and b. publish only the raw score boundaries between the ratings. This will be much more intuitive for the team as a whole and will feel fairer! As a background comment: Remember that the only exposures 99% of us have had to normalization of performance scores was when college professors "grade on the curve". That always resulted in normalization scores going up, not down. Thus, our system is not intuitive; does not seem fair; and puts tremendous downward pressure on morale and retention of the best talent!
2.	For me, one of the biggest paradoxes of season TY23 is talk about a simpler, more focused rating/ranking system when it looks like we have more than tripled the number of metrics we have to manage and be evaluated by.

Whether full-time or seasonal you feel seen & heard. They provide amazing benefits for seasonal employees giving you the opportunity to take advantage of the 401K & ESPP plans. You receive a performance based bonus at the end of the season. 

The opportunity for growth into higher & full time position is encouraged, if you wish to do so. 

The knowledge & experience you gain from working with tax experts all over the country in unapparelled. Intuit also provides the opportunity to further your education, encouraging and providing classes for uncredentialled experts to get their Enrolled Agents license.

Overall my experience has been amazing.

The old culture has seriously deteriorated. Edward Jones used to be about always doing the right thing, taking care of family and community, not making money the reason for your life "money has never been my god..."
The home office used to treat advisors like they served the advisors. It was a respectful collaborative effort. Now it feels like policy, how you operate your office, what product and how you push clients to those products is emphasized. Too many people focused on increasing revenue from existing clients. 
Home office people can often be rude, home office associates can occasionally be found that "talk down" to advisors. The culture of respect and collaboration are largely dead. reviews.advice: You are expected to learn from a bunch of modules and a few zoom meeting with several other brand new BOA’s. You are literally pitched into the job the first day and expected to answer calls and navigate through the system with nobody to show you anything. Having a rotating BOA like an experienced On Call to come and train the first week would be extremely helpful but the FA’s don’t want to pay for it and neither does the company. If you end up working for an FA that doesn’t want to come in to work much you are left dealing with making up excuses to the clients why they can’t speak to the FA when they call. The attitude of the FA can either make the work environment good or miserable and you have no idea what you will end up with when you get hired.  The company itself tries to make a good work environment but when the FA does whatever they want in their own office you don’t benefit from what HQ is trying to implement. Several other BOA’s I met in my region seemed to be struggling with FA attitude issues. So it seems like getting a bad FA is more likely than getting a good one.

Don't just communicate to us what great leaders should be doing at Jones, but instead ensure that leaders are actually living up to the standards. Get rid of the weeds.

Jekyll and Hyde. reviews.advice: There is literally no hope for this company unless the board decides to fire most of the C-level executives and directors.  This place is a lost cause.
reviews.cons:
Let's talk.

The company has been growing like crazy, and one thing that was never thought about was "can we actually hire at a sustainable rate, and scale accordingly?"  The answer was no on both counts.  Software engineers at Wayfair have a history of disappearing.  People who enter labs have an especially low success rate (70% make it through, and less than 50% last a whole year).  It's basically their way to run people through a burnout gauntlet, and see who survives.  And then you have the stories of the people who come in to work and are just asked to resign.  You'll see hints of it here on Glassdoor if you dig, and it's even worse than what you read.

They actually gathered all the engineers for a big meeting at the beginning of this year.  And they said that they were sorry that people felt scared and were sad that people felt like management didn't care.  Which is exactly how we felt.  They promised that their door was open, and they were going to work hard to set things right.  One person out of 500 stood up and asked a really cutting question.  AND THEN THEY FIRED HIM!  And there were 3 completely different official reasons given about it.  It's crazy.

The leaders also started up an engineering meeting to keep everyone on the same page and answer anonymous questions.  One time someone asked why we couldn't get snow days off, because it was tough to shovel for 3 to 4 hours and still work an 8 hour day.  So the leaders proceeded to talk down to us and reprimand us for even thinking about asking a question like this.

Turnover has been high over the past year, and the best people are leaving.  This worries management, but they still have no idea that the problem is actually them creating a terrible environment.

So if you're a good person who cares about the person next to you and leaving things better than you found them, don't bother applying here.  But if you're not, and you just want to keep your head down and not question anything, then this is the perfect place for you.  And if that's what you want, Wayfair gets 5 stars.  

Amazing career opportunities if you want to have the same job forever.  
Incredible senior management that value untrustworthiness.  
A fantastic culture of watching people next to you disappear.  

It's truly a perfect company.

employerResponses.response:
First, I wanted to thank you for providing feedback. Second, I am very sorry to hear that your experience was far from ideal. I know it can be hard to give feedback if you feel management is the problem, but leadership would love to learn about these issues to refine the Wayfair employee experience. We do try to create an open and transparent environment; one thing we’ve started doing is department-wide anonymous surveys. This has been helpful in identifying issues where people don’t feel comfortable speaking up for whatever reason and pinpoint where any issues may exist.

As you noted, the company is growing very quickly - our Engineering team alone has grown tenfold over the past five years. I won’t pretend we get it right all the time, but we do aim to scale our teams and our systems reasonably to meet the rapid growth of our business, and we rely on employee feedback to refine these processes. To that end, we’ve put a lot of time and energy into our interview process. And, we closely track our voluntary and involuntary attrition rates to make sure we are keeping high employee retention and so that we can immediately nip any potential issues in the bud. For Wayfair Labs, we’ve made huge strides since the beginning of this program, and our average success rate is now over 90%, with several classes at 100%. We also run management trainings on giving, receiving and soliciting feedback. In these trainings - and in general - we encourage respect for all teammates and partners, communication and collaboration, and we try create opportunities for people to take on new challenges. 

I am very excited about the work we’re doing to solve tough challenges and there’s an exciting opportunity for our employees to do big things – our goal is to build a team that feels encouraged and empowered to do so. I’m very sorry you didn’t have the experience we try to cultivate. 

Once again, thank you for this feedback.

reviews.advice: Be more transparent, talk with more junior folk, and see if there are ways to bring more empathy to your communications.
reviews.cons:
Wayfair is a retail company, not a technology company. There isn't a lot of attention or understanding of technology, especially in senior leadership inner circles. 
The company is trying very hard to cut costs and as a result has gone though multiple rounds of layoffs, as well as moving more positions to Bangalore. There isn't much of an understanding on the implications and churn quickly moving a large percentage of the workforce to a vastly different time zone creates. There will likely be more layoffs and moving of roles offshore, so would suggest anyone looking for a mid-senior position really dig into whether they think the role at Wayfair will last before accepting a job.
Finally, trust in senior leadership is at an all time low. A lot of the messaging from senior leadership (c-suite) has seemed obtuse, some of it even landing the c-suite in business insider for claiming people needed to work harder to keep up.

reviews.advice:
After almost 6 years of working here, in the same position and the same department, I don’t think there is anything constructive I can say that would realistically address the issues I’ve experienced. It’s a culture problem, and the culture has become almost cult-like in its structure. “You’re either with us or against us”, and god bless you if you’re in the latter group…

I’m sorry, but I refuse to drink the koolaid and subscribe to the “boy’s club” mentality that you seem to think is the only way to successfully motivate your employees. It’s disgusting, it’s exhausting, and it’s disheartening. I can’t believe I could work for a company seemingly doing great, life-saving work and yet leave site every day feeling absolutely terrible about myself.
reviews.cons:
- The promise of ease of movement within the company is a blatant lie. Especially if you start in manufacturing, it is notoriously difficult to move to another department to further your professional development - either you’re doing too poor of a job that no one else will want you, or you’re doing too good of a job that they don’t want to have to replace you. 

- Unsurprisingly, once you start to struggle with maintaining a healthy work/life balance, management and HR will pounce at any sign of weakness and use it as an excuse to withhold promotions. They’ll blow smoke up your butt and commend you for going “above and beyond” and being a “go-to person” for any extra work they need doing, but will feign concern and empathy when you need support and accommodations. 

- Little is ever done to alleviate concrete issues between two employees working on the same shift, and the overwhelming mindset at Regeneron is that everyone should be able to work with everyone or you’re deemed a “problem employee”. I’ve had to endure over a year of gaslighting and antagonistic behavior from a male coworker who’s work performance has proven to be regularly subpar (while mine is constantly commending for being high), and when this quickly began to take a toll on my mental health, I was invalidated time and time again. My honesty was used against me, I was told I was making excuses (which made me afraid to even be forthright with the issues that inevitably continued), and my (25 year old) HR BP went so far as to bring me into a meeting to tell me that “it seems like [I’m] on the verge of a mental health crisis” to which her solution was an e-mail to me with copy and pasted “resources” (most of which were so obviously not applicable to me at all) so that she could check a box off and convince herself that she had done her job well. 

-If someone, especially someone in your management chain, doesn’t like you - RUN. Move to a difference shift, a different department, or a different company altogether because a target has been painted on your back and nothing good will come from you staying where you are. It really is about who you know at Regeneron, and even more so who you’re friends with. Word travels fast, including personal and biased accounts of you through the lens of whomever has a problem with you.

- As soon as you make it known that you aren’t completely and 100% satisfied with everything, you fall into the category of the “red, frowny face people” (current employees should get this). Once that happens, the powers that be could not care less what you have to say, and are basically waiting for you to leave. If you leave Regeneron for any reason, good or bad, you are dead to them.
reviews.pros:
- There are two kinds of employees in manufacturing - ones that drink the koolaid and ones that don’t. If you find yourself on a team with your kind of people, then that will increase your likelihood of not having a crappy day at work because you’ll be spending at least 40 hours a week with those people.

- As someone who really benefits from weekly therapy sessions, I’ve really valued the health benefits thus far as my insurance leaves me with no copay, making every session completely free to me.

- The commute from where I live (in downtown Albany) is about 5 minutes, and about 15 minutes when I lived in downtown Troy.

reviews.advice: If you're not part of the solution then you're part of the problem.
reviews.cons: I worked here for almost 6 years and it was a dream come true for me. I couldn't believe how horrible it turned out to be. At first it was fun and exciting, but it quickly turned into a more toxic environment than anyone could imagine. I can speak to the on-air production side as well as the business side, not to customer service or anything like that. The culture there is that employees are treated like it's rush week at a sorority. Regardless of their level, the employees that have been there longer than you are condescending, mean, and manipulative. Unexpectedly, the men here were actually the only ones who were normal and sane, all the women above entry level (except literally 2 or 3) were very much "I suffered to get here so now I'll make you suffer". I want to be clear that this wasn't normal catty attitudes/behavior, this was fully hostile work environment, laughing at you while you're crying, ridiculing kind of stuff, invading your privacy/asking for details about doctor appointments, counting minutes you're not at your desk, just basically constant harassment. The worst of it was within merchandising but the toxicity runs deep and throughout the entire site, including human resources, marketing, programming, planning, etc. I went to HR, requested it be off the record and that no action be taken, after months of dealing with it to try to figure a way out of the situation and anything I could do to cover my bases. They immediately met with my entire team from my immediate supervisor all the way up to the vice president of my department, HR didn't even tell me but my team did. It's actually insane. I don't know if it's something taught at the Florida state colleges or what. This wasn't my first job, this wasn't me being too soft, this wasn't me expecting to be given the world. I'm pretty tough and rebound quickly, but I haven't rebounded from this. When I left I took a necessary break from working at all because it was truly traumatic. But it's been years now and I still haven't been able to go back and work for corporate America again because of this place. It sounds SO dramatic but ... this is the truth. I wouldn't recommend this company to anyone, ever.

reviews.advice:
Respected CEO,

I believe that organizational culture stems from the leadership. I noticed a disapproving glance from you when I entered a group meeting late and took a seat in the front row. Although you didn't verbalize your disappointment, I sensed it. I had a valid reason for my tardiness, but it seemed unimportant to you.

You strike me as someone who doesn't entertain excuses, and I appreciate that trait. My point is, it's crucial to gather all the facts before forming a judgment.

Furthermore, I want to bring to your attention that there is negative talk circulating about you within the workplace. These discussions happen freely and without hesitation, and while some criticisms may hold merit, much of it is detrimental and unprofessional. I understand if this doesn't concern you.

I express these observations with the utmost respect.
reviews.cons:
With all due respect...

COVID took a toll on AvisBudget Group. Many long-serving employees I encountered, with 15 years or more of tenure, seemed burned out, reflecting in their attitudes. Those who didn't display this burnout often seemed insincere, in my view.

Morale is at an all-time low, with seasoned employees feeling burned out, leading to toxic and negative behavior. Positive conversations about the company are rare during casual discussions.

To their credit, AvisBudget tries to boost morale with occasional "appreciation" days. However, my group perceived these efforts as artificial and insincere.

Certain employees who should retire are still present. They've mastered using Performance Improvement Plans (PIPs) to dismiss new employees who challenge their tenure or don't align with their management style.

HR's interventions are minimal, and they have procedures that allow managers to target and justify terminations easily.

Again, I express this with all due respect...

If you anticipate a fair and constructive Mediation session or PIP, you'll likely be disappointed. If they decide they want you out, you'll be let go regardless of your dedication. The company prioritizes metrics over its employees.

I felt undervalued and unappreciated during my time there.

Challenges and setbacks are part of life. It's a continuous learning process; either you grasp the lesson or step away.

AvisBudget must learn from my departure, or they risk repeating similar issues.

Once more, I share these thoughts with all due respect.

reviews.cons:
Pay: Leadership will tell you that you will be paid market rate, but this has been an ongoing issue for years. Whatever they pay you is less than what you should make. They manipulate the description of your role to minimize it, to the extent of referring to it as an "entry level" position but it is anything but entry. They tell the market you do less than what you do, and they get away with paying you less as a result.

Leadership: Leadership constantly lies about the direction of the department. Part of it is genuine dishonesty but the majority of it is a constant change of leadership. It is similar to politics where each president comes in with their ideals and is replaced by someone who functions the opposite. This leaves progress in the department at a halt. Managers cycle out as well. They come in with a new idea, implement it, tell their leadership "It worked" and then add it to their resume so that they can leave the department. It is essentially a self-fulfilling prophecy. The result is obvious with even a hint of foresight. You end of creating roles that are over encumbered with no clear delineation of tasks and no clear scope of job responsibility. This becomes even worse when considering punishment as it can be unclear if you are even the person at fault for customer frustration or system issues. Although billing is key to any insurance company, Unum's billing department functions as a steppingstone for leadership to grow and develop themselves rather than their teams.

Difficulty: The systems you will use will be antiquated outside of Salesforce. You will be working with macros that require a lot of hand holding. As a result, the learning curve is steep and the even seasoned team members have to ask for help daily. This is especially hard on new team members. This also means that the systems you are learning are not very transferable in regard to skillset.

Training: If you feel that you are not learning or feel unprepared it is likely because you are. You will have learning material to read through and will have some 1 on 1 time but there is so much to learn that you could be familiar with the systems ahead of time and you would still struggle. Expect to constantly ask questions to your more seasoned team members. You will have to wait for a response from them but once again your peers will be kind and helpful. With this being said, definitely reach out to them and do not feel like an irritant. They are well aware of your circumstances and will go out their way to help you.

The Deal: When you accept the position, you will be locked in your role for 18 months. It is not unusual for a role to require new hires to stay in role for some time especially if there is high attrition, but you have to ask yourself why a year and a half. It is because of attrition and difficulty of the role. People who have managed to last the 18 months are posting out rapidly. If you are hoping to use this role to get your foot in the door at Unum, I would suggest finding any other door. Other departments are not like this one and you will be fine there. Unum as a company is well organized but not all departments are equal.

reviews.cons:
-The workload is EXTREME for a position that pays sub 50k. You will work non-stop and the claims never stop coming. There is no lull in business. There is no down time. It's like waking up to run 2 marathons every single day.
-Cultish corporate culture. Some people that work there are very into Unum the company, and have somehow taken on their job as part of their personality.
-The training is inadequate and you probably only learn about 25% of what you need to know in order to perform your job. 
-The amount of knowledge that you must retain and access every single day is intimidating. They advise you to use "workflows", but there isn't a workflow for MANY situations. Because of this, it's almost impossible to approve a claim without involving another person.
-There are a lot of team meetings that take away time from everyday work. 
-I was easily working 12+ hours a day to keep up with my activities. Activities are little tasks that pop up in your view for you to complete on your claim load. These activities can take anywhere from a few seconds or 30 minutes to complete and I routinely had more than 100 activities to start my day every day, with more being added to the list as the day progressed.
-You will have a hard time doing your job without waiting for input from other employees. There's no good way to manage your workload because it's all dependent on someone else agreeing with you and adding their piece.
-It's insurance work and that comes with approvals and denials. You will probably be talking with a lot of medical professionals to explain claims decisions and sometimes those phone calls are incredibly tense. It's also very tough explaining the medical rationale Unum's nurses and doctors reached to deny a claim when the claimant's doctors are heavily disagreeing with the decision, and you are not the person that made the decision.
-The claimants can be incredibly hostile. You will be yelled at eventually. Claimants have your extension and can call you at all hours. It doesn't matter if you have a billion hours worth of work to do, if a claimant calls you have to prioritize that call. The company tracks your call metrics and you can get in trouble for not answering your phone enough. You will also get transfers from the customer service reps.
-On top of your regular work (activities) and incoming phone calls you're receiving, you're also getting a steady stream of emails from within Unum as well as from the claimants HR managers, doctors, etc. 
-There are a lot of employees at Unum that like to pass the buck, and because the DBS role is one that requires you to know a lot about a lot of things (the details of specific policies, medical knowledge around approving/denying claims, tax implications, state disability policies that often offset the benefits Unum provides, etc.) many people feel comfortable forwarding you emails and telling you to take care of something outside your scope of duties. 
-Open Concept office is abysmal. They tried to sell it as, "we're getting with the times! This environment will spur teamwork and collaboration!" What they actually did was doubled the amount the employees they could fit into a room and made a very noisy, germy and distracting environment for people who don't actually need to "collaborate".
-Chronically under-staffed. This role is incredibly demanding and burn-out is high. I saw many fellow employees file disability claims for themselves because of the stress of the job. Productivity is through the roof but you will not be compensated fairly. This role is classified as exempt, so you will not receive overtime once you are no longer a trainee.

It’s literally turning into a high school complete with lockers. Employees went to college to be professionals. But yet leaders treated us all as if we were children again. These employees worked so hard during Covid. And leaders rewarded with a bait and switch then act shocked when engagement scores keep going down.

The severance package was nice, but I was absolutely devastated, by the way it all went down. Just my manager and this new HR employee in a conference room. They broke the news, I sat there in shock, and then was immediately followed to my desk to pack my things and leave. They told me someone would send me everything I left behind at my desk, but I should’ve fought to collect all my belongings because there were some items I never got back, and when I followed up I was told my desk had been completely cleared, which in my mind means they just tossed everything else. The ending 100% sucked, but I’m still glad I worked there in the end because I gained valuable experience.

* Product at Expedia can be a hit or miss depending on your team. There's opportunities to do impactful work and feel great with your own team- but the folks in your team need to be up for that too. * Product management at Expedia requires stepping on a lot of toes and self-initiative to create great products, there's so many people working at different paces and across different time zones. reviews.advice:
Foster Open Communication:

Encourage transparent and frequent communication between leaders and employees. This includes regular updates, open-door policies, and town halls where employees can voice concerns and provide feedback.

Invest in Leadership Training:

Provide ongoing training and development opportunities for leaders to enhance their management skills, emotional intelligence, conflict resolution abilities, and understanding of diversity and inclusion practices.

Supportive Leadership Style:

Shift towards a more supportive leadership style that empowers employees, acknowledges their contributions, and fosters an environment of growth and development. This includes mentoring programs and regular performance feedback.

Promote Employee Well-Being:

Prioritize the well-being of employees by implementing work-life balance policies, mental health support programs, and wellness initiatives that help reduce stress and prevent burnout.

Establish Clear Goals and Expectations:

Clearly define roles, responsibilities, and expectations to prevent confusion and ensure that everyone is aligned with the organization's goals and objectives.

Enhance Conflict Resolution Mechanisms:

Develop robust mechanisms for addressing workplace conflicts promptly and fairly. Ensure that all employees feel heard and respected when issues arise.

Implement Fair Compensation:

Regularly review and adjust compensation packages to ensure they are competitive and fair based on industry standards, employee performance, and cost of living adjustments.

Strengthen HR Practices:

Reinforce human resources practices to ensure they are transparent and effective in dealing with employee complaints and grievances. This includes training HR personnel in best practices and legal requirements.

Encourage Team Collaboration:

Promote an environment that values teamwork and collaboration. Implement team-building activities that foster trust and camaraderie among employees.

Lead by Example:

Leaders should model the behavior they expect from their employees. By demonstrating integrity, respect, and dedication, leaders can inspire their teams to follow suit.
reviews.cons:
Organization and Leadership:
The role exists within a framework where organizational structure often appears undefined and may present challenges in streamlining processes and decision-making. Leadership support is limited, which may impact employee engagement and satisfaction.

Work Environment:
The working environment is frequently described as intense, with instances of hostility that are not adequately addressed, creating a challenging atmosphere for teamwork and collaboration.

Human Resources and Complaints Management:
There is a noticeable gap in how human resources and senior leadership manage and respond to employee grievances. Issues are often not addressed transparently or effectively, which can affect morale and trust within the organization.

Compensation:
The compensation for this position is below industry standards, which may not correspond with the demands and expectations placed on the role.

Work-Life Balance:
This position currently offers limited flexibility, demanding significant time commitment that extends beyond typical business hours, which can impact personal time and overall work-life balance.

There is a fair amount of chaos in IT leadership. We've had senior leadership recruited and quit in the same calendar year. They do deep layoffs in their IT tower every few years. These are mandated from on high and IT leadership doesn't have much say in these which leads to some interesting problems. A few years back they laid off every single project manager along with everyone who had admin rights on the ticketing system. In the latest round, they laid off several dozen employees from IT and hired back at least a few as contractor at 60%(approx) of their salary. That can be galling from a company who makes a big deal about how we're all "a village". As you'd imagine, morale among the survivors isn't great and gets worse with every new round.

A toxic QA manager alienates team members. We no longer feel like a cohesive unit working toward a common goal. The sense of belonging that fuels motivation and creativity dissipates under their leadership.

Autonomy is essential for job satisfaction. Unfortunately, the QA manager micromanages every aspect of our work. We’re treated like cogs in a machine, devoid of the freedom to make decisions or contribute meaningfully.

5.	Purpose Eroded:
A sense of purpose drives us to excel. However, our QA manager’s toxic behavior chips away at that purpose. We’re left wondering why we bother when our efforts fall on deaf ears.

We’re left questioning our sanity after each meeting, wondering if we’re the problem.

reviews.cons:
The lack of training that you will experience at this company is laughable. In my experience there was NO formal job training before you were handed claims you had no idea how to handle. Once you stumble and crash your way through enough, you will develop your own way of handling them. Formal systems or standards for claim handling….non existent, you will have better luck reading a subreddit for claims adjuster's. It is a common occurrence in this position to realize “oh I was doing this wrong” through word of mouth from a coworker after you have been doing it the wrong way for MONTHS. 
NOTHING is a priority to management until it becomes an issue and then it’s an all hands on deck emergency that has to be resolved immediately. 
This leads me to my next point, workload. The workload is absolutely disgusting. You will be handed a never ending number of claims and exposures of increasing difficulty regardless of how inundated you are. The onslaught never slows down and the claim train has no brakes. Imagine putting your mouth around a fire hydrant and having somebody knock the top off. That is the best way to describe the workload you will experience. By my estimation you are assigned roughly 8.5-9 hours of work on a normal day with 7.5 paid hours to do it. On a busy day which is at least once or twice a week you receive around 10 hours of work. It is common and expected for adjusters to work 1-2 hours every night after hours to include time on the weekends and taking additional vacation days just to CATCH UP on work. The company psyop of convincing adjusters to think they should be working more than their paid hours while not receiving compensation for it is quite successful.
No posted maximum amount of work you can be assigned and if you ask management will shy away from the question. Seriously if you heed no other warning about this place BEWARE the workload…
Insert your quarterly arbitrary meeting from corporate about how you are spending too much money and need to improve your claim management while you just spend every day trying survive and avoid getting screamed at. Add it all together and buddy you have a two star job on a good day.

reviews.advice:
Start offering job appropriate training course to excel workers skills or offer to pay for outside job appropriate training. 
Put in place process and procedures that are consistent and clear. There are allot of duties that should be clear across the board but they are not, therefore, everyone is doing it differently and it creates a mess. 
Pay attention to the workload level that is being plead on your employees and ensure that they are being properly compensated for the level of work they are performing.
Start performing reviews so employees can work toward goals and see opportunities ahead.
reviews.cons:
Not much room for growth in the KC office, which is the headquarters. Most people have been there for YEARS and don't plan to go anywhere anytime soon (thats saying allot right there). There are overseas positions and positions with some of the subsidiaries like Butterball, Seaboard Marine, Seaboard Foods, and PS, International. 
Although its nice to not have anyone over your shoulder all the time, it is also nice to get feedback and reviews but unless you are high-level executive you don't receive reviews and you don't get feedback unless you ask for it. You have to branch out to expand your job or no-one seems to know what you really do. 
Allot of the employees workout which you think would be good BUT then you find that if you don't workout, you don't belong. There are actually cliques for those that workout, those that smoke, and the younger crowd that forgets to get fully clothed before going to work. If you don't workout over lunch with the majority of the building you can feel really looney because they will outcast you quickly. 
Senior-level management is often heard joking about other employees, their personal lives, and how provocative they dress, etc. The majority of Senior execs are men and the HR department is all women and one man. The man will always share your personal business, nothing confidential is actually confidential.
reviews.pros:
Benefits are not the greatest but they are okay. Work loads always seem to expand, however, compensation makes up for it; your job expands then your pay does as well. The assistant positions are for the higher executives only and the pay is above average for executive administrative positions in the Johnson County area. 
When I worked there, what I loved most was that you have a guideline to your job description but they let you make the work your own and no-one was standing over your shoulder. 
The executives are down to earth and you would have no clue you were standing next to billionaires. They are absolutely wonderful. 
Lots of activities, team happy hours, Royals games, sponsored runs, habitat for humanity, etc. There is a gym in the building and you also get a discounted rate at a nearby gym.

I don't even know that I have advice for the new person in charge, because he doesn't appear to be someone who will listen. People are numbers to him.  The two people in charge of our office, meaning the new  C-Suite local leader and the C-Suite person who hired him and who he reports to are both equally as disconnected from the needs of their employees and what is sad is, I don't think that they care. The one who hired him, who visits the office periodically, can't even be bothered to speak with employees when he comes in. He only speaks to those with a title. You could literally be walking in the same hallway as him and he doesn't engage with you. How do companies put leadership in place that don't even know how to speak to people and how to make them feel valued? He comes across as very much "I am up here and you are down there," mentality. There are a couple of leaders at our office that really care and have a good balance and we know who those people are and we appreciate them.  The two leaders in charge of our office (the one local person who is the new leader and the one who visits/hired him) could learn from those leaders in the office that I mentioned that are the only a couple of leaders that really get it  (one male and one female).But, I feel like those people two good leaders who care will move on because while they smile, you can see the strain on their faces and tell they wish they could do more, but they can't. 
1. Listen to your employees 2. Listen to your employees 3. Listen to your employees 4. Pay better 5. Offer yearly bonuses to all employees. 6. Go back to putting WFH back in the hands of your local department leaders  or at the very least, keep the 3/2  WFH schedule rather than the change you indicated you are making (reducing the days). 7. Offer an anonymous box where employees can bring their concerns. 8. Understand that how employers treat employees is news that travels fast and it can be the make or break of an organization because the employees you really want, will not be interested in a company where they don't feel valued at. 9. Treat employees as thought they are a vital piece of your organization and that means treating them as if them having balance in their lives matter. 10. There are employees who literally work 12 hour days, work on weekends and have done this for years, it is not too much to ask to give us back some of the time we have given the company. This company is owned by a family and yes, they can certainly do what they want, and have every right, to do that, but in this time that we are in with so much happening in the world, you would expect some understanding of the importance of balance. I applaud those companies that are on the forefront of showing their employees they are valued. Companies that don't get that will at some point ultimately be left behind. The poor ratings is based on the new leader and the person who hired him, they are both C-Suite executives. I realized over the last few weeks, that we are just workers to them, we are no longer considered valued employees. This is why diversity at the top, diversity at the local level and diversity of thought matters. Even economic diversity matters, because when you have leaders in these roles who are so far removed from employees who are doing the job, they don't understand the every day challenges of people who don't make what they make. Where there is diversity, there is understanding and where there is understanding, there is more human kindness. Saying you care about employees and doing it are two different things. When you are a leader who is continuing to shout from the rooftop that other companies are bringing people back to the office and not want to hear why WFH and balance is important, than you have already shown who you are. Disconnected.
reviews.cons: I have worked at this company for several years and this is not easy for me. I have always tried to find the positive in everything and have always been a team player, but there comes a time when you have to be honest. This company has transitioned to a new leader as of April 2023 and it doesn't appear that he cares about the employees and the sole focus is on business. While we all certainly understand we are in the business of making money, that doesn't or shouldn't come at the cost of the mental health of your employees. We went from having a much more flexible WFH policy to one that was less flexible after COVID and now, as of a recent announcement a couple of weeks ago, we are going to a much more rigid policy, which essentially offers only one day. To add insult to injury, as we voiced our concerns about the policy what we got back is "We want people that want to be here." What kind of leader who understand the value and importance of people says that? Another ill conceived remark was , and I am paraphrasing but this is pretty accurate, "I am not giving people a Mon or Fri WFH day, because I don't believe employees should have a long weekend." Who says that? Someone who is disconnected from their employees. Comments like these, even if you think it, have no place being said and certainly should not be in the workplace. We just lived through a time where people lost their lives to a pandemic and there is a premium placed on quality of life, yet some employers don't get it. Sure, they will walk around and smile at you and authorize a FUN event every now and again, but that is it. When it comes to understanding the needs of the staff, there is no understanding. WFH helps parents, caregivers, students and even employees who may be battling a health issue and while we understand we have jobs to do, that should not mean that our lives don't have value. It should not mean that we are only numbers. Most of these decisions are made by older males, of a certain group who can't fathom that life doesn't revolve around a job. We are supposed to work to live, not live to work. What's worse, is that somehow when we ask to be treated with some basic understanding of the quality of our lives and how balance is important and can help, we are made to feel like we are ungrateful, unprofessional and that we are complainers. There is no value for the lives of the employees anymore here. When you bring up WFH, you are labeled as not being a team player, or told "We want people that want to be here." As if just asking for some balance means that we don't want to be here. This is the difference between new school leadership and old school thinking and many of those leaders that think like this, are so disconnected from employees many level under them nor do they understand the importance of those employees. Many of those leaders have no understanding of what true leadership is. This company has gone downhill since a very kind man who was the often called the "conscious" of our previous leader, left for another opportunity. He was a good man who left about two years ago.  We have a new company leader of this office and while you always want to give people a chance, you can already see three months in, that how employees feel is at the bottom of the list. People are literally coming in now and smiling and acting like things are fine and quietly looking for jobs. We have already lost some employees and I am certain we will lose many others.

reviews.advice:
Poor leadership can have detrimental effects on both individuals and organizations.  

here are some pieces of advice to help you become a better leader:

Self-awareness: Take time to reflect on your strengths and weaknesses as a leader. Acknowledge areas where you may be falling short and be open to feedback from others.

Communication: Improve your communication skills, both in terms of clarity and empathy. Ensure that your team understands expectations, goals, and feedback. Listen actively to their concerns and ideas.

Empowerment: Trust your team members and empower them to take ownership of their work. Delegate tasks appropriately and provide the necessary support and resources for them to succeed.

Lead by example: Set a positive example for your team by demonstrating integrity, accountability, and professionalism. Show that you are willing to roll up your sleeves and work alongside them when needed.

Recognition and appreciation: Recognize and appreciate the contributions of your team members regularly. Celebrate their successes and milestones, and provide constructive feedback when necessary.

Continuous learning: Commit to continuous learning and professional development. Stay informed about best practices in leadership and management and be willing to adapt and evolve as needed.

Empathy: Show empathy and compassion towards your team members. Understand their perspectives and individual needs, and be supportive during challenging times.

Conflict resolution: Develop skills in conflict resolution and mediation. Address conflicts and disagreements promptly and fairly, and work towards finding mutually beneficial solutions.

Vision and direction: Clearly articulate a vision and direction for the team or organization. Help your team members understand how their work contributes to the larger goals and objectives.

Seek feedback: Regularly solicit feedback from your team members and other stakeholders. Use this feedback to identify areas for improvement and make necessary adjustments to your leadership style.

Remember that becoming an effective leader is a journey, and it requires ongoing effort and commitment. By prioritizing self-awareness, communication, empowerment, and empathy, you can work towards becoming a better leader and positively impact those you lead.
reviews.cons:
My experience with NVR has been nothing short of disappointing and disheartening. If you're hoping for fair compensation that reflects your dedication and hard work, you'll be sorely let down.

Despite promises of merit-based raises and opportunities for advancement, the reality falls far short of expectations. Raises are not only infrequent but also miserly, failing to keep pace with inflation, let alone adequately rewarding employees for their contributions.

The company's approach to compensation seems not only outdated but also insulting. Employees are undervalued and underappreciated, with raises often amounting to mere pennies, if anything at all. This paltry increase in pay fails to acknowledge the rising cost of living or the increased responsibilities shouldered by employees over time.

Moreover, the lack of transparency surrounding the criteria for raises fosters a sense of frustration and disillusionment among staff. Without clear guidelines or feedback, employees are left in the dark about what they need to do to earn a meaningful increase in compensation, leading to a sense of stagnation and resentment.

It's evident that NVR prioritizes cost-cutting over employee satisfaction and retention. By neglecting to offer competitive raises, they risk losing talented individuals who seek fair compensation for their efforts.

In conclusion, if you're seeking a company that values and rewards your hard work with fair and meaningful raises, I would recommend looking elsewhere. NVR falls short in this regard, and employees deserve better treatment and recognition for their contributions.
