reviews.cons: I worked on one of NVR's regional marketing teams, and while the experience had positive moments and I met some good people in my time there, I could not and would not recommend it to any marketing professional looking to grow in their career. NVR, across all levels all the way up to executive leadership, has fostered a culture of bullying. Fear tactics are used to improve performance, there is constant gossiping and rumor spreading, demotions happen routinely whenever leadership is unhappy with the sales numbers -- all in all, it will feel a lot like a high school cafeteria. I was in attendance at numerous meetings where individuals were targeted, berated and dog-piled on by leadership in front of many colleagues. As a marketing professional, your performance will be based on sales numbers exclusively, which means if the market is experiencing a downturn, you will be given a negative performance review even if your work that year was above average. The individuals who thrive at this company are those who have no problem stepping on others to boost themselves up the ladder, and it shows. HR is basically non-existent -- when I resigned from my position, the HR rep asked to have a exit interview where I could explain why I was leaving and then never followed up to actually schedule it when I agreed. There is zero flexibility, and they take pride in harmful mantras like "It takes what it takes," and "NVR isn't for everyone," (why be proud of a lack of inclusivity?!). This company is a classic example of the "rise and grind" culture that is finally dying out, thanks to an evolving corporate landscape where the employee holds more of the power. You have the power to choose a company that views you as a human instead of a number on a spreadsheet, cares about your mental health and overall well-being, and will value the skills that you bring to the table. NVR is not that place.

In addition to the heightened sense of accountability, we are given more and more directives, goals, and tasks, however the support staff, funding and resources are not provided in order to either keep the people safe nor achieve the goals we have set. Eastman has a lot of great 'ideals' and 'acheivements' they share with the world, but within the gates we are all burdened with more work than we can handle, are asked to raise the concerns which we do, and then are told to work 'more efficiently.' At some point if this company is serious about keeping people safe and acheiving world class chemical company goals around safety, reliability, asset integrity etc, it will need to provide the staff, capital funding, and knowledge rentetion to enable their people to do this. It a great place to be surrounded by wonderful people while you burn yourself out trying to meet unachievable goals and expectations.
reviews.pros: The people at Eastman are some of the nicest, hardest working people I've ever had the opportunity to work with.

reviews.advice: Open the books to employees on their own salaries. Don't brain drain the company by under-compensating world class experts (and those aspiring to become ones). These are smart people, and they can see a bad deal a mile away (also they listen to shareholder calls, so don't outright lie to them).
reviews.cons: Corporate is constantly chipping away at financial incentives to work here in a technical role. Benefits aren't great value (health insurance is among the worst in the industry), advancement opportunities are very limited for individual contributors, and there's no transparency about how your compensation is determined each year.
reviews.pros: The people who work in engineering are top tier: in their integrity, in their knowledge, and in their genuine friendship. Couldn't ask for better coworkers. Also, plenty of challenging and interesting projects with a good balance of employees vs management determining what they work on.
reviews.summary: Excellent people in engineering, corporate limits their growth

reviews.advice: I would encourage management to be careful about groupthink.
reviews.cons: The most unfortunate thing about Eastman is that it seems stockholders are all that matters. At the corporate level, you live and die by the stock price. If it doesn’t look like they’ll be able to meet what was told to investors in Q1, you can guarantee there will be headcount reductions in Q4. Eastman has been a pillar of the local community for over 100 years. At times I think they have lost sight of that. There were headcount reductions 4 out of the 5 years I was there.
reviews.pros: Overall it’s a great place to work. Always something new to learn. The company does a lot of really cool things as well - new technologies, new products. Benefits are good as well.

reviews.advice: Stop rewarding the leadership team so richly for less than mediocre performance.
reviews.cons: Rudderless people in charge (would be an insult to call them leaders). Hang around long enough, and eventually you will be laid off. Circular economy has consumed all resources and bled all available capital. Plant reliability on everything else will suffer.
reviews.pros: Few and far between….it is a paycheck
reviews.summary: Get Out While You Still Can…

reviews.advice: You're serving two entities. The board ultimately owns us, but the employees keep us running. The board wants to milk cash from us short term, the employees and community we live in depend on Eastman being healthy and profitable for years to come. Please please please prioritize tomorrow, even if it makes the shareholders unhappy for a few quarters. We HAVE to keep this plant running. Take care of maintenance, address REAL safety concerns. I'm talking fatigue and ANCIENT equipment, not "holding handrails." Reward your employees. Every layoff and denial of improvement projects to meet the bottom line is at the expense of our future.
reviews.cons:
Huge focus on quarterly financial results has led to large cost cuts and layoffs that are bad for moral and may eventually cause the plant to shut down due to ignored upkeep. Eastman's biggest asset are its people, and the layoffs and poor raises and bonuses have made them feel underappreciated. HUGE effort and personal sacrifices were made by a significant % of employees to being the new recycling plant over the finish line, and the majority of them were not recognized in any genuine way. Retention is poor and we are losing valuable employees. Finally, town halls and management announcements do not focus on positives, they always open up with excuses for why results aren't better, just filled with pessimism and the same mantra of "poor demand... de-inventorying... challenging economy.... yada yada yada."

Let's just focus on making sound decisions for the future health and function of the plant, and reward our talent. Financial results will follow.

If you are uninterested in working around a salesy-salon atmosphere you won't get anywhere with this company. 

The operational side of the business isn’t even included in the "trifecta" (aka the new business moto). In contrast, operations demand the most amount of physical labor and general workload, intellect when it comes to software/process systems, overtime, accountability, etc. The job never stops. The merchandising manager position has also taken a backward step and now the company has redefined the role as a "lead tasking" associate. As the least paid manager in the store, Merchandising Managers are essentially operation managers who are relied upon to finish endless job expectations on one hand and to be a sales manager in the other. The task associates get paid less than the beauty advisors. Simply said, they do more work and need more common sense.

reviews.cons:
Working in this job has been a mixed experience due to the management style of the District Manager (DM). On one hand, the DM expects employees to be well-versed in every aspect of the job and holds them accountable for what they don’t know, yet claims it’s not a learning position. This creates a confusing and frustrating dynamic for employees.

The DM’s approach is inconsistent, as she is very hands-off and lazy in some aspects, only superficially checking in with some stores while meticulously scrutinizing others. This lack of consistency undermines morale and creates a sense of unfairness among employees.

reviews.advice: Our success for so long has been our ability to move ideas into actions quickly, and we should never lose that!
reviews.cons: 1. (For some) You will have to work. At some companies with 20k+ employees, you can sort of skirt by doing the bare minimum and your lack of effort can hide amongst the volume. At Chewy, you'll get sniffed out pretty quickly. As kind as everyone is, we are also goal-oriented and you can't sit idle here - we move too fast, This is a con for "big company people" who want to rest for 10 years before retiring. If you're motivated and focused, you'll love it. If you're not, this will be a major con for you. 2. (For some) There are a lot (and growing) of inspection mechanisms. And while they may add value and be important for scale, document writing is the way decisions are made at Chewy, and it's a big upfront level of effort to present or support an idea. If you enjoy very high autonomy, the ability to move super fast and only 'check in with a PPT slide or two" at the end of a quarter with a couple fancy graphics that distract from results, Chewy may not be the place for you. In current state, data-driven, crisp, long-format document writing is more than a task, it's HOW we work. For someone who is great at 'doing' but weak at explaining their ideas, and the how/why in written format, or someone who doesn't like to be questioned and inspected continually, it may be stressful. Great place for those who like strong upfront alignment, clear decision-making thought process and ongoing discussions about our effectiveness, but would not recommend for the 'casual, let me do my thing and don't inspect me' type of person.
reviews.pros: 1. Everyone actually cares about the customer experience - and not just product teams shipping customer-facing gizmos...on-site facilities teams care about welcome experience for guests, IT cares about the experience of employees submitting request, etc. It's an extremely customer centric organization and it's thoroughly engrained at all levels. 2. Everyone wants to help. Sure, there are busy times when there are bandwidth issues like anywhere else and you might feel like you don't have enough resources, but by intention, everyone is in everyone's corner. This isn't a cutthroat place where your success has to mean someone else's failure - everyone can succeed. 3. People are nice. Crazy thought, right? People are SO nice. Like, everyone. Run into someone in a break room? Friendliest conversation ever. On a call with a C Suite leader, you walk away thinking "WOW, I wouldn't have assumed they'd be so nice". It's just a company of really kind people who actually care how you're doing when they ask. 4. You get the OPPORTUNITY to have shifting priorities. Sometimes people complain "We keep changing priorities." To which I say, "So? Would you rather work for a company that can't switch priorities and instead goes out of business because you didn't adapt to new information and customer demands?" Your paycheck stays the same if your priority shifts. It's ok. You will have the opportunity to work on many different projects, and while it sometimes seems tiring, it's pretty cool to look back after a year and say "I got to work on 15 different impactful things " Chewy has a high "I get to do a lot" quotient. 5. Everyone gets a say. This isn't a "VP+ gets a voice and we all march" sort of place. Every team member at any level has the opportunity to voice their POV and share an idea, and the great ideas are used. They are involved in bringing it to life, in building on the idea, and even presenting it. I've seen many leaders at Chewy start in entry level positions and soar to senior leader roles in a matter of a few years by having well founded ideas and seeing them through.

reviews.advice:
Improving as a manager at Chewy involves a combination of skills, mindset, and understanding the company’s culture. Here are some actionable steps:

Embrace Chewy’s Operating Principles:
Chewy operates in accelerated “Chewy Time,” where they achieve more than others think is possible. Clear scope and objectives enable fast decision-making and action. Be comfortable with failure, learn, and iterate swiftly1.
Tip: Align your management approach with these principles to drive results.
Listen to Your Team:
Regularly engage with your team members. Understand their challenges, ideas, and feedback.
Tip: Create an open communication channel where employees feel heard and valued.
Invest in Training and Development:
Continuously improve your skills. Attend workshops, read management books, and seek mentorship.
Tip: Encourage your team to participate in training programs as well.
Lead by Example:
Demonstrate the behavior you expect from your team. Be punctual, respectful, and committed.
Tip: Set the tone for professionalism and work ethic.
Empower Your Team:
Delegate tasks and responsibilities. Trust your team members to make decisions.
Tip: Encourage autonomy and foster a sense of ownership.
Prioritize Employee Well-Being:
Understand work-life balance. Support your team during challenging times.
Tip: Show empathy and flexibility when needed.
Stay Updated on Industry Trends:
Keep abreast of e-commerce, pet industry, and management trends.
Tip: Attend conferences, read industry publications, and network with peers.
Address Challenges Proactively:
Identify bottlenecks, inefficiencies, and areas for improvement. Collaborate with cross-functional teams.
Tip: Be solution-oriented and drive positive change.
Learn from Feedback and Mistakes:
Accept constructive criticism gracefully. Use it to enhance your leadership skills.
Tip: Regularly seek feedback from your team and superiors.
Promote a Positive Work Environment:
Foster camaraderie, celebrate achievements, and address conflicts promptly.
Tip: Create a supportive atmosphere where everyone feels motivated.
Remember, being a great manager is an ongoing journey. Adapt, learn, and grow to create a positive impact at Chewy!

reviews.advice: Dear CEO, BOD, and Senior Executives I wanted to take a moment to address an important aspect that often goes unnoticed within organizations - the impact of management on the overall culture of a facility. It is crucial for us, as leaders, to recognize that our actions and decisions directly shape the environment in which our employees work and thrive. Mismanagement can inadvertently foster a negative culture where employees may feel demotivated or undervalued. Therefore, it is essential to take responsibility for the culture we create through effective management practices. By creating an inclusive, supportive, and positive work environment, we can empower our employees to reach their full potential, resulting in enhanced productivity and overall success for our organization. Sincerely, Burned Out
reviews.cons: Working for a company that fails to value employees' time and gaslights them can have significant negative effects on both personal and professional aspects. Firstly, it creates a sense of frustration and demotivation among employees. When their time is not respected, it can lead to increased stress levels and a lack of work-life balance, ultimately affecting their overall well-being. Moreover, gaslighting employees undermines their confidence and self-esteem, making it difficult for them to voice their opinions or concerns. This toxic environment hampers creativity, innovation, and collaboration, as employees may hesitate to share their ideas or take risks. Ultimately, it erodes trust and loyalty within the organization, leading to high turnover rates and difficulty in attracting and retaining top talent. A company that disregards the value of its employees' time and gaslights them risks not only damaging their reputation but also hindering their growth and success in the long run.

reviews.advice: You are happy to throw out ideas: "we need to do this", "this needs to change", "we need to implement x, y z". How about you pull yourself away from your PowerBI module, get a project management certification, and actually implement some initiatives rather than just pressuring undertrained supervisors who are just clinging on for dear life into doing everything for you?
reviews.cons:
- Not given any tools to succeed: know-nothing warehouse manager pressuring me to increase order picking performance by 1.5-2x when we lack the resources to train new associates, lack sufficient picking equipment, and experience constant shortages of the tote boxes that we pick into. Meanwhile I'm being barraged with emails from leadership working remotely "wHy aRe tHeY PicKiNg sO SlOwlY??", when I bring up the obstacles I am swatted down and told they are just excuses.

- I received zero on-the-job training: I was continuously told by the manager that he had developed some kind of training matrix blah blah blah that he would roll out this Friday blah blah blah fast forward two months later no training. Was told in my first week that I would be sent to cross-train in December but that never happened either.

- 12-14 hour days are the norm here: The logistics leadership at this company has ZERO voice and gets bent over constantly. They will agree to fulfill any and all orders, even if they are not achievable because they are lacking the necessary analytical and negotiation skills opting rather for a "put our heads down and get it done" approach. This results in 55-60 hr/wk as a norm with little hope for change. Things brings me into my next point.

- Ineffective leadership: The operations management that I have dealt with in my short time have been laughably bad. The warehouse manager has a theoretical understanding of how things should work, but he constantly neglects working on big-picture, value-add topics in favor into jumping into manual functions like wrapping and stacking pallets when things are tough (which is every day). He is also cold and fatiguing to interact with, he never lets up talking about the job for even two seconds and every conversation is a one-sided, unfocused monologue regarding how things were in his previous facility in Florida. The director of operations has not been present in our facility since October, preferring to oversee things from Florida, despite the fact that our building is the lowest-performing nationally. It is humorous when he chimes in virtually in meetings nitpicking small oversights, not realizing that myself and the team have worked 13 hrs/day for months. The fill-in director who covers from time to time IS HORRIBLE, he tucks away with a laptop under his conveyor belt and slams us with emails in broken English demanding that we push the associates to pick faster and does nothing more than that. Having worked at several distribution centers and interacted with many directors, I was stunned when I observed this guy and realized that he has zero skills outside of just refreshing a production dashboard in PowerBI.

- VICIOUS CYCLE: Associates get hired on, do not have any sense of attachment to the role due to lack of training and terrible compensation despite being surrounded by numerous competing warehouses that are always hiring. Associates begin to burn out with the hours and then start calling out. The brilliant manager's only solutions are to A. terminate the burnt-out team members for attendance B. write up the burnt-out for performance which leaves the site consistently understaffed, underperforming, with low morale.

reviews.cons:
To put it bluntly, DO NOT work for this company. I started here in July 2015 at 19 years old and was fired 3 days before Christmas 2023 due to my FIRST company vehicle accident, which had occurred 10 days prior. **To those who read this, please do not discount me as a disgruntled (ex)employee. Me getting fired just fast tracked my resignation** 

With that being said, they’re just another company to add to the list of ruthless corporations who would have your position filled before your funeral. When I first started here, it was an entirely different company than when I was fired. There was leadership, structure, accountability, and decent opportunity to make a livable wage. I can only speak up to the end of 2023, but that is no longer the case. Mastec has little to no opportunity for advancement, as over the past 4 years they’ve done nothing but eliminate managerial positions. With streaming becoming more relevant every day, DirecTV has become less and less relevant annually, and Mastec leaves little to no solutions for its employees to compensate the lost wages. The solutions they do provide such as taking on contracts for other business lines (I.e smartaira, ADT, AAS) pay LESS than the dwindling DirecTV work that it would be replacing on any particular day. They will send you hours away from your home multiple times a week, and expect that time to be free. They force you to clock a lunch break on any day you work more than 5 hours whether or not you have the time to actually take a break. There’s absolutely no structure within the management. My manager worked remotely from 6 hours away; The supervisor doesn’t really care about anything, and nobody takes him seriously when he does try to correct an issue (and when that happens he just gives up and doesn’t follow through). You get shorted on equipment every pick up day, not at fault of the warehouse manager but instead the technology they use to determine how much equipment we’re installing in between pick ups. When you live 1.5 hours away from the warehouse, that becomes more than a minor inconvenience. They make it extremely hard to have a work/life balance, as every day is different. You could be done at 3:00 pm 25 minutes from home, or 7:00 pm 2.5 hours away from home; and you never know until you wake up and see your route in the morning. The turnover rate is absolutely ridiculous, and nowadays techs stay for 90 days @ $20/hour to collect their $1000 bonus, and then they quit. Meanwhile, the guys who do stay around get paid piece rate and could work an 8 hour day to go home with $30. With that being said, there’s TONS more minor inconveniences that I could complain about but I think the point has been made. 8.5 years of sacrificing a ridiculous amount of my youth for a company whose HR rep said “it is what it is” on the PHONE CALL telling me I was fired just confirmed everything I had learned about Mastec in that time. I knew how badly I was being treated at Mastec, but I stuck around to maintain a schedule with my child and because I was scared of change. I now work for a small, family run business and my eyes have been opened to just how badly I was treated. So again, DO NOT put yourself in that vicious cycle with this company, THEY DO NOT CARE ABOUT YOU.

This company is going through financial problems. The ELT (Executive leadership Team) over paid for the Dupont Materials & Mobility acquisition last year $11 billon. None of the ELT members that signed off on this deal are loosing their jobs. 

The Dupont business unit they bought uses Nylon and Nylon prices have fallen in the marketplace. The deal was signed with Dupont thinking that Nylon prices would remain at FY2021 levels. In FY2022 Nylon prices started to come down and the prices have not recovered. 

In response to demand problems and Nylon prices, the ELT is laying off allot of really good people all over the company. They are more worried about their million dollar bonuses and hitting Wall Street's EPS and Revenue targets than they are about their employees. 

Sr. Management has cut all discretionary spending (fruits, coca cola and bottled water in breakrooms). They have also cut all corporate travel.

reviews.advice:
Advice for management - return to your roots, actually care about your critical workers.

Stop paying lip service to your field employees. Actions speak louder than words. Everyone understands that most field oil and gas workers are employed as contractors because the riskiest jobs are heavily outsourced. But actual Diamondback field employees should not be an afterthought. 

Recent example, the 2021 Midland Christmas Party for the corporate workers. The people focused big bosses purposely scheduled the party on a thursday so anyone wanting to attend would need to use PTO for the friday the day after. Anticipating us field workers not showing up, they got the small convention center, got limited food, and even though everyine knows many of us coming from the delaware basin or surrounding towns near Midland get hotel rooms to attend the party, the big bosses purposely ignored this.

As the company has grown, the big bosses have stopped coming out to field, so much so that it's a surprise if they even know anyones name anymore. Unfortunately, the culture has come undone (everything that made Diamondback a great company) as the VPs kick back and count their money and ridiculous number of shares they award themselves at the tall city twin towers.

Compensation - talk about it with your friends, you'll be surprised how wildly your pay varies. It's eye opening how much people are valued, or undervalued by supervisors. 
Bonuses (Cash/Stock) - big bosses will tell you they're transparent, but they're not. How is your bonus calculated? God only knows. (If it seems like a BS game, it's because it is. Trust your instincts!)

Career Opportunities - not so good if you're hispanic, black, or asian.

reviews.cons:
There are a lot. For one, the accounting team isn't actually in the beautiful main building in Atlanta. Of course they don't tell any of the new employees this, but you only find out on the very first day when you show up to work. Instead, you are in a old concrete building off to the side of the main building with rows of cubicles and little to no natural sunlight (extremely damaging to mental health). To compensate they offer "free breakfast and lunch" which is just delivered cold food from the main building cafeteria. 

Management provides little to no training. All of the training for my tasks was given by the other accountants. While these accountants are extremely nice people, it is not their job to be good teachers or trainers. Some of them were extremely bad at explaining their tasks, especially the ins and outs. 

Managers provide zero effort to provide more assistance to employees struggling early on in their position. They would rather fire you than take any extra time to work with you on ways to improve, regardless of how eager you are to learn, grow, and succeed. You are expendable and can be let go at any time if your work is not up to par with their standards. 

I was fired after only 4 months, randomly out of nowhere, without given any chance to improve and grow and develop as a young professional. I was fired over zoom, and both HR as well as my manager kept their cameras off the entire time. I work with you every day for almost 5 months and you don't have the human decency to look at me while you are firing me? I think that says enough about management.

Don't expect any sort of formal training or guidance. You are mostly on your own, and asking coworkers for help is frowned upon by management.

I worked there for six years, I absolutely loved the company, but as they got more and more successful over the years, management got a bit full of themselves.  Only seem to care about the bottom line anymore even though they tout themselves as being all about their employees.  While that used to be true, it has become a pretty selective thing now.  After working for six years with the same company, having success in a few different roles, my controller left the company, they dumped all of his work on me and laid me off shortly after.  It ended up being a blessing as I was promoted via another company and am now able to actually work and spend time with my young family every evening.  Pay is okay, but they are pretty stingy when giving out raises to people already in the company.  Unless you get a big promotion of course.  I was stuck on the same salary for about 4 years.  And as the national average grew, my salary stayed the same.
reviews.cons: Poor Work/life balance; inconsistent direction from leadership; Disregard of employee loyalty

reviews.advice: As an international company, your documentation suffers from grammatical and voice issues on a consistent basis. Going forward, you have the opportunity to improve this by leveraging AI. The future of documentation isn't a document, it's a set of algorithms that code for conceptual data that can be added to an AI as downloadable modules that can be included with products. Writers won't write the documentation; they'll train the AI by correcting it and fixing the verbiage. That 'training' is then compiled into the module. Other companies are already moving in this direction, but it is bleeding edge at this time. Will MSI jump onboard?

reviews.pros:
This is my first Glassdoor review ever and I am VERY honored to illustrate it with all viewers. Everyone at Motorola Solutions is genuinely passionate about what we do here. We each play an integral part in the organization and move to the same beat. I've worked with upper and middle management including peers on the ground floor and everyone here at MSI has been very helpful and welcoming. No one has shown an ounce of rank/title/superiority over another and have treated everyone with the utmost respect and inclusivity. Work is not trivial and is taxing to an extent but in a feasible manner. Work/Life balance is on point. Management sends weekly surveys to check the pulse of its employee's satisfaction (this is genius as it prevents cancer from growing). Company promotes 10% days for you to continuously learn and evolve your craft in your work life. This is a simple notion but very effective. Management continuously encourages troops to take as much time off as they can as long as it's appropriate to do so. They have inhouse mentorship programs which I've been fortunate to take part in. Good to have comradity with other individuals that have veteran experience and have been through the ups/downs of an organization. They don't guide your path but show you the forks in the road so you can avoid them. All of these company attributes just portray to employees that management truly cares about your evolution in career, knowledge and physical well being.

The CEO, Greg Brown is one of the most compassionate, empathetic and "good hearted" leaders that I've ever had the privilege to listen to. His All Hands and Town Hall meetings are very informative, unscripted, raw/unfiltered which is truly a breath of fresh air. The Senior Management Team's transparency is very open which is unheard of in the tech corporate world. There is a reason why the Senior Leadership Team is not constantly churning like other organizations that I've lived through. They are all cut from the same cloth which is powerful to witness.

Finally the products/solutions... This ALONE gets me excited to wake up in the morning. We are using technology to save lives and "solve for safer." This is a powerful mission and brings meaning to an employee. The engineering, support, marketing, ops and sales teams are all a bonus on top. I haven't seen any rivalries or animosity towards any departments. This is again, unheard of. We champion one another and advocate for greatness. There is no competition that I've witnessed among peers. It's clear from our CSAT and NPS scores that we provide white glove treatment to every customer that comes under our umbrella. Our brand name is evident and I see this company sticking around forever. Again, I don't see this as a "job" and on the flipside nor do I see this as a "family" (hate when organizations say that) but I will say it comes as close as ever to one... GO MSI!!!

reviews.advice: This would be advice for corporate in Minnesota: it is past due to clean management house. Start at the plant manager and hr manager. The culture of Huntsville Polaris is toxic, and it starts at the top. But if corporate truly cared, they would have already closed down this plant. Unfortunately, the all-mighty dollar is winning the moral dilemma.
reviews.cons:
The cons are overwhelming at this location:
-Quality. If you are familiar with Six Sigma, you will have a stroke here. Process and part variation is rampant. Most units don't roll off the line complete, and are reworked out of process at an off site warehouse. The term "Lean" is thrown around very loosely. 
-The production schedule. Some corporate person created the build targets for this facility. Because anyone who works in the facility, knows they are impossible to attain in an 8 hour shift. The entire supply chain design is flawed (programs, "processes", replenishment strategy, and the lousy excuse for a 3PL Universal).
-Safety. The "EHS" team is a joke. All actions are reactive, with zero proactivity to make the facility safer. When safety violations are brought to managements' attention, it will go months without being addressed, and then closed without resolution. 
-Toxic culture. There is complete lack of leadership in this facility. This has lead to an overwhelming toxic culture. Basic employee code of conduct is not enforced. This has lead to a culture rife with lies, deceit, and numerous inappropriate relationships that are "conveniently overlooked". 
-Turnover. In my professional career, I've never seen the employee turnover that HSV sees. Polaris has chewed through the entire area workforce already (hence why they have weekly job fairs). 
-HR. HR is the snake of management. Two faced, liars, that do not care about employee well being and just protecting the company. You've been warned. 
-Management. Management is a rag-tag group of leftover hacks. Anyone with experience and education has come and gone. This has left those without any other options as the managers (they've outlasted everyone else, not that they are qualified or an expert in that position).
reviews.pros:
-There aren't any pro's. If you are experienced and have an education, you will be rode hard into the ground. Your hours will be stretched with weekends and holidays becoming mandatory. This will make the compensation package not make financial sense. 
-Also, be wary of the "perks". These can be relinquished on a moments notice by HR, without compensation reimbursement.

reviews.advice: Management isn't genuinely interested in your advice - they will convince you that they want it during the interview process, but from day one you'll be expected to assimilate into "the Vertex way" and "our special culture". With over half of the company now being new, external hires, I'm sure those employees will all enjoy being told to fall in line. Good luck with that.
reviews.cons:
The performance review cycle is an absolute joke. Stakeholder feedback is completely anonymous, which is fantastic for a company that operates on talking secrets about its employees behind their backs, and then lets them go for "underperforming" when there was never a word uttered to that employee nor an opportunity to improve ever truly given. 

Like that? You'll also love that in cases of a 'Building' rating, one where improvement is needed, you are also not guaranteed an actual written performance review that articulates the ways in which you didn't meet your primary work objectives. Even better when the company's own analytic tools provided demonstrate that you met and/or exceeded all but one. From what I have seen and experienced, HR can't even treat their own employees with respect or integrity through this process.
reviews.pros: The only thing Vertex has going for it is its science. The company is successful despite itself. Unfortunately the EC can't get out of its own way, nor can the countless senior leaders who all waste time, resources and employees' sanity pandering to them. Longstanding Vertexians, and those who do well managing up to longstanding Vertexians, will do well. It's hands down survival of the fakest.

reviews.advice: Stop promoting people who clearly have no interest in or aptitude for management into management because they’re stellar ICs; just make them fellows and cut them loose to do what they’re actually good at.
reviews.cons: Quite toxic management culture, especially around career development. There is a cohort of golden children being fast-tracked up the org at the expense of everyone else. Admittedly all very bright, but an outstanding IC does not necessarily make a good leader. If you have a PhD from a non-elite university, or outside one of a few narrow fields, you will have a hard time being taken seriously at the start; if you have a lowly MS, people will look at you in astonishment and ask whose badge you stole to get in the building. Lots of empty talk about DEI while only considering candidates from the top R1 programs. Lots of silos. Lots of orgs who absolutely need to be talking to each other, who are instead talking past each other, if they’re even talking. Lots of institutional inertia and resistance to change. Management is very clear that compensation is at or below that of their peers, and use “great benefits” as justification.

reviews.advice:
Empower lower level employees to make decisions.  It takes so long to get some decisions made and the organization could be so much more nimble and efficient if every decision didn’t have to go to vp level. 
Please rethink the 3 day mandatory on site.  Most people will not complain about 2 days mandatory on site.  Technology is so advanced to enable F2F interactions even if not co-located.
reviews.cons:
-Leadership is bureaucratic- decision making is not done at the appropriate level. Everything needs to run up the flagpole to VP+ level for decisions that lower level employees should be able to make. No empowerment. 
-Hybrid employees are mandated to be on site 3 days per week. Not usually an issue but this means the hybrid employees are not really trusted to do their jobs. Example: 1. if you have no meetings and could focus and work with no distractions on projects at home, you still must commute in to sit at your desk to meet the 3 day requirement. 
2. If you aren’t feeling well enough to go into the office but ok to work at home, you will have to use sick time rather than work from home and be productive otherwise you risk losing your job for not meeting the 3 day requirement.
3. Commuting into work is more than the 2 hours average round trip- it’s organizing your family and getting yourself presentable for the office which eats into time that could be spent working. What could be a 10 hour workday at home becomes 8 hour workday when onsite coupled with the stress to get your family where they need to be and get yourself to work.
- Vertex is an environment that is probably better suited to people who don’t have children or any other commitments or interests outside of work. Work-life balance is a big challenge.

Williams Sonoma is a company of entitled people who provide iems of questionable quality to entitled people. They pay less than average wages to employees and expect the employees to be the professional punching bags for them. They make it clear that customer service can be mistreated, besmirched, lied to and cussed at as long as the customer never reaches a supervisor. If the customer does hang on long enough to get to a supervisor, the supervisor will then give the customer whetever they want, break policies, send gift cards, whatever as long as the customers are happy. The fact that the customers then give low ratings to "teach the reps a lesson", knowing that it could harmfully impact the representatives employment is amazing. The customers want free items, and as much money back from the expensive items as they can. This demographic is well coached on getting their way. I have never worked for a company that believes its ok for a diamond status customer to talk down on employees based on the sound of their voice. 

If you have children, elderly parents, or have anyone to take care of, please do not work here. The work life balance is based on the customer's need for free shipping. As long as people are calling about free shippoing, nothing that is going on in your life matters. There are blackout dates that you cannoot take off, and yopu also cannot take off any other days. Any days off outside of your schedule can lead to termination. They give you a fake bank of hours to take, but will never let you take the days off that you need to live your real life and use them. No matter why you need a day off, they charge you a point. People miss court dates, weddings, funerals, birth of their kids, etc because of business needs. Why is there no one available to answer calls if Chris wants to witness his first son being born? Why does Jemma have a failure to appear because she couldn't go to a court date Because Kelli needs vendor information that we cannot legally give or because Sonya needs an Easter basket liner. Kids sick at school? let CPS take them because business needs will have you unemployed, and you won't have any recourse. 
Immediated supervisors look out for themselves. All they care about is your daily rating. I have a special needs child. My supervisor told me to look for the company policy on ADA. Thepolicy says that only the employee is considered. Not a disabled family member that you care for. So Dr Appointments, meetings, etc are not supportive of business needs, and therefor the company will not support you. Factually, they only openly support LBGT issues. They say that they support other groups, but not families, not children, not single parents, not disabled. They may contribute to causes to show social accountability, but on the inside the employees with children or specail circumstances are not even given options for scheduling that would help them out in their actual non WSI lives. The 40% discount is a joke because if you are not in SR management, you cannot afford to purchase the items, even with the discount. 

If you need extra seasonal money, go for it, If your life is not the standard, cut and dry, suburban American, two earner household, living will be beyond difficult with this company.

They need to vendor out and find another CMS that is better streamlined so it doesn't take minutes to do one task or having to jump into 2-3 different systems to do one task. Again inefficient. And stop expecting your tomorrow to work 10-15+ hour days and weekends to get the job done on a constant basis. This is not a healthy work-life balance as this gives you employees less time to decompress and enjoy their families. Also, if this is what is expected from your employees, then GB needs to pay more. Your HR department is not helpful as far as needing to speak with a live person about their benefits and other company policies. This corporation is too big to be running very mediocre at best.
reviews.cons:
This is the most disorganized, chaotic complex institution I ever worked for. They have very high turnover, which doesn't help with the claims that need to be handled. They allow their workloads to pile up and when they hire new employees, they expect them to come in and play clean up. They have cases where the previous adjusters have done lackluster investigations, excepted compensability on files that clearly should have been denied and they're paying/wasting thousands of dollars on claim files on employees that are milking the system that should have been shut down. Their CMS is complicated and for what reason, the new employees can't figure out but those who have shockingly remained with the company more than a year just go along with it. The training is minimal at best and instead of giving you new claims to start in to get familiar with their systems and procedures, they throw everything at you and expect you to fix it and get them caught up on their behind work. And this is work that is behind like 4-5 months. It is unrealistic and they seem to can't comprehend why they cannot keep valuable employees. 

The benefits are okay. I haven't had the chance to use any of them. I think the pay needs to be more if they want new people to come in and fix their mess. The organizational breakdown of GB and the other carriers they work with is complex, to many hands and opinions in the files. Adjusters feel like they can't do just that, adjust. They also want you to have work meetings about your claim scores on each file and enjoyed why people can't keep up with the work. The constant file reviews for so many companies is ridiculous and again, takes time away for doing the actual work. I can understand the frustrations of past adjusters that have left. They expect you to write up all of these reports for these clients and carriers, which leaves very little time to do the work. Adjusters just want to do that adjust claims, get these injured workers help with treatment and back to work.

This better way was to bring online managers who didn't understand the business or the products and believed forcing people into multi-hour meetings was the secret to getting results. reviews.advice: Slow down. Invest in data foundation so you can actually validate what the priorities of work should be. The CEO should be listening to his people - the people he hired to do a job - rather than making top down decisions arbitrarily based on his 'gut'. This isn't a design firm, it's an ecommerce business. Allow for upward feedback on leadership and actually take it seriously. Create an environment where people feel like they can speak up and they won't risk retaliation. Be open to diversity of thought and ideas.
reviews.cons:
Culture Culture Culture

They take themselves way too seriously and there is no margin for error. The environment is toxic, oftentimes speaking to people in disrespectful and rude tones. I was literally screamed at and spoken down to as if I was nothing. 

It's very much decision by committee, but the most popular person - not the best idea - wins. I cannot tell you how many times I would advocate for something, have my idea turned down only for leaders to present it as their own idea just a few months later. 

Work/Life balance doesn't exist. Because everyone is remote, they expect you to be available at any and all hours. My boss literally emailed me on Christmas and New Years Eve. It.Never.Stopped. And they would share a firehose of documentation, rarely with context, and by the time you had a chance to review any of it they would have already moved onto the next thing with a whole new set of disorganized documentation - then in the same breath talk about needing to streamline all the documentation. It was like a fire drill orchestrated by an executive with ADHD every single day. Truly maddening. 

They work incredibly fast paced - which can be a great thing - except they don't ever have moments of thoughtful reflection and/or planning to ensure that the work they're so diligently focused on getting out the door is 1) done well or 2) the right thing to be spending resources on in the first place. They pivot so often, you spend most of your time planning, no time deploying, only to have the plans thrown out. 

For being a digitally native company, it's really sad how little they actually understand about digital best practices and getting data on anything is like pulling teeth.

reviews.advice: My advice to Management is to listen to your drivers when they bring up issues that are legitimate safety concerns, and make changes accordingly. Don't ignore them, or make excuses. It was very disappointing and frankly embarrassing to be a part of this company that I used to think so highly of. After months of dealing with these loads and the pallets and the risk to my license, my career, I had enough and decided this wasn't where I wanted to invest years of service.
reviews.cons: 1: The loads: I understand in this industry, there's a lot of varying materials of different shapes, sizes, etc... so it can be a challenge to load the trailers. It's understandable to have some funky loads sometimes. But you shouldn't be dealing with these issues on a regular basis: -Units that aren't flush, but just thrown on there sloppily; stickers left on top the the load or in places you couldn't see from the ground; items on top of the load that needed to be shifted or rearranged so they could be properly strapped (I was regularly climbing on the load to rearrange or move something because it would've been dangerous to ignore or strap it like it was). -Having material scattered throughout the load so the receiver you're delivering to has to move a bunch of stuff to get to theirs. Sometimes this can't be helped due to size and weight of material, but there were many many times that it just wasn't necessary. It's as though some of the loaders use their paperwork to gather all the delivery items and then they ignore the paperwork delivery order and just throw everything on the trailer to get it done, rather than taking the time to try to keep items in a certain order. -Pallets falling apart because they weren't properly and securely wrapped, so they'd end up falling apart while driving down the road, leaving loose boxes and hardware on the trailer. 2: Management: They pretend to care about your input but then ignore or downplay what you have to say. They listened to my concerns and those brought up by other drivers, but they didn't make any improvements or changes. I tried to brainstorm with them how the pallets could better be wrapped - nothing changed. They kept wrapping the same way. For all their preaching about "safety", you would think they'd take these issues seriously, when there's a huge potential for hardware or boxes to fall off the truck into traffic. 3: The trucks: They have all automatic T880's with terrible Paccar motors - constant check engine lights, break downs, wear and tear. I think they are moving in the right direction because their newest truck has a Cummins so hopefully they keep ordering those. When I received the truck I was taking over, it was disgusting - FILTHY from the previous driver. It needed a deep clean which the company should've taken care of - a new driver shouldn't be the one scrubbing and cleaning and fixing things to make it presentable. The windshield was cracked along the entire length and wouldn't have passed inspection. The insurance and registration paperwork was disorganized and missing the registration papers for half the trailers, one of the internal cab lights was dangling from the ceiling, the driver's seat was broken, etc. I spent several hours cleaning it, fixed what I could and to their credit, the Boise mechanic ordered and installed a new seat... But I mean, COME ON PEOPLE. Very unprofessional.
reviews.pros: They have adequate pay, good benefits and amazing pto (4 weeks per year to start). Some other pros are they have auto chains (with manual chains as a backup), a mechanic on-site, and no driver-facing cameras (they have the outward facing dash cam and one rear facing camera on each door, which I was totally fine with. It's the driver facing camera I don't agree with so I really appreciated their decision in this area). Another pro for me is I was regularly getting about 8-10 hours of overtime per week. So, there are definitely some good things about working for Boise.
reviews.summary: Ok pay, good benefits, great pto, but terrible loads, unreliable trucks

reviews.cons:
Upper management disconnected from day to day of in store employees, show bias in offering opportunities and promotions to preferred "inner circle", not equitable. Unrealistic sales goals impeded bonus (necessary to achieve livable wage). Poor business decisions on corporate-level affecting profitability of stores leading to smaller bonus earning. 
Yearly raises supposedly based on "merit", i.e. employee performance, but in reality the highest rank (4 out of 4 stars) is never granted and bonuses are capped for each location--so if every employee at location deserves the max 4% raise (well below inflation %) the store cannot grant them this which results in a lower % raise, no matter the employee's work. Effectively, staff makes less year over year as a result. 
Rigid availability requirements harmful to work/life balance (Floor Leaders must be available to work EVERY Saturday/Sunday, Inventory leaders must be available to work EVERY week night Monday through Friday AND a weekend day.)

There should be a minimum number of hours guaranteed for all employees each week or pay period, and more consistency in the schedule. This is a good way to avoid frequent call-outs because then we wouldn't have to work 2nd or 3rd jobs. 
Give part-time employees real health insurance!
Maybe standardize the training process and make sure everyone is on the same page with SOPs
reviews.cons:
Hours are inconsistent. Scheduling beyond a month is impossible. Sometimes this makes it feel more like a casual gig than a real part-time job. 
Pay is not enough for the amount of work we are expected to do. In general, we are understaffed. The company is obviously trying to cut costs by reducing employee compensation/availability, meanwhile, we are trained to accommodate the customer's every need--even if that means eating costs. I believe it comes out of our paychecks.
We have to confront harassment/frequent robberies/organized retail crime daily Customers will be wonderful or condescending/rude, and anything in between.
Also, there is so much waste! plastic plastic plastic 
But maybe this is true for any retail operation...
reviews.pros:
Great coworkers. Nice store environment. Decently organized with standard operating procedures across multiple locations. Very flexible schedule/easy to pick up shifts... really depends on management--each store is different. 
Employee benefits include a monthly stipend for athletic pursuits, 401k + employer matching, and store discount.

Most of the people were wonderful to work with but there were some difficult co-workers and supervisors who created a very toxic work environment.  Gossip, back stabbing, lies and passive aggressive behavior to just name a few issues.  Some of this behavior came from the supervisors too.  Some of the Mid-level Managers tried to address these issues but the offenders often complained to HR when they were confronted for their behavior.  HR tended to side with the aggressors.  

Work load was not evenly or fairly distributed.  Many of the more competent employees were stuck with the burden of doing much of their co-workers work, causing a lot of stress and burn out.  When supervisors received complaints about workload, they usually disregarded or ignored it until the person had a full meltdown or simply left.  

AP was also treated as an inferior dept within the company.  For example, the budget for team & morale building events were severely reduced to the point that the Managers had to fund some events using their own money.  Budgets for other depts did not seem to be effected.  Hard not to feel disgruntle when other depts are going out to expensive dinners and golfing while AP is gets a potluck that they paid for out of their own pocket.  Also, most of the other depts were allowed to wear casual dress, including jeans, while AP had to dress business style.  I believe this has since changed, but it still caused a very low morale when it was happening.

reviews.advice: I shared my thoughts during my exit interview. Transparency is needed for how the training process occurs in the beginning. It will save a lot of time for all parties.
reviews.cons:
The interview and onboarding process was slow and time-consuming. The first interview was over 2 hours. Waited over a week for the next interview, again almost two hours, and was not informed it would include two separate processes. The third interview was scheduled via Zoom at the office. There also is a fourth interview, but that portion was waved. From my last interview to my first day was almost a month. I was told it was a formality and they just needed to prepare. They also stressed I would probably want additional time off as a "break". I was currently unemployed at the time so I did not need a break. My start date continued to be pushed back with the reason of my background check had not cleared yet. However, with the background check you can follow the progress so I could see that it had cleared. 
Finally, I started and after asking repeatedly what the training schedule would be like, I was provided the information. 12 weeks of training, with 4 weeks performing ridealongs 3x a week. It was not what I had been hired to do. I can see both sides of this as it is important to gain a full understanding of the company and how it works, however, I was not applying to perform manual labor and physically could not make it through the training requirements. I also got the impression through my first week of training that schedules were not consistent. People were working very long hours to try and catch up on the workload. I just felt overall the information provided during the interview process and onboarding did not match up with what was actually occurring once hired.
reviews.pros: Employees and staff were all very welcoming. Safety culture is 100% across the board. Many long-term employees are dedicated to their jobs. Company is showing amazing growth.
reviews.summary: Lengthy interview process and training requirements

reviews.advice: De-emphasize sales. Instead emphasize building working solutions and actually listen to customer’s complaints to fix existing issues instead of trying to cram more product down their throats, and don’t throw your account teams and support groups under the bus to clean up problems that you actively encourage your sales org to create chasing what you perceive as easy money.
reviews.cons:
This company is run by people who are career salesmen. And sales is all that they care about. This is reflected in almost all levels of the culture. Sales teams are often (and exclusively even) given the best perks and benefits, and are almost always the only ones being recognized by executive leadership on the all-hands calls. 

Meanwhile NCR invests laughably little (about 3%) into innovating the vast array of legacy products it constantly misrepresents as being cutting edge, and the actual newer products are also often years ahead of being working and viable solutions, but are sold anyways.

Execution and delivering on promises to customers is a distant second priority. That is until this rush to the sale’s finish line mantra complicates another sales opportunity, and leadership will then throw all hands on deck to (temporarily) fix said problem to keep the customer on the sales hook.

You will constantly hear executive leadership saying “the customers are first”. It’s all nonsense. What they really mean is “the sales pipeline is first”. And these aren’t just my words, at least three high level customer contacts (c-suite and director) have told me this same thing over the years.

reviews.advice:
1. Make quoting easier so sales reps can give pricing on the spot.

2. Improve training and management of overseas teams so billing / support work is not dependent on sales reps moving mountains.

3. Invest heavily in R&D to improve older legacy solutions rather than yearly re-orgs
reviews.cons:
The biggest challenge for the NCR SMB Hospitality is aging technology. NCR Aloha was the clear market leader a decade ago but the resources were not invested to keep it current. This is resulting in much of the SMB market going to Toast.

Also, the support and billing were moved overseas. These people are nice but often aren't properly trained. This leads to very angry customers over long support holds and duplicate billing. They are trying to make NCR Silver (Aloha Cloud) the future but it needs much more investment to catch up with competitors (like Toast & Square).

All that being said, I enjoyed my time at NCR because of the people. There is still a place for NCR in larger chains. If you only have restaurant experience and want to get a corporate business job, this is a great place to start.

For those fresh out of college, NT isn’t a bad launching pad for your career, offering a decent work-life balance with reasonable hours. However, don’t expect the traditional grind of a banking institution—NT leans more towards the culture of a tech company, favoring personal charisma over proven expertise in its hiring practices. If you’re young and have the right look, you’re more likely to be in favor. 

Tenure at NT is commonplace, and while this implies a level of job security, it also points to a stagnation of industry-relevant knowledge and talent. These long-term employees maintain their positions not through current expertise but through the inertia of NT’s workplace culture, which seems resistant to turnover. They're unable to find work elsewhere. 

The hiring process at NT explicitly aims for diversity, with sex and race being decisive factors, often to the detriment of Caucasian candidates. This isn’t speculation; it’s a fact I’ve verified through conversations with those who still work there. This policy, while common knowledge internally( among managers only) is delicate and potentially contentious if discussed beyond the company’s walls.

reviews.advice: Ameren used to be a destination employer. People would start and end their entire careers there. That's no longer the case. years and years of slashing pay and benefits and staff, now the rest of the pack has caught up to them. but long-timers and leadership hasn't realized this yet. To them, Ameren is still the old Ameren.. For a young/mid career engineer, it's a decent place if you like stability (utilities are notoriously stable in times of economic strife). But it's not what it once was, and gets worse every year. Still a pretty decent place though. But if you're ambitious, there are other opportunities out there. It's a good company overall. reviews.cons:
The company leaves some of its departments understaffed, resulting in more work to be done than can possibly be handled and sets performance expectations at unreasonable levels. For example, a team might have a task that can sometimes be completed in 5 minutes, but other times might require 20 to finish, but team members will be expected to meet a quota as if the task only takes 7 minutes to complete on average, which is only possible to achieve when the vast majority of the tasks that come in are of the 5 minute variety, but that is rarely the case.

These practices lead to sloppy work, and some employees spend more time finding ways to exploit the system to make their numbers look good without actually doing any of the work.

Couple that with the annual layoffs that often see the best employees being shown the door while the worst are kept on because their numbers look good, and the perennial bouts of corporate restructuring that eliminate jobs and drop the workloads of those positions onto others, and you are left with a high-stress job and no sense of security.

Work-Life Balance: The biggest challenge I faced was maintaining a healthy work-life balance. Due to the nature of the industry and project deadlines, long hours and weekend work were common, which can be draining over time.

Corporate Culture Issues: While the company is making efforts to address these, during my tenure, there were moments where the corporate culture did not align with modern workplace expectations. Issues around diversity, inclusion, and workplace behavior were areas needing significant improvement.

Communication Barriers: Despite being in a communications role, there were occasional barriers in internal communications. Hierarchical structures sometimes slowed down decision-making processes and hindered effective cross-departmental collaboration.

reviews.pros: At many very large companies it can be hard to pinpoint one's impact, but at Activision Blizzard we have the chance to see many direct and tangible impacts on products that reach a tremendous amount of people on a global scale. This company leans on its extensive resources to provide some very strong combinations of benefits and compensation - while perhaps not exceeding that of the start-up or mature tech industry, benefits + compensation are compelling for the games industry. Many folks have positive outlooks and want the best for each other, our players, and the company. It feels both meaningful and challenging to focus on talent acquisition for video games that are millions of people's favorites and to work with folks at some of the highest standards in the industry. I get to work with brilliant people from a wide variety of different backgrounds and lives. These different backgrounds are appreciated and sought after for perspective and advancement of our studios. I have regularly seen folks being valued for their abilities and achievements - many of which have resulted in promotions.

reviews.advice: Walk the halls, physically or virtually, instead of exclusively communicating through large forums. Be wary of making too many tactical requests that erode teams' decision-making abilities in pursuit of a strategic goal. And do everything you can to eliminate the "us vs. them" dynamic that the matrixed org chart seems to encourage.
reviews.cons: The decentralized structure of the company fosters power struggles, crossed incentives, and conflicting efforts to pursue common goals. Work flexibility is entirely dependent on your specific team. The pathways to resources, technical or otherwise, are overly complex and difficult to learn for new employees. The negative moments in the company's recent history seem to weigh on everything and everyone, creating a tremendously risk-averse environment that prioritizes perceived liability over customer satisfaction. And the pending merger with Microsoft has encouraged short-term tactics at the risk of confident, long-term strategy.
reviews.pros: Everyone I work with, directly and indirectly, has proven to be friendly, talented, and wonderfully experienced at what they do. The company is great at providing technical resources to support work—laptops, phones, software, etc—and it never feels like reasonable asks are rejected. Compensation and benefits are strong. Conduct expectations are high. Strategic goals are clear. And whether they're gamers or not, everyone is excited about the work they do and who they're doing it for—you simply can't replicate that.

For upper corporate management: a biorepository is a service.

Businesses that provide services rely on the abilities and knowledge of those who perform the labor of the service and greatly benefit from happy, well-trained, and experienced workers who see a future at the company they work at. When you employ the "churn and burn" retail model that relies on a constant cycle of new hires, you burn out the people who are constantly training new people who quit a few months later. reviews.advice: Turn to your employees and acknowledge their hard work. Many of them are prioritizing their work over their family, which shouldn't be the case. Offering praise for a job well done or engaging in casual, personal conversations about their loved ones can make a significant impact. Demonstrate the same level of care for your employees as you do for your role in the company. Being personal and emotionally involved are distinct, so focus on genuine care without letting emotions cloud your judgment. Foster trust with your team by genuinely caring for them, without crossing the line into excessive emotional involvement. Set realistic expectations and establish goals that prioritize family. Advocate for your employees by pushing back against unrealistic expectations from higher-ups. Avoid using intimidation as a primary management style. Recognize the dedication of excellent employees who are willing to invest time and effort and ensure that their contributions are valued.

reviews.advice:
Please adopt more developer friendly practices and rely less on low-code platforms.

When you hire someone to solve a problem, and they offer you a solution with lower cost and better performance, instead of outright turning it down, consider enabling them to at least build a quick Proof of Concept.

I was told repeatedly that we can't do any custom dev work because then someone has to maintain it, and "what will we do if you decide to leave?"....  but the same applies to low-code tools.  Even worse yet, the entirety of SAP development work is "maintained" by offshore Deloitte contractors.  Almost none of their work is documented and nobody in house reviews or knows how to use their low-code platform.   How is 100 lines of Python code considered a bigger risk than this?
reviews.cons:
- Expect for most dev roles that your skills will deteriorate. If you don't skill build on your own, you'll struggle finding your next job.
- There is a strong fear of in-house development. If you ever encounter a scenario that has business value and would let you use your skillset, expect them to prefer outsourcing to a vendor (not even the best vendor), to a contractor, or for them to just change their mind and decide it isn't actually valuable.
- There are little to no developers at the company. Don't let the 9000 employee count fool you, you're pretty much on your own.
- The development practices are very immature and bureaucratic. Programmers don't get access to local admin for downloading libraries. It's a huge hassle to develop any Proof of Concepts. The company expects thorough approval before taking any productive action.
- Managers are not very technical or proactive, expect to find yourself being your own manager, finding your own use cases, setting up meetings with stakeholders, tracking down emails, playing secretary for menial tasks, etc. And on top of that, you'll need to work on explaining what you're working on to your manager and hope that they listened.
- No meaningful chances for mentorship, again you're on your own as a dev.
reviews.pros:
- You won't be forced to churn out code constantly/stay late
- The pay is okay
- Most people are fairly nice
- There have pension and really good 401k matching

reviews.advice: Get back to how Equinix was running in 2015 to 2020 when it actually seem to really care about their employees. It seems everything is now just a number and how they can please the street. Focusing on DEI and how much one volunteers does nothing for our stock price and revenue for the company and stop following all the other big tech companies with this (it's not working out like they hope)
reviews.cons: Cons are- low compensation and based salary compared to most other similar roles at other big tech companies. Always changing the comp plan for the worst. Every year the comp plan is cut down and try to make it as complicated as possible. You will work harder and bring in more revenue but get paid less every year. There's a lot of guessing into how you will be paid and half the time the comps aren't paid correctly or have to wait months. Equinix in the last 2 years has really focus on commission pay outs and making sure they can claw back as much as possible. As a global company they have made cross selling with other regions difficult so they do not have to pay full comp if their are multiply reps involved which in a lot times multiply reps are needed! Also, for the last 2 years, Equinix seems to have really focus this effort and money on DEI. I am all for diversity but it's a point where it's in your face 24/7 now. Volunteering is being pushed harder every Q as it seems now it is more mandatory within the company. If you are comfortable in your AE position it looks down upon as you should aspire to be a manager or director one day. There a lot of great team managers and there are few who should not be managing a team. Equinix is huge on promoting within which is a huge pro but a lot times they will promote AE's to management level with no experience or training and seems to be based on how much they like you and not so much your performance. My former manager constantly canceled calls, was late and half the time was somewhere else (why her team was the worst performing). Equinix does not care about loyalty at all! No severance package for tenure reps that have been with Equinix for many years. It's a shame as Equinix was once a great place to work but the Cons now outweigh the Pros and they are chasing away great people. Just another corporate America company where you are just a number, nothing less, nothing more.
reviews.pros: Pro's are Paid time off and roles over each year with a max of 250 hours. Equinix offers ESPP and RSU's are typical. All the sales reps I have came in contact are great. Equinix does a great job at hiring the best sales people. In almost 9 years I never had one issue with any other coworker and quite a few have become lifetime long friends. Yearly sales kick off to Vegas is an awesome experience that Equinix puts in a lot of effort and money into. P-Club is also another amazing experience that Equinix puts a lot of thought an money into. Equinix is the best of the best when it comes to anything Data Center related and that why they can demand such premiums. Decent offices.

Salary in my opinion is pretty decent and maybe even a little above average.
